News.title: Nurse who stabbed her 8-year-old disabled daughter 96 times ‘out of desperation’ after receiving school report is jailed
News.content:
KILLER MUM Nurse who stabbed her 8-year-old disabled daughter 96 times ‘out of desperation’ after receiving school report is jailed

A NURSE has been jailed after stabbing her disabled daughter 96 times in a horrifying attempted murder-suicide, cops say.

Mum Sarka P was driven to kill her eight-year-old out of “desperation” over her care, the Prague High Court heard.

During the trial, the nurse chillingly confessed that she could only remember the first four wounds of her stabbing frenzy.



But prosecutors say the girl was knifed 96 times with a 20cm long kitchen knife while she tried to fight back – reportedly attempting to snatch the knife from her mother.



Police raced to the family apartment in October last year – and found the child dead and the mother unconscious and “seriously injured” according to emergency service spokeswoman Monika Nováková.

Sarka P had already swallowed pills in an attempted suicide – before reportedly deciding to end her daughter’s life alongside her own, the court heard.

Harrowing testimony from the mum recalls the final terrifying moments of her daughter’s life.



“She looked at me and noticed that I was holding a knife in my hand”, Sarka P told the court.

“She started to stand up and stretched out her arms towards me. She wanted to hug me. So I hugged her.

“I said that we would leave together, that I would not leave her here to her fate. With her gestures, she indicated to me that she wanted to take the stuffed animals with her, with tears in her eyes I told her yes.”

The horror unfolded after Sarka P found out that her daughter was struggling in school, would need more care and would also be moved to a class for children with learning disabilities.



The revelation reportedly tipped her over the edge as she told the court that she lived alone without the help of the girl’s father.

She told the court: “I stopped going to social events to take care of her.”

Her lawyers argued that she was exhausted and desperate – and that the notice from the school was the final trigger.

The mum says she cannot believe she attacked her daughter so many times – and does not remember the brutal murder.

But prosecutor Zagarová slammed the nurse, saying: “She was angry that she had extra work to do.”



Zagarová also doubted the alleged memory loss – claiming it was a tactic to get a lighter sentence.

Experts in court stated the nurse did not have a mental disorder – but that she was “emotionally unstable”, reported to Czech paper Denik.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The motive was a combination of frustration and helplessness,” said the expert, who was not named in the report.

The mum pleaded guilty in court – and was handed an 18 year prison sentence.

News.title: US blasts Iranian tankers in response to Tehran’s attack on Navy ships after ‘evacuate immediately’ threat
News.content:
US forces have struck Iranian oil tankers after Tehran threatened to target ships in Kuwait and Bahrain.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard ordered tanker crews to flee “immediately” as the explosive stand-off over the Gulf escalated.



The warning came after Iran launched ballistic missiles at US warships on Saturday, according to Washington.

American forces struck three Iranian oil tankers in retaliation.



The latest strikes targeted multiple tankers linked to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard around Kharg Island and near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz.

A US official told Al-Monitor: “American forces have struck multiple Iranian tankers tied to the IRGC in response to more attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship.”



Iranian media reported a small tanker was hit off Kharg Island, with its crew evacuated and no casualties reported.

A second tanker was also hit near Jask, with its crew said to have escaped safely.

The IRGC then issued a chilling warning to crews in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports.

“All oil tankers in Kuwait and Bahraini waters must be evacuated immediately,” it said.



It warned the vessels would be targeted whether they were “at anchor or at the docks”.

Iran has also boasted of a new Qassem Basir ballistic missile, claiming it has been “tested” against a US warship.

The missile is said to have greater range and accuracy and carries a half-tonne warhead.



Meanwhile, the White House has rejected Iran’s proposed “exclusion zone” around the Strait of Hormuz.

Washington says the crucial waterway remains open and under US control.

The US military also says it has cleared mines from the strait, while 94 commercial vessels have been redirected and three disabled.

The tit-for-tat attacks come as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues, piling pressure on Tehran’s oil exports.

The new barrage follows US forces blasting three Iranian oil tankers last week after missiles were reportedly launched towards navy warships.



US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it “permanently disabled” M/T Downy off the coast of Iran’s Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz.

American forces also “completely destroyed” the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman, CENTCOM said.

The statement, posted on X, said the tankers were part of a shadow network funding Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies.



Kharg Island has been repeatedly targeted during the war, including US strikes on military sites there in March.

The strikes came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm.

Trump has raised the prospect of a US strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site as the conflict with Tehran rumbles on.

The US president brushed off the widening war as “small potatoes for us”.

Iran’s nuclear programme was one of the key issues behind the conflict that erupted in February.



Diplomatic efforts to resolve the row collapsed shortly after Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tehran has since gained leverage through the Strait of Hormuz – a vital artery for oil and gas shipments.

US forces are now helping vessels navigate the waterway as the Iranian regime tightens its grip and continues targeting ships.

News.title: Blind man with no licence nabbed for drink driving on M6 after doing 150 miles in two hours
News.content:
DRINK RAP Blind man with no licence nabbed for drink driving on M6 after doing 150 miles in two hours

A BLIND man with no licence was nabbed for drink driving on the M6 after doing 150 miles in two hours, a court heard.

Anthony Hall, 50, told police he retains some “light perception” so he used other vehicles’ tail lights to guide him.



At one point, a service station attendant helped him refuel on June 29.

Officers stopped him as he weaved over the road in Cumbria on his way to Scotland after taking his partner’s Vauxhall Minerva without consent.



He told them he was registered blind and knew the risks but wanted to “get far away from his home life” due to rows.

Hall, of Huddersfield, gave a breath alcohol reading of 50mg in 100ml.



The limit is 35.

He admitted drink driving before Kirklees JPs and got 36 weeks’ jail, suspended for 18 months.

He was disqualified for 12 months.

Prosecutor Damian Walsh told Kirklees magistrates’ court that Hall had been driving for more than two hours when he was stopped.



He said: “The officer observed the vehicle weaving in lane one, drifting onto the hard shoulder and back and then drifting into lane two and back.

“The officer guided the defendant to the back of his patrol car. As the officer was speaking to the defendant, he could smell alcohol on his breath.

“Hall admitted he had drunk some wine.

“The officer then asked the defendant if he was blind and he said ‘yes’.

“He can see some light and he told officers that he had followed the red lights of a HGV.



“However, he overtook the HGV and was looking for another marker to assist him.

“He told officers he had driven from his home in Huddersfield to where he was now stopped. Officers checked that distance on Google maps and that came out to be 150 miles.”

News.title: Jeremy Corbyn and leftie pals BANNED from Israel as nation hits back at Labour’s sanctions
News.content:
A DOZEN left-wing political figures have been barred from Israel after the country imposed retaliatory sanctions on Britain.

It follows the UK’s ban of imports from illegal West Bank settlements and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s accusation that some settlers were guilty of “ethnic cleansing”.



Barred politicians include Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott, Zarah Sultana, John McDonnell as well as all five Green Party MPs.

The Greens claimed to be “proud” of their MPs for “standing up for Palestinian rights”.



Israel also said it will close the British consulate in Jerusalem and eject UK officials from a Gaza support centre.

Other moves include ending British training of Palestinian Authority forces and banning London-based, pro-Hamas law firm boss Fahad Ansari from Israel.



Labour MPs Richard Burgon and Naz Shah have also been banned from the country.

A US backlash was also feared after Foreign Secretary Mr Miliband called settlers “terrorists”.

His claims were branded as lies by furious Israeli leaders after Labour announced an import ban on goods from illegal West Bank settlements.

Writing in today’s Sun, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch says Labour has thrown British Jews “under the bus . . . to win back Islamist votes”.



She adds: “At a time when Britain faces a serious terrorist threat, deliberately damaging relations with a country whose intelligence helps saves lives here in Britain is madness.”

Mr Miliband told MPs yesterday: “The British Government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank — perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse — members have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians.”

Mr Miliband said he is a “proud Jew” and added Israel had every right to defend itself after the October 7 terror attacks that killed 1,200, but announced a “reset” of relations.

News.title: Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlers in West Bank plays into the hands of antisemitic pro-Hamas mob
News.content:
Grow up, Mili

ED Miliband’s sanctions are better suited to student politics than the grown-up business of international diplomacy.

His allegation that Israeli settlers in the West Bank are guilty of “ethnic cleansing” was designed to win the approval of the hard Left.



His wrong-headed decision to boycott goods from those settlements will only damage trade and could end up punishing ordinary Palestinians — as well as Brits reliant on Israeli-made medicines.

It has also upset our closest allies in Washington and Tel Aviv at a time of rising global tension, leading to the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem.



Why has Labour done this now — especially as Israel plays a key role in providing vital security intelligence and defence tech to help keep Britain safe?

It smacks of being a nakedly partisan stunt to win back Gaza-obsessed voters from the Greens ahead of Labour’s party conference, and next month’s by-election in Holborn and St Pancras.

By doing so, Miliband has played into the hands of the antisemitic pro-Hamas mob who have already brought enough division and hate to our streets.

Yesterday, the Chief Rabbi called it a dark day for British Jews, while the Jewish Leadership Council said the Government had made them an “increased target”.

All so Labour can win cheap points with pro-Palestine activists and Leftists.

Lock ’em up

WHEN even the notoriously soft UN thinks Britain is failing on illegal migration it’s time for a radical change of course.



From handing £1billion to France, to the shambolic one in, one out scheme, NONE of it has stopped the boats.

It’s clearer than ever that what an angry public wants is for all illegal migrants to be detained on arrival.

Putting them in camps would curb the migrant crimewave and make women feel safer.

Even the useless Home Office would know where every migrant was instead of losing track of the tens of thousands who disappear every year.

Crucially, if migrants knew they were going to be locked up — instead of enjoying free housing and healthcare — they wouldn’t come here in the first place.



Tech airheads

WHAT the hell is going on at our airports?

Thousands of passengers were left stranded yesterday by a “technical fault” in the air traffic control system — the THIRD major incident in three years.

National Air Traffic Services boss Martin Rolfe, paid £1.3million a year, is facing calls from furious airlines to quit.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Rolfe claimed he was “persecuted” after the major outage in 2023.

Passengers might like him — and his creaking computer systems — to be a whole lot more resilient.

News.title: Family pay tribute to ‘inseparable’ couple found dead by their carer as cops question man over horror stabbing
News.content:
FATAL STABBING Family pay tribute to ‘inseparable’ couple found dead by their carer as cops question man over horror stabbing

A FAMILY have paid an emotional tribute to an “inseparable” couple who were found dead in a flat by their carer – as cops question a man in his 40s over the fatal stabbing.

Ismail Ahmed Leli, 80, and Fatima Leli, 78, were pronounced dead at the scene after cops arrived at the address in Blackburn at 8.22am on Monday.



Both of them had sustained devastating stab injuries, prompting cops to launch a murder investigation.

A man in his forties was arrested on the same day and remains in custody for questioning.



Heartbroken family members described the pair as an “inseparable couple” who were “devoted to one another”.

They said in a statement: “On behalf of our entire family, we are heartbroken to share that we have lost our parents, the oldest and most cherished members of our family.

“Married and inseparable for over sixty years, they were the very heart of who we are — devoted to one another and loved by everyone who knew them.

“Their loss has left a void that words cannot describe, and we are still coming to terms with what has happened.



“At this incredibly difficult time, we wish to express our deepest gratitude to the police for their diligence, professionalism and compassion.

“We are also grateful to our local councillors, to the wider community and St Luke’s and St Phillip’s Church, whose kindness and support have meant a great deal to us.

“In particular we thank Masjid-e-Quwwatul Islam, which has been a source of strength, comfort and practical support to our family throughout.

“We now ask, respectfully, that our family’s privacy be respected, so that we may grieve and mourn in accordance with our faith.

“We would be grateful for the space and understanding of the media and the public during this period.



“We thank everyone for their prayers and condolences.

“Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un — “To Allah we belong, and to Him we shall return.”

The street remains cordoned off as the investigation continues and a forensic tent is still outside the property.

Neighbours were shocked to wake up to a large police presence in the area, with officers carrying out door-to-door enquiries.

One resident described the couple as “very private” and said they were members of the local mosque.



A couple, who lived in the next block on the street, said: “When we got up, just after 8am, we looked outside and it was all there then.

“It was a bit of a shock”.

A Lancashire Constabulary spokesperson said at the time: “Our thoughts are with their loved ones at this distressing time.

“We have a dedicated team of officers assigned to this case, carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic enquires in the area.

“There is currently a scene at the property and will remain in place over the coming days.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“You will continue to see an increased police presence in the area, as we conduct enquiries and provide reassurance.

“If you have any information or concerns, please stop one of our officers for a chat.”

News.title: Inside village branded ‘ground zero’ of UK illegal immigration crisis where locals fear migrant camp DOUBLING in size
News.content:
A PRETTY village branded the “ground zero” of Britain’s illegal immigration crisis is demanding answers over fears a local migrant camp could ­DOUBLE in size.

Newly-seen documents suggest that 3,510 asylum seekers — up from the 1,256 specified in the official application — could be housed yards from tiny ­Piddington in Oxfordshire.



But the Home Office last night insisted that they were just early drafts, despite being dated 2026.

The fresh twist for the 350 villagers battling to halt the arrival of the migrant camp has poured new petrol on an already tense uprising in the most unlikely of places.



Images of men in black balaclavas shutting down the port of Dover for hours last weekend were rightly shocking.

As was footage of the ­hundreds of local residents spontaneously blocking new boat migrants leaving Portsmouth in the early hours of Monday morning.

Both scenes pointed to a government losing control over the growing backlash against Britain’s illegal immigration disaster, with ministers and cops braced for further unrest.

PM Andy Burnham insists that all parts of the country “must do their part” to handle the massive influx, despite not a single vote being cast in favour of his ideas.

Yet when people take to the streets, questions of what that means in practice are going to be far harder for the Labour Party to try to bat away with cries of racism.

In this quaint corner of England, the anger is boiling from the ground up and from the most unlikely of revolutionaries.



“We are definitely ground zero for this problem,” says Piddington parish council chairman Tim McNally.

Softly spoken in a check shirt and trainers, McNally says he used to spend his days “fixing benches, potholes and roads” in this beautiful thatched bend in the road in the rolling hills just north of Oxford.

Now, he references Spartacus and looks to US chief Donald Trump for inspiration.



McNally has spearheaded the ­campaign against the housing of male asylum seekers in an old Ministry of Defence base some 750 metres away from scores of family homes.

He has even sought to hold a ­referendum on leaving the UK in a desperate bid to show Westminster how seriously his village objects.

On July 4, America’s Independence Day, he got the nod from 175 locals to push for a full vote in the village, due to be held next week.

And he believes that, despite the ballot on ­September 15 having no legal bearing, it will help others fight the Government’s new policy of shifting asylum seekers from hotels directly into communities.

With support from around the world, including from Elon Musk, McNally’s campaign lit up the internet this summer, but so far it has fallen on deaf ears at No10.



And the council leader is still seething with anger over the day his life was turned “upside down”.

That day in July was when the Home Office gave notice that MoD Bicester, a stone’s throw from his house, would be a major test case for asylum accommodation policy.

“This notice says your life’s going to turn upside down, and it was that day I realised we’ve got to do something about this,” he told me just yards from the security fence of the site, which backs on to the local kids’ playground.



“I can’t just sit back and let it happen. We’ve got to find a way forward.

“The village was depressed — mentally, shocked. They felt trapped and they had no way out.”

On the road into the tiny hamlet, signs have gone up declaring this would-be republic a hotbed of ­resistance. “We talk about Spartacus, right?” says McNally.

“That is the fact that we’ve got others behind me wanting to ensure we’re delivering against this.

“We did this in solidarity for ­American Independence, respecting their situation 250 years ago.



“And for us, we’re now being shut down in our democracy, and I think it’s a message back to the world.”

Appealing directly for Donald Trump to take up their case, McNally says: “He’s a leader in terms of ­shoring up and controlling borders, and every man and woman should be able to do the same. We should be in a controlled and safe situation.

“He’s making that his primary statement. We should be doing the same.”



And McNally warns this revolutionary spirit will spread across the country unless the Government urgently rethinks its proposals.

He adds: “This is giving people the confidence to actually say, ‘I’m going to speak out. We don’t like this’.

“And we have a blueprint on the website which helps other ­parishes do exactly the same.”

Home Office proposals for the Bicester site are deeply redacted and offer little real insight into who is coming and what safety measures will be put in place for the villagers.

McNally says the 1,256 arrivals face “challenges in their home territory, and I feel actually we have a ­problem in our home territory because we don’t have any right to examine all of the content that we should be entitled to examine. All avenues for us to review are hidden, and that puts us in a really difficult situation.



“How can a government do this to us? Our children — our children’s lives — are the ones that are being undermined.”

A fresh row has broken out this week after published documents showed the Government had scoped out using the site for 3,510 migrants — more than ten times the ­population of the village.

The Home Office insists that the number was a preliminary draft published in error, but for the ­villagers it is yet another chilling element to this dangerous farce.

Joe Marshall, a local resident and planning expert, warns the infrastructure is completely unsuitable and the Home Office is hiding the true costs and potential impact.



Millions will have to be spent installing power, beds and internet at the camp for the new arrivals.

Oil-fuelled generators, temporary sewage treatment plants and streams of buses risk turning Piddington’s single lanes into a noisy, polluted and dangerous spot.

“We’re expecting there to be some promises,” Joe says, “some risk assessments, some things saying we’ve looked at this and it’s safe.

“And actually, the application is full of inconsistencies. There’s typos.



“And there’s some really crucial ­documents missing.”

But it goes back to safety, with the young dad warning: “We’re not scared of the high number; what we’re scared about is the low number that may have ill intentions.

“And obviously, if they come out with the intention to do harm or look to satisfy themselves, it’s going to pose a big risk to our village. We’re sitting ducks. The police have come and had a look and said that we’re sitting ducks, and we’ve not been given any reassurances.”

In another bizarre twist, locals have been warned that their streetlights will be turned off between midnight and 5am as part of the county council’s push to reduce its carbon footprint.

Local mum Victoria Hubbocks says: “It doesn’t matter at the moment if the lights get turned off because we all know each other, and if you walk down the street at night you feel safe.



“I go for runs at 5 o’clock in the morning and I don’t feel scared. I will have to change that.

“And having no lights at all is just crazy.”

She warns that the current plans will effectively be a death knell for the village, telling The Sun she is “scared, sad, frightened — all of those things”.

She adds: “I think it effectively takes away my children’s childhood. My eldest is 11 and he’s at the point where he will come down here by himself to walk the dog, and that will no longer be possible.

“I just think it will completely change our lives. This year has been our ‘yes year’ for him.



“We’ve slept ­outside. We have done all of those things because I don’t believe that we will feel safe enough to do that in the future.”

Local dad Mario Terzino agrees.

“I’ve got an 18-year-old daughter,” he says. “She likes to walk the dog on her own.

“We’ve already had a conversation with her, and she won’t be able to walk the dog on her own if this goes ahead.”

He adds: “We’ve got no shops. We’ve got no public transport. We’ve got no pub. There is nothing here.



“It’s not about who’s going to the base. It’s about the scale. We’re talking about 1,250 people, or males, going into a site which is literally ­adjacent to our playing field. It’s just bonkers.”

Taking aim at Andy Burnham’s order that everyone has to step up and play their part, Victoria sums up the feeling of betrayal in ­Piddington: “Step up? Fair enough, but ten men to each woman in ­Piddington isn’t a fair proportion in any way, shape or form.”

A Home Office spokesman said last night: “It is categorically untrue to suggest we are seeking to house 3,510 people at MoD Bicester.

“As our planning application clearly states, we are considering the site to accommodate up to 1,256 asylum seekers.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms.



“That is why we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites.”

News.title: Boy, 4, plunges to his death from family’s six-storey apartment as brother desperately tried to save him
News.content:
FALL TRAGEDY Boy, 4, plunges to his death from family’s six-storey apartment as brother desperately tried to save him

A FOUR-year-old child has died after plunging from the sixth floor of an apartment building seconds before his older brother raced to save him.

The little boy, named Ilyès, toppled from the balcony of his family’s home in a southeastern suburb of Paris.



He lived together in the flat in Choisy-le-Roi with his parents, his twin sister and three older siblings.

At around 6pm on Saturday, the youngster wandered off onto the balcony and began to clamber up the railings.



Spotting his treacherous position, the four-year-old’s elder brother rushed outside and scrambled to grab hold of him.

“He tried to grab him by the hair, but it was too late; the little boy fell”, recounted one distraught neighbour.

One witness recalled the harrowing moment he heard the fall and went to investigate.

“I heard a boom” he said, adding “I went down to the street and saw the little boy on the sidewalk.

“He wasn’t crying, he wasn’t screaming, and he was still breathing…”

Wiping away tears, the man recounted: “I called the fire department and the police, then I brought some sheets. The fire station is just across the street.



“They came running. And they actually climbed over the garden fences that separate us from the station to get there faster.”

Emergency services raced to the scene and rescucitated the child before rushing him off in an ambulance.

But the youngster tragically passed away the following morning.

The entire neighbourhood of Fernand-Pelloutier has been rocked by the tragedy with the mayor visiting the scene that same evening to speak to traumatised residents.

In a public statement, Mayor Tonino Panetta wrote: “It is with immense sadness and deep emotion that the City of Choisy-le-Roi learned of the tragic death of Ilyès.



“The elected officials, the City employees and I extend our most sincere thoughts and deepest condolences to his family and loved ones.”

A psychological support helpline has been launched and the child’s teachers have been instructed on how to speak about the child’s death to classmates.

A mum who knew the boy’s mother from the schoolrun said: “She was a very devoted mother to her children, she cared about them all the time, and she took their return to school very seriously.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Choking up with emotion, she added: “What happened on Saturday was a tragic accident. It could happen to anyone.

“It only takes a few seconds… No one should judge.”

News.title: More flight delays expected after hundreds cancelled by air traffic control glitch
News.content:
Flight delays are expected to continue on Wednesday after an air traffic control problem cancelled hundreds of flights across the UK.

Tens of thousands of passengers were affected by the disruption and tracking website FlightRadar24 said up to 1,000 flights were cancelled after a glitch affecting air traffic control provider Nats.

Its boss Martin Rolfe apologised, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after Nats said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped".

With few aircraft able to take off, it is understood landings were restricted, leading to some flights being unable to depart overseas airports.

The fault was widespread across the UK, and beyond, with airports in Scotland and Ireland also reporting disruption. EasyJet made 200 cancellations and British Airways more than 100.

It is not the first time disruption has blighted Nats' control system. Ryanair and Wizz Air called for an overhaul of the organisation, with Wizz Air saying Nats was "not fit for purpose" in its current form.

When asked whether he was considering his position, Rolfe said there would be "lots of time for that later" but his focus now was on making sure the problem was solved.

Europe's busiest airline, Ryanair, reported on Tuesday that more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed by up to eight hours.

At Heathrow, one of the busiest airports in Europe, departures were initially paused around lunchtime. Traffic then resumed, before facing further disruption in the afternoon.

It is understood the airport ran out of space for incoming flights during the afternoon because planes had not been departing.

Thirteen Heathrow-bound flights were diverted to other airports in the UK and Europe.

News.title: US forces hit five Iranian tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan
News.content:
US forces struck five Iranian tankers in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship over the past two days, US Central Command (Centcom) has said.

The US attacked oil tankers linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) in the Gulf of Oman, as well as a tanker near Kharg Island, a major oil terminal off Iran's Gulf coast, Centcom said on Tuesday night.

Iran retaliated by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan, though Jordan later said that it had shot down 18 of the 20 missiles with its air defence systems.

Tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have escalated over the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.

Oil prices rose in early trading in Asia. Benchmark Brent crude was up by 1.5% at $99.41 (Â£73.39) a barrel, while US-traded oil was 1.6% higher at $94.55.

According to Centcom, Iran targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles, which the US "successfully evaded". No American troops were harmed, it said.

Following the US retaliatory attack, Tehran also warned of further strikes on US ships in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports.

The IRGC Navy Command warned all oil tanker crews near Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports linked to the US to "immediately leave their vessels whether at anchor or at the ports because they will be targeted".

Two of the missiles fired by Iran towards Jordan fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said.

Centcom has claimed that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".

Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil.

Some 90% of the country's crude oil comes through the island, transported through pipes from the mainland.

News.title: The trail of clues that our planet might be heating faster than we realised
News.content:
This July, during Britain's record-breaking hot summer, a curious row broke out on X over climate science.

Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit".

He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim.

The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon.

Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs.

Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming.

News.title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
News.content:
The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk.

Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women.

Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say.

Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C.

The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature.

Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool.

"But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said.

Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer.

But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk."

A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above.

According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C.

Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee.

News.title: RNLI boss says volunteers facing 'unacceptable' abuse
News.content:
RNLI staff have faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse since anti-migrant protests at the weekend, the charity's chief executive has said.

On Sunday, police faced off with demonstrators who blocked roads in Portsmouth in an effort to stop 140 people who arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area with the RNLI's assistance.

Chief executive Peter Sparkes said the abuse of volunteers was "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

He said there had been "deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding" about the charity, and condemned threats by "those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard".

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

Footage was subsequently posted on social media showing volunteers of the Poole-based charity labelled as "traitors".

News.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
News.content:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost Â£408 including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , external

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

News.title: LIV files for bankruptcy protection with $45m owed to players
News.content:
LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (Â£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.

A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday.

The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (Â£5.5m).

Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - Â£4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - Â£4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - Â£3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - Â£2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (Â£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (Â£33m).

A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts.

The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (Â£74m-Â£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (Â£370m-Â£739m).

LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.

However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.

News.title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns
News.content:
There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner has warned.

A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time.

She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need".

The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally.

Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data.

Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools.

It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions.

And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions.

The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them.

Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic.

She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent.

She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored".

"It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said.

News.title: Police warned a day before Dover protest, force says
News.content:
Kent Police previously said the protest was "spontaneous", and it did not have any intelligence to suggest a demonstration was going to happen.

Dover District Council deputy keader Edward Biggs called the announcement from Kent Police "very worrying" and "really poor".

He added: "It's very disappointing. We rely on the police providing us information so that we can inform the community and take whatever steps we need to take."

Kent Police said the information it received "would not have prevented the lawful protest from taking place, nor the disruption experienced by the town, port and wider community".

It said it had asked the College of Policing to independently examine the processes involved, so it can learn from its response.

Kent's police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said he welcomed the independent learning review by the College of Policing.

He said he had asked that it examined both how information is triaged and the communications strategy the force deployed in response to the event.

He said he would ensure the chief constable was held to account with regards to any recommendations made.

He added: "It is essential that we understand how this happened, and that lessons are learnt.

"This is separate to the response of officers, staff and specials on the ground, who did the best they could, in the circumstances they were presented with, to bring the disruption to an end as soon as they did."

Demonstrators told the BBC on Saturday they did not want to talk to the media, although one said "send them back" and another said "stop the boats" when approached.

No arrests were made on the day of the protest, police said previously.

Although no boats arrived on Saturday, eight did on Sunday, carrying 625 people, Home Office figures revealed.

The day after the protest, several officers were injured and vehicles damaged in Portsmouth at a demonstration sparked by the arrival of 120 migrants.

Both protests have been linked to Danny Thomas, a long-term campaigner against migrants more commonly known as Danny Tommo.

News.title: New law to force tech firms to stop children taking or sharing nude images
News.content:
The government has said it will introduce a new law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking or sharing nude images on mobile devices.

Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, were given three months in June to block access to nude images on smartphones and other devices used by under-18s.

But culture secretary Lisa Nandy MP told MPs on Tuesday that despite "significant commitments" from both companies, current proposals "do not meet the scale of this crisis".

She said ministers would look to legislate "as soon as they can" - with the caveat it may reassess these if firms develop and implement solutions sooner.

Alongside making tech firms block nudity on devices used by children at device-level, the government said its draft legislation would also make providers of apps used by children introduce similar blocks on nude imagery.

"This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world," Nandy said.

She told MPs that Apple and Google had already made "meaningful changes" to block nudity on smartphones used by children at the core of their systems, but more action was needed.

An Apple spokesperson said it launched its Communication Safety feature in 2021 to help stop children from seeing or sharing imagery containing nudity - and had since "continued to expand its capabilities".

"We share the UK's commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe," they said.

A Google spokesperson told the BBC it was an "industry leader in combating non-consensual intimate imagery and advancing child safety across our products".

They added Google was pleased to have "made progress" and remained committed to working on efforts to keep children safe online.

News.title: Harry and Meghan 'surprised' by King's letter making clear they remain non-working royals
News.content:
A spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex says the couple were surprised to see a letter sent on behalf of King Charles clarifying that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The spokesperson said the couple, who have recently moved back to the UK, "were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance".

But royal sources say Prince Harry and Meghan were made aware of the letter, sent on Monday afternoon, before it was made public.

It is also understood a security committee, which includes Home Office representatives, is meeting this week to look at the level of taxpayer-funded security that should be given to the Sussexes who are now resident in the UK.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - decides security for royals and public figures and Prince Harry has previously complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK.

The Home Office does not comment on such decision making - and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting.

"The UK government's protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals' security," said a Home Office spokesperson.

In terms of Prince Harry and Meghan being "surprised" by the King's message on Monday - it's understood that reflects the lack of time given to them to respond.

They were believed to have had only had sight of the letter about an hour before it was shared with the media. By the time his team had made contact with Prince Harry it's understood the letter was almost published.

News.title: Trump shares misleading video of King and fainting worker
News.content:
US President Donald Trump has shared a misleading video on social media which appears to show King Charles shrugging and walking away from a man who fainted during a royal visit.

The footage, which has been edited, features in a video shared by Trump on his Truth Social platform which appears to show other world leaders being disrespectful. The video goes on to show a montage of clips where Trump is seen honouring fallen US troops, hugging veterans and shaking hands with law enforcement officers.

The clip of the King was taken from a longer video when, as Prince of Wales, he was visiting an Asda supermarket distribution centre in Bristol during the Covid pandemic in July 2020.

The full footage, which Trump did not use, showed Charles reaching out to the man as he fell before remaining close by as he received medical attention. The video posted by Trump edits out the King staying close to the worker.

Buckingham Palace said it was not something it would comment on. The White House has not responded to a request for comment.

News.title: England up in reading, maths and science rankings as Scotland and Wales fall behind
News.content:
English pupils have pulled ahead of the rest of the UK in international reading, maths and science tests, new data suggests, with Scotland and Wales falling further behind.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) saw reading and maths scores slump in each UK nation except England, while all four saw an uptick in science, with that rise again most notable in England.

The latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills.

Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said.

The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families.

Run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Pisa tests assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire.

Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy".

News.title: Argentina to file criminal case against oil company operating in Falklands
News.content:
The Argentine government has said that it will file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.

The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.

Reacting to the news, Foreign Office Minister Kirsty McNeill insisted that there could be "no doubt" about the British government's commitment to the Falkland Islanders.

Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.

Speaking in the House of Commons on Tuesday, McNeill said that "the decision by the Falkland Islands government to pursue hydrocarbon production is a commercial decision for them to take alongside the commercial companies involved".

She added that "the future of the Falkland Islands is for Falkland Islanders to determine".

The simmering dispute between Britain and Argentina over the Falklands heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands.

Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.

In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."

The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.

He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.

Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".

News.title: Guinness 'heist' CCTV footage of two men released
News.content:
In each of the clips, a person emerges from the driver's side of the vehicle and approaches a building at the entrance to the depot, where they appear to have a brief exchange before barriers to the site are lifted to allow the lorry access.

It is estimated the total value of the items stolen, including the trailers and the Guinness, was about Â£205,000.

The trailers were found in Skelmersdale, Lancashire, last week.

One was left in the Hall Lane area shortly after 03:05 BST on Tuesday.

The second was dumped in the Gillibrands Road area shortly after 12:00 the next day.

Det Sgt Gary McClatchey said: "We will not settle for anything less than the full recovery of the near 900 stolen Guinness kegs and the locating of the offenders behind this brazen heist.

"As our investigation continues, we are now looking to identify the two men captured in the CCTV footage as we believe they hold vital information.

"I'd urge anyone who recognises these men [to] contact us so that we can progress with our investigation and I would also strongly encourage the men in the footage to please come forward."

He continued: "As we have previously stated, these kegs are stolen goods that are looking to be sold on by criminals.

"So we are continuing to urge anyone who is approached by any prospective Guinness sellers to remain cautious and, as always, report any suspicions to police."

News.title: Prince George begins first day at a rainy Eton College
News.content:
Prince George arrived on a rainy morning for his first day at Eton College, accompanied by his father and mother, the Prince and Princess of Wales.

Prince William and Catherine carried umbrellas as they brought George, wearing a jacket and tie, to be welcomed by the head teacher, Simon Henderson, and provost Sir Nicholas Coleridge.

"Welcome, good luck and enjoy," said the head teacher, shaking hands with Prince George.

They made small talk about the bad weather before the new pupil, parents and staff disappeared inside the historic school, where 13-year-old George will be a boarder.

George, who had travelled the short journey from his home at Forest Lodge in Windsor, was seen with his parents arriving at Eton's school yard, overlooked by the school's Tudor landmark of Lupton's Tower.

He was later photographed wearing the school's uniform, with black tailcoat, waistcoat and a stiff white collar.

The future king follows in the footsteps of his father in attending the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around Â£65,000 a year.

ABC has dismissed claims that Jimmy Kimmel’s late-night show is ending next year.

Just as the comedian was returning from summer break on Tuesday, Page Six reported that his upcoming season will be his last.

“His contract is not getting extended,” a source familiar with the matter told the entertainment publication.

Jimmy Kimmel Live!, which has been on air for nearly 24 years, will remain in the ABC lineup at least until May 2027 after the host signed a one-year deal, as reported by multiple outlets last December.

But an ABC spokesperson said in a statement shared with The Independent that Page Six’s reporting that the show will be canceled next year is “inaccurate” and that “any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative.”

open image in gallery ABC has dismissed claims that Jimmy Kimmel’s late-night show is ending next year ( Getty Images )

Kimmel has been a longtime critic of Donald Trump, but his jokes targeting the president’s MAGA base in the past year or so have grown increasingly controversial.

His show was briefly suspended in September following comments he made on air about the fatal shooting of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. When he returned about a week later, Kimmel shared his regrets for his remarks, choking up as he said, “It was never my intention to make light of the murder of a young man.”

Trump, then 79, called for Kimmel to be fired in April after the late-night host joked on his show during a parody of the upcoming White House Correspondents’ Dinner about First Lady Melania Trump, then 55.

“Mrs. Trump, you have a glow like an expectant widow,” Kimmel said at the time.

The real event abruptly ended after a gunman tried to storm into the ballroom of The Washington Hilton, where Trump, Melania, several members of his administration and D.C. journalists were attending the gala.

“I appreciate that so many people are incensed by Kimmel’s despicable call to violence, and normally would not be responsive to anything that he said but, this is something far beyond the pale,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

Kimmel said the joke was “about their age difference “ and “it was not by any stretch of the definition a call to assassination.”

open image in gallery 'Any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative,' an ABC spokesperson said ( Getty Images )

Page Six’s sources say that the move to cancel Kimmel’s show would be unlikely to be related to Kimmel’s adversarial relationship with the Trump administration.

“It wouldn’t have anything to do with Trump,” one source said.

ABC is also in a legal battle with Trump’s Federal Communications Commission.

The network and its parent company Disney filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC after the agency demanded an early review of the broadcast licenses of eight ABC-owned stations. The FCC has asked the court to toss out the lawsuit.

Donald Trump has intensified the U.S. trade war with Canada by banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from its neighbor, the White House announced on Tuesday.

The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion in U.S. imports earlier Tuesday.

President Trump also moved Tuesday to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term U.S. government contracts as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs took effect and Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States.

Trump directed the U.S. General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for those contracts until Canada allows “full and fair reciprocity″ for American products.

Carney said Tuesday Canada’s strategy was about becoming more independent. “It’s about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live.”

open image in gallery A truck crosses into the United States on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan ( AFP/Getty )

The rupture has upended one of the world’s closest relationships. On Aug. 22, the U.S. imposed 50 percent tariffs on about 5 percent of Canadian imports, charging that Canada had unfairly treated the American dairy, alcoholic beverage and auto industries.

The U.S. and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and its subsidies for producers of softwood lumber. But they remained friends and staunch allies.

Under Trump, U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated rapidly. In addition to imposing tariffs on Canadian products, Trump has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about making Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney came to power in a come-from-behind political victory last year by promising to stand up to him.

Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of U.S. alcoholic products — a move that prompted the retaliatory U.S. ban on Tuesday.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Mark Carney has vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States ( Reuters )

Canada is exploring ties with the European Union that could stop just short of membership, a Canadian official familiar with the discussions said.

Options could include expanding existing agreements, negotiating a new treaty or creating other forms of cooperation. The official said Canada is already consulting provinces, territories and labor groups about what a deeper relationship with the EU could look like, but no model has been chosen.

The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the talks publicly.

Carney is due in Strasbourg, France, next week, where he will attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address Sept. 16 and address the European Parliament the following day.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making a whirlwind 24-hour trip to speak at the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders this month because “there is no option” after New York’s mayor urged his arrest over the war in Gaza, Israel’s U.N. envoy said Tuesday.

Ambassador Danny Danon accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani of “doing politics” when he called the prime minister a “war criminal” and called for his arrest, which he had to withdraw because New York City does not have authority to take Netanyahu into custody.

“You know, it became very trendy to do politics by blaming Israel,” Danon added. He stressed, “For us, it’s important the prime minister will come.”

Netanyahu has become an increasingly polarizing figure over Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza. Mamdani, whose office did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment Tuesday, has pointed to the arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes tribunal against Netanyahu in November 2024, accusing him and another Israeli official of crimes against humanity.

The International Criminal Court warrant said there was reason to believe Netanyahu used “starvation as a weapon of warfare” by restricting humanitarian aid and intentionally targeting civilians in the campaign against Hamas — charges Israel denies.

While New York City does not have legal authority to execute an ICC arrest warrant, Mamdani has encouraged the federal government to do so. The U.S. and Israel are not members of the court, and the Trump administration has imposed a series of sanctions on ICC staffers in a campaign to dismantle the tribunal.

Netanyahu is scheduled to arrive in New York late on Sept. 23, address the U.N. General Assembly the afternoon of Sept. 24 and fly back to Israel that night, Danon said.

Danon noted that the meeting of leaders from the 193 U.N. member nations is taking place during the Jewish holidays and an election campaign as Netanyahu tries to keep his job as prime minister.

Danon said protests against Netanyahu would “create more chaos” on New York streets during the high-level meetings the week of Sept. 22-28.

Last year, there was a mass walkout from the U.N. General Assembly hall when Netanyahu started to speak from the podium. This year, Danon said, “I expect that there will be something like another show.”

But the ambassador said Netanyahu is experienced, “and I’m sure he will deliver his speech despite those attempts.”

CBS News is pushing back against online claims that a promotional photograph for the upcoming 59th season of “60 Minutes” was digitally altered or artificially generated.

The image, captured by photographer Mark Seliger at Grand Central Station’s Oyster Bar, features the program’s new lineup.

Following its publication, social media users highlighted several visual anomalies, drawing particular attention to reporter Lesley Stahl appearing to lean against empty space, overlapping feet that critics argued would compromise balance and an unclenched left hand gripping nothing.

“There’s a table behind her,” Jeremy Adler, the senior vice president of communications for CBS News, told The Daily Beast.

Seliger defended the portrait, noting the difficulty of getting a large group into a single frame.

CBS News is defending a promotional image for the 59th season of ’60 Minutes’ following social media claims that the photograph was digitally edited or artificially generated ( Getty )

“Bringing ten people together in one frame can be a challenge, but with this team there was an immediate chemistry and a real sense of connection,” Seliger said, according to CBS News. “You could feel the history of 60 Minutes, but also the energy of where it’s going. That’s what I hoped would come through in the photograph.”

The shoot location was intended as a tribute to network pioneers Edward R. Murrow, Walter Cronkite and Douglas Edwards, who broadcast from Grand Central when CBS maintained studios in the terminal between 1939 and 1964. According to the network, the historic studio was situated directly above the Oyster Bar, though “60 Minutes” did not premiere until 1968.

The backlash comes as the program prepares for its first full season under the leadership of Bari Weiss, whose appointment following the May departure of longtime executive producer Tanya Simon has drawn continuous controversy.

Critics have accused Weiss of censorship and shifting the program’s editorial stance, while the upcoming season launch features an interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Many users on X tied the picture's apparent glitches directly to ongoing frustrations with the broadcast's direction, with one calling it a “fake or poorly AI’d photo.”

User Darin Yates labeled the program “Liberal Propaganda and Fake News,” adding that “even your photo is fake.”

Other accounts questioned the staging entirely.

X user David Andersen asked, “Do they dislike each other so much they won't take a group photo?”

Commenters also zeroed in on specific physical awkwardness in the portrait.

Drinking very hot beverages increases the risk of developing oesophageal cancer, the largest study into the subject has found.

Financed by Cancer Research UK, researchers analysed data gathered from across the nation and established clear evidence connecting hot drinks to the disease, although the overall threat remains very minimal.

While prior studies have pointed to a similar correlation, this latest project provides the most thorough examination of the issue to date.

Participants who reported enjoying hot drinks faced roughly 1.7 times the cancer risk of those who preferred warm beverages.

That figure rose to approximately three times the risk for individuals who drank them very hot. Consuming six or more hot beverages daily also elevated the likelihood compared to drinking fewer than six per day.

Although exact temperatures went unrecorded in the study, the International Agency for Research on Cancer declared beverages above 65C as "probably carcinogenic" back in 2016.

Experts agree that adding cold milk or simply allowing drinks to cool before drinking can negate the risk.

The new study said the temperature at which coffee and tea is drunk in Western populations is estimated to be around 60C.

Fiona Osgun, head of health information at Cancer Research UK, said: “While the risk of being diagnosed with this cancer remains relatively low in the UK, this research does add to the evidence that drinking very hot drinks could increase the risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

open image in gallery Letting drinks cool down before drinking or adding cold milk can negate the risk, experts have agreed ( Alamy/PA )

“There is however a simple step people can take – let a cuppa cool down a little before taking a sip.

“And the most important ways to reduce the risk of this cancer type are not smoking and cutting down on alcohol.”

Experts believe very hot drinks may damage the cells lining the oesophagus, which could increase the chance of cancer developing.

For the new study, experts from Oxford Population Health at the University of Oxford looked at data from around 980,000 adults by combining two large UK studies – UK Biobank and the Million Women Study.

The two main types of oesophageal cancer are adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).

While drink temperature affected SCC risk in the study, there was no obvious impact on adenocarcinoma risk.

Overall, there are around 9,500 cases of oesophageal cancer in the UK every year.

People in the UK have around a 1% lifetime risk of being diagnosed with SCC.

Dr Keren Papier, lead researcher and senior nutritional epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health, said: “International research has shown for some time that drinking beverages like mate at very high temperatures, as is typical in South America, is linked to increased risk of certain oesophageal cancers.

“What was less clear, was whether this also applied to the temperatures at which hot drinks are usually consumed in Western populations.

“This is now the largest study to look at that question in a UK population, where many people drink tea and coffee daily.

“It adds to existing evidence that drinking very hot drinks could increase the risk of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

“More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk.”

Ads for three travel firms have been banned for making misleading claims about the “eco” credentials of their holidays.

Thomas Cook, loveholidays and DialAFlight ads all broke advertising rules by using terms such as “Eco Resort”, “Eco Hotel” and “eco-conscious resort” without making clear what those environmental claims were based on.

A Meta ad for DialAFlight, seen in July for Jumeirah at Saadiyat Island Resort, said: “Reconnect with yourself and your surroundings at our eco-conscious resort …”

DialAFlight said the claim “eco-conscious resort” had been taken from a factsheet provided by the accommodation, while the hotel provided the ASA with a list of environmental initiatives and activities undertaken at the resort.

Two Google ads for loveholidays, also in July, promoted the “Green Garden Eco Resort” and the “Marvida Family Eco Hotel”.

The online travel agent explained that in both cases the term “Eco” was part of the accommodation’s name rather than an environmental claim formulated, adopted or endorsed by loveholidays.

Thomas Cook explained that the “Sandos Caracol Eco Resort” changed its name in July 2025 and the travel firm had taken steps to block “Sandos Caracol Eco” as a search term to prevent it appearing in future searches.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) found that consumers were likely to interpret the claims as meaning the accommodation had environmental characteristics or benefits, but were not given enough information to understand what those were.

ASA director of complaints and investigations Miles Lockwood said: “For people looking to make more environmentally conscious choices when it comes to booking their holidays, it’s important that they can trust the claims that they see in ads.

“Today’s rulings make clear that if a hotel or resort is described as ‘eco’ or ‘eco-conscious’, advertisers need to be clear about what that means, so people have the information they need to make an informed choice about where to book.”

A loveholidays spokeswoman said: “As an online travel agent, we do not own, operate or manage the accommodation we sell. The hotel names displayed in our advertising reflected the trading names of the properties, rather than environmental claims made by loveholidays.

“We have updated the listings for the hotels concerned and removed the s. We will continue to review our processes to ensure the information we provide to customers is clear and transparent.”

More than half of people who have had money stolen through fraud in the past two years feel the experience has negatively affected their mental health, according to Which?.

The consumer group commissioned a survey of more than 1,500 people across the UK who had lost money to scams in the past two years.

Unauthorised fraud was the most common type reported in the survey, with people having their bank account or card details harvested (44%), or losingtheir physical card, mobile phone or other device to opportunistic thieves (16%).

Impersonation scams accounted for 35%, with victims having been groomed into authorising payments to fraudsters purporting to be trusted organisations or individuals. The remaining 5% was made up of other types of scams.

People reported their experience had a negative impact on their stress levels (63%) and mental health (54%) as well as their financial situation (47%).

One person told Which?: “It has made me feel stupid and ashamed.

“I haven’t fully told my family. I have tried to cover up the full financial loss.”

Another said: “I was so nervous and stressed. It had a big impact on my marriage as well.

“My husband thinks I don’t have enough knowledge to maintain my finances. I’m so depressed.”

A third person said their mental health “was affected very badly”, adding: “I feel like a failure.”

A Facebook user who fell victim to a scam on the platform felt the situation “was handled very poorly”, according to Which?

Which? argued tech giants should be doing more to combat scams on their platforms.
