Sports.title: Audi signals appeal over Tsunoda’s Italian GP non-penalty
Sports.content:
The Audi Formula 1 team has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against Yuki Tsunoda's non-penalty in the Italian Grand Prix.

Amid confusion over where he was supposed to line up on a lap 6 restart, Tsunoda parked in his correct 14th grid slot, but at an angle towards the inside wall. Race director Rui Marques was "not comfortable" with Tsunoda's position, so imposed an extra formation lap.

According to Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations, "any driver who caused an extra formation lap, and is then able to start the, or any subsequent, extra formation lap must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and must start ... from the end of the Pit Lane."

But according to the FIA race stewards, Tsunoda didn't technically cause the extra formation lap because the race director acted out of an abundance of caution, Tsunoda wasn't out of his grid slot and didn't impact other competitors. The crux of the issue is that race control hadn't informed Racing Bulls that its driver had caused the extra formation lap either, so therefore the team had no reason to tell Tsunoda to start from the pitlane.

Tsunoda escaped a stop-and-go penalty and went on to score the final point in 10th. The decision not to punish the Japanese driver impacted Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, who crossed the line in 11th.

As a result, Audi has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against the non-penalty for Tsunoda.

"Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there," Audi said in a statement. "The Stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

Gabriel Bortoleto would have gained a point in Monza if Yuki Tsunoda had been handed a penalty. Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Per article 15.4 of the FIA's International Sporting Code, competitors have one hour after the stewards' decision to notify their intention to appeal. That does not mean Audi is actually appealing against the verdict just yet. But it gives the team an additional 96-hour time window to further study the case to see if there is an element to appeal against before following through on it.

In their verdict, the stewards wrote: "The extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22.

"Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and start from the Pit Lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop and Go penalty is imposed.

"In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the Pit Lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

"A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the Pit Lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap."

The stewards added: "The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the Pit Lane.

"Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action."

Sports.title: Why Mercedes didn't pit Russell under virtual safety car in Italian GP
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli's sensational win from the back of the grid in the Italian Grand Prix was thanks to a great drive, but perhaps also a little help from strategy and a timely virtual safety car.

The Italian was the only Mercedes driver to make a pitstop during the race - and ultimately defeated his team-mate and championship rival George Russell.

Mercedes split the strategies between its drivers, putting Antonelli on mediums after the early red flag. That was the only option for the Italian to go to the end without stopping, having started the race on hards. Russell, on the other hand, started on mediums and switched to hards after the race was stopped following Charles Leclerc's crash - and stayed on that tyre for the rest of the distance.

For Antonelli, Mercedes used the opportunity to put him on a new set of mediums when Lance Stroll's stoppage caused a virtual safety car on lap 27.

By that point, Antonelli had already made his way through the field and was battling Russell for the lead - although Mercedes asked him not to attack his team-mate after the initial phase of the fight, allowing them to try to build a gap to Max Verstappen.

Then came the call for Antonelli to pit. And although the Italian was able to come back and overtake his team-mate on fresher tyres, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said the team itself didn't know which strategy would ultimately prove better.

“We didn't know what was the better strategy," he told the media, including Autosport, after the race. "At that stage, the system said that the one-stop [for Russell] comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but wouldn't catch. So that's what the software said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“It was also the right thing to split the strategies because it was unknown what the better one would be. In the morning meeting we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it and you can see with George it was a forever tyre but it didn't have the performance that of the medium.”

The decision to stop Antonelli was made despite him reporting that his tyres were in good shape.

“We didn't talk to Kimi about the stop," Wolff confirmed. "We asked for the state of the tyre and he said, 'Well it's actually good' but it was clear that we saw abrasion and I think it was on Lewis' car. We saw some abrasion on a McLaren. So it was the right thing to do. And that's why it didn't need any big discussion.

“But then having said that, Kimi was able to extract 35 laps or 40 laps from that tyre in a consistent way and that's certainly his skill.”

Russell himself believes he had enough pace to win the race had Antonelli stayed on the same strategy.

"I would have loved to have continued on the same strategy," he said during the post-race press conference. "Because I felt in a good position in that battle. I knew exactly what I needed to do with the energy management to defend but also when to attack and make those moves and I put a lot of preparation into this race in that regard.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"Then of course when the VSC came out, it came out at that perfect point for the drivers to pull the trigger and take the pitstop."

Asked whether he had considered stopping for fresh rubber at that point, Russell said: "I didn't. I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well but I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pitwall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"When we had Max in the mix as well from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios. So, today Kimi did a great job.

"I was on the hard tyre and Kimi was on the medium tyre. So if either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC, because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre.

"But, it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether. It would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC."

After the race at Monza, Russell trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship.

Sports.title: After Antonelli’s Italian GP win, is the F1 title fight over? Our writers have their say
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s Italian Grand Prix win from 19th on the grid was a statement performance and extends his lead in the Formula 1 world championship to 66 points.

With a maximum of 10 rounds left – subject to the Qatar and Abu Dhabi GPs and the situation in the Middle East – the Italian driver is in a supremely strong position to seal the 2026 world title.

So, is the 2026 F1 world title fight over? Our writers have their say.

It’d need to be a generational choke for Antonelli to lose it from here

I don’t want to say it is done and dusted before the European stretch of the season is over but this felt monumental. To go from 19th on the grid to victory, against the likes of George Russell and Max Verstappen at the front of the pack, is going to go down in history as the first moment Antonelli demonstrated his F1 world champion credentials.

A gap of 66 points with 10-ish rounds to go isn’t impossible to overturn – just two DNFs and the pressure is right on top of the 20-year-old – but he just doesn’t seem phased by any of it and, if anything, is driving better now than at any point in his burgeoning career in F1.

Antonelli has shown already he can bank solid results when needed, and also charge for the win when it is there for the taking; he effectively did both one after the other at Monza this weekend.

Yes, finishing second to Russell in every race still isn’t enough to mathematically seal the title, but with his team-mate expected to serve a back of the grid penalty for an engine change in Azerbaijan, he has a great opportunity to make that scenario a reality.

– Haydn Cobb

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

It’s not over – but Russell will need luck

Antonelli definitely dealt a sizeable blow to Russell’s title hopes in Monza but, as of today, there are 10 rounds to go – 258 points to score.

Russell’s deficit is up to 66 points, and the dynamic isn’t favourable to him, as frustration will understandably be growing – though he was very gracious in defeat on Sunday.

In order to make up such a substantial gap, Russell will need the stars to align. Antonelli doesn’t have many off days; in 13 grands prix so far this season, he has finished on the podium 11 times to Russell’s seven.

That remarkable consistency typically leads to a world title, with few examples to the contrary. Coincidentally, it happened just last year. Oscar Piastri also had 11 podiums from the first 13 rounds, by which time he was 16 points ahead of team-mate Lando Norris and 81 points clear of Max Verstappen, but he ended up outscored by both.

Other than that, the most recent one was Nico Rosberg in 2014. The German had recorded 11 podiums in the first 13 races, but team-mate Lewis Hamilton had 10 podium finishes himself and was just 22 points down in the standings. Three times fewer than the current gap, in other words.

So, such a recovery wouldn’t be unprecedented, as shown by Verstappen – but it wasn’t comparable given Russell and Antonelli have the same car, unlike the Red Bull racer and the McLaren drivers last year. So, while there’s hope, the Briton really is a long shot by now.

– Ben Vinel

Antonelli’s rivals have too much to do

There’s really very little to suggest anything can still stop Antonelli from clinching the title this year after his Monza victory. If anyone had doubts before, this weekend probably removed the last arguments for predicting any other outcome - barring something going completely wrong for the Italian off track.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

After all, Isack Hadjar didn’t exactly plan to miss a couple of races. So, as long as Antonelli stays away from boxing gloves for the next couple of months, he should be fine. If he shows up on the grid - regardless of where he starts, apparently - he looks set to become world champion at the age of 20.

It’s not only about Antonelli, either. Russell, still his closest rival, doesn’t just need to close a massive points gap - he has to do something even more difficult: maintain the belief that he can still beat Antonelli on any given weekend.

Given how this season has unfolded, and the speed of the Italian’s progress, it must be daunting for the Briton to see just how brilliant his young team-mate has become.

Monza also confirmed Ferrari is probably out of the picture. Charles Leclerc never really was in it, and now he’s simply too far behind to seriously think about the title. And Hamilton doesn’t appear to have a car capable of challenging the Mercedes drivers consistently. The same applies to Norris and McLaren, whose weaknesses were exposed again this weekend.

– Oleg Karpov

I am going to call it here

I just don't see a way back for Russell. I really don't. Yes, there are a lot of points on the table, stranger things have happened in F1, and those formidable Mercedes power units have been glass cannons. I get all that.

But the manner in which Antonelli has been amassing race wins, and collecting whichever result is available when Mercedes doesn't enjoy its usual supremacy, is a quite a marvel for a 20-year-old.

Russell is turning things around, but even that doesn't appear to be enough to be beating Antonelli on a regular basis and that's exactly what he would have to do. Not keeping pace, as he is roughly doing now, but battering Antonelli.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

I just don't see it happening, because I'm afraid Russell has met his match in the young Italian.

What's more, the Italian Grand Prix was supposed to be Antonelli's mulligan, his joker race where taking his fifth power unit meant an exercise in damage limitation. Instead of sustaining damage, he has dealt Russell a mental hammer blow. Meanwhile, Russell still has to take his engine penalty later on, and there isn't a circuit left where overtaking will be this easy.

The conclusion to last year's title race has shown that 10 races is an eternity, but that was when the best driver of his generation was doing the chasing. Now, the best driver of the next generation is out in front, and he looks bulletproof. I am going to call it here.

– Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: Will Matchroom Keep Alan Chaves After Garcia Loss?
Sports.content:
“I have one more fight left with Matchroom, so it will possibly be in December,” Chaves said to La Casaca Boxing Club.

Winning that fight alone might not be enough. He may need to look exceptional against a credible opponent to persuade Matchroom that he remains worth another contract.

Hearn visited Chaves in the dressing room before the Garcia fight but did not see him afterward or join him in the ring. Chaves said his promoter, Georgina Rivero, was unhappy about Hearn’s absence.

Initially, Chaves claimed it did not bother him, but his later comments revealed that he noticed.

“There are many people who disappear when these things happen, as in this case with the promoter,” Chaves said.

The timing is difficult to ignore. He received promotional attention when he was knocking out opponents and being presented as one of Argentina’s brightest prospects. Once Garcia beat him, Hearn was no longer there.

None of this proves Matchroom has already decided to let Chaves leave after December. It does show how quickly a young import’s position can change after the zero disappears. Promotional enthusiasm is easy when a prospect is producing knockouts. The real test comes when the company must determine if it wants to spend money rebuilding him.

Matchroom has already learned that Chaves is not ready for a top lightweight. Now it must determine if his weaknesses can be repaired or if it merely bought an inflated record.

Chaves deserves credit for accepting responsibility, but his explanation also raises serious questions about his corner.

“They studied me 100 percent, and we as a team made the mistake of watching very little of Eridson,” Chaves said. “From the little we watched, we imagined he would come out and do the same thing.”

Preparing for a significant fight in Newark without properly studying the opponent is inexcusable. Chaves and his team assumed Garcia would come forward and trade because that was how he had fought in the footage they watched. They did not prepare for movement, counters, or changes in rhythm.

“I trained to go forward because that was what had worked for me in all these fights,” Chaves said. “We didn’t have a Plan B, Plan C or Plan D other than going forward and exchanging.”

Once Garcia refused to cooperate, Chaves had nothing else. He followed him around the ring, struggled to cut off his exits, and walked into counters throughout the fight. Even after four knockdowns, neither the fighter nor his corner found a different approach.

What happened was more than a bad performance. It was tactical negligence built on overconfidence.

His 19 knockouts in Argentina encouraged the team to believe that aggression and power would travel without the supporting skills. Garcia showed what happens when a puncher accustomed to compliant opposition meets a crafty boxer who controls distance and refuses to remain in front of him.

The knockout percentage concealed Chaves’ mechanical weaknesses. His feet did not position him to trap Garcia, his attacks became predictable, and he lacked the defensive awareness to enter safely. Those deficiencies were always there. Garcia was simply the first opponent skilled enough to reveal all of them.

Hearn now has two bad matchmaking options. One route is to give Chaves a ham and egger, allow him to score another knockout, and advertise the performance as a successful return. Fans will recognize that rehabilitation job immediately. Stopping someone selected to lose would not show that he learned anything from Newark.

Instead, Matchroom can match him against a capable lightweight who can move and counter. Such an opponent would give Chaves a genuine chance to redeem himself, but it also risks another one-sided defeat that ends any discussion about a new agreement.

A top opponent is not necessary. Chaves does need someone good enough to test the areas Garcia punished. Matchroom must find a fighter who forces him to cut off the ring, control his aggression, and change tactics during the fight.

A decisive win under those conditions would give Hearn a reason to consider another deal. Knocking out a soft target would leave the questions unanswered. Another boxer taking him apart would likely finish his Matchroom run when the contract expires.

An immediate rematch with Eridson is not something Chaves believes he deserves. That is another honest admission. He knows he must earn it by beating someone else first.

December is not merely a comeback date. It may determine if Chaves remains a Matchroom fighter or becomes another heavily promoted puncher whose value disappeared once his record met a real test.

Sports.title: Usyk Camp Rejects Tyson Fury’s Backup Plan
Sports.content:
Usyk’s manager, Sergey Lapin, was unimpressed by the public offer.

“Usyk is not Tyson’s backup plan,” Lapin told Sky Sports. “If Fury needs an opponent, he should visit the Ready to Fight platform. They can help him find a worthy opponent there. Oleksandr is always open to big challenges. But serious intentions are backed by a concrete offer, not statements in the press.”

The Joshua negotiations have not stalled because neither boxer has formally refused to fight. Both men signed individual contracts, but their teams remain divided over the venue.

Joshua and Matchroom want Wembley Stadium, which they believe was included in the agreement. The organizers and broadcast partners favor Madison Square Garden in New York, where the event can be staged at a more convenient hour for Netflix’s American audience.

A Wembley event designed around United States viewing hours may require an early morning ring walk in London. That creates transportation, licensing, and logistical issues while asking British ticket buyers to attend a fight at an unreasonable hour.

Declaring the fight dead and naming Usyk gives Fury a way to pressure Joshua into accepting New York without admitting that the original contest remains under negotiation.

It is unclear how serious Fury is about pursuing the trilogy. Calling out Usyk gives him another famous name to mention while the Joshua event remains tied up over its venue.

Actually fighting Usyk would be a far greater risk. Fury lost both previous meetings on points and came close to being stopped in the ninth round of their first contest. A third defeat would make the Joshua event an even harder sell. The contest is already based largely on nostalgia. Both men are former champions in the later stages of their careers, and each has suffered damaging defeats.

If Fury lost to Usyk again, he and Joshua would hold a combined record of zero wins and five losses against the Ukrainian. Promoters would then be selling a meeting between two aging British heavyweights who repeatedly failed against the same opponent.

Having vacated his remaining heavyweight belts, Usyk can now select the final fights of his career without mandatory obligations controlling his schedule. He has no sporting reason to rescue Fury’s November date through a hastily arranged trilogy.

A pair of victories already settled matters in Usyk’s mind. Stepping in again calls for massive purses, extensive camp preparations, plus contract clauses honoring the undisputed winner of their first two bouts. Lapin’s reaction guards those advantages. The champion keeps possibilities open without letting Fury treat him like an easy backup while Joshua talks stall.

Ultimatums, false retirement vows, and substitute names constantly pop up whenever Fury sits at the bargaining table. This callout fits the usual routine: fabricate panic, point fingers, then pretend another blockbuster remains ready to sign. A trilogy could still materialize eventually. Yet a social media challenge hardly counts as an actual contract talk.

The real threat facing Fury and Joshua is letting this matchup disappear altogether. Without championship belts between them, another setback for either man would instantly erode their commercial draw. Every prolonged holdout simply turns the contest into a nostalgic showcase of past glories rather than a fight that matters in the present.

Until Fury’s team sends Usyk a concrete proposal, the trilogy callout is best understood as leverage in the Joshua venue dispute.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Gets Second IBF Title Chance
Sports.content:
Raymond Muratalla surrendered the belt after struggling to make 135 pounds for his recent defense against Robson Conceição. He plans to continue his career at light welterweight, creating an opening for the IBF’s two highest-ranked available contenders.

Cruz (7-1, 4 KOs) lost a majority decision to Muratalla in January after challenging for the championship in only his seventh professional appearance. Muratalla’s pressure and activity became increasingly effective during the later rounds, showing that Cruz’s extensive amateur background had not fully prepared him for the physical demands of a hard professional fight.

The 31-year-old Cuban returned in July and stopped late replacement Abraham Montoya in three rounds. His brief comeback gave no clear indication that he had corrected the weaknesses exposed by Muratalla.

An exceptional counterpuncher with world-class reflexes, Cruz often depends on distance, quick reactions, and single clean shots. Those tools can control shorter amateur bouts. Over 12 rounds, repeatedly changing direction and escaping exchanges can drain a fighter who is not comfortable holding his ground or working inside.

Subkhankulov (12-0, 6 KOs) will try to force that type of contest. The 34-year-old Russian southpaw earned his position by stopping Bakhodur Usmonov in the 12th round of their April eliminator. Usmonov went down four times across the final three rounds before the referee ended the action.

His southpaw position will also test Cruz’s lead foot placement and ability to land the right hand without remaining in range for counters. Subkhankulov is unlikely to be discouraged by feints or a difficult opening six rounds. His best chance is to attack the body, keep Cruz working, and turn the final third into another test of stamina.

There is history between them. Cruz defeated Subkhankulov by split decision when they met in the semifinals of the Ústí nad Labem Grand Prix in May 2019. The three-round amateur result offers Cruz some familiarity, but it says little about how their styles will interact over a professional championship distance.

The October 7 deadline may determine more than the fighters’ pay. Cruz has spent his professional career fighting in the United States, while Subkhankulov has done much of his work in Russia and on IBA-promoted cards. If negotiations fail and Subkhankulov’s side wins the purse bid, Cruz may have to pursue the championship far from his usual surroundings.

This is still a favorable route back for Cruz. He avoids another meeting with Muratalla and faces someone he has already beaten. However, two championship appearances within his first nine professional outings show how aggressively his career is being pushed.

At 31, Cruz does not have years to spend developing against mid-level opposition. Winning the vacant belt against Subkhankulov may be the calculated shortcut his team needs. Losing would show that the rush from decorated amateur to professional champion asked too much of him too quickly.

Sports.title: Jack Dempsey Escapes Without A Verdict Against Miske
Sports.content:
At 22 years of age, Dempsey was tearing through the heavyweight division with his aggressive style and crushing left hook. Miske, 24, had the benefit of fighting before his hometown supporters, but he was far more than a protected local attraction.

Dempsey weighed 187½ pounds, while Miske came in at 182.

Known as the “St. Paul Thunderbolt,” Miske was a fast, clever boxer who understood how to block punches, smother attacks, and work at close range. Those skills gave Dempsey one of his hardest tests during his climb toward Jess Willard’s heavyweight championship.

The local favorite supplied a tactical lesson for smaller fighters facing dangerous punchers. Instead of continually backing away, he stepped into Dempsey’s punching range and crowded him. Retreating would have given Dempsey space to drive forward, build speed, and launch his leaping left hook. Miske took away that leverage by getting close, controlling Dempsey’s arms and preventing him from completing his punches.

The rolling movement associated with Dempsey’s attacks depended upon momentum. He bobbed his upper body from side to side, shifted his weight, and sprang forward with hooks from changing angles. An opponent who backed away gave that attack time to gather force.

Meeting Dempsey chest to chest changed the exchanges into an arm wrestle. His long swings lost much of their force as Miske blocked the hook, jammed the punching arm, and answered with short shots before tying him up.

Quick punches inside prevented the younger man from finding a steady rhythm. Dempsey had productive stretches in the second and third rounds, but Miske answered with a hard right cross in the third.

Years later, Dempsey admitted that Miske was landing more punches and building what looked like a lead. He also recalled being hurt during one exchange and struggling to remain upright until the bell.

“Miske had landed more telling blows than I had,” Dempsey recalled. “He suddenly came at me with a volley that nearly put me out.”

It was a revealing admission from a fighter remembered for overwhelming opponents. Raw aggression had run into a boxer who understood distance, timing and leverage. The visiting fighter finally produced his strongest attack in the seventh. A heavy left to the body followed by a right to the jaw troubled Miske and helped Dempsey recover ground. Neither man scored a knockdown, leaving the newspapers to decide which work they valued more.

Miske’s approach was almost the opposite of the one Jess Willard used against Dempsey in Toledo the following year. The 6’6″ champion tried to control the challenger from long range but remained too upright and stationary.

That distance allowed Dempsey to leap forward with hooks and overhand punches. Willard became an easy target once the challenger closed the distance, leading to seven knockdowns during the savage opening round.

Such a runway was never available against Miske. He moved toward the danger, shortened the punches, and forced Dempsey to work without full leverage. Willard waited at the end of Dempsey’s forward rush, while Miske intercepted it before the punches reached full speed.

The St. Paul fight showed that smothering Dempsey was safer than surrendering the ring and waiting for him to attack. Gene Tunney receives credit for solving Dempsey in 1926 and repeating the result one year later. Miske had exposed several of the same weaknesses eight years earlier. Their tactics were not identical. Tunney relied more heavily on footwork, his jab, and movement at long range. Miske was more willing to hold his position, work inside, and smother Dempsey physically.

Both remained composed when Dempsey attacked. They refused to become stationary targets at his preferred distance and punished him when his forward movement became predictable.

Before their first fight, Tunney studied films of Dempsey and brought former opponents and sparring partners into camp. There is no firm evidence that Miske personally supplied Tunney’s plan, but the St. Paul contest had established the central principle: Dempsey became less effective when an opponent denied him momentum and forced him to restart his attacks.

Miske supplied the early evidence that denying Dempsey momentum made him less effective, and Tunney later produced the polished championship version.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press surveyed eight writers at ringside. Four favored Dempsey, one selected Miske and three scored the fight even. The newspaper published the bout as a draw, although other reports awarded Dempsey a narrow newspaper decision based on his aggression and heavier punches.

A later collection drawing upon additional newspaper sources produced seven verdicts for Dempsey, four draws and one for Miske. That broader tally included reports beyond the eight writers questioned in St. Paul.

Such disagreement exposed the weakness of the no decision era. A boxer’s official record remained untouched after a distance fight, even when most observers believed he had lost. Local sports editors became unofficial judges without a uniform scoring system or any requirement to agree.

Reports from St. Paul do not support the claim that hometown writers simply protected Miske. Four of the eight surveyed writers favored the visiting Dempsey, while only one selected Miske. Regional loyalty may have influenced individual accounts, but the split also reflected a genuinely close fight.

Miske landed more often and controlled long portions of the contest, while Dempsey delivered the harder individual blows. Some writers valued activity and craft; others favored aggression and damage.

Promoters benefited from the uncertainty. Dempsey survived a difficult night without receiving an official loss, allowing his handlers to continue selling him as the next threat to Willard. Miske also avoided a formal defeat and remained a leading heavyweight attraction in Minnesota. Jack Kearns wanted knockouts that would sell Dempsey to a national audience. Taking him into Miske’s hometown against a fast, experienced boxer was a serious gamble.

The no decision format reduced the danger because only a knockout placed an official loss on the record. It did not remove the promotional risk. A decisive beating reported across the country still would have damaged Dempsey’s growing reputation.

Kearns learned that clever defensive fighters presented a different challenge from the large, slower heavyweights Dempsey destroyed. His fighter continued facing dangerous opposition, including Fred Fulton, Battling Levinsky, Bill Brennan and Miske himself, but the first fight supplied a warning. Dempsey’s power did not automatically solve every style.

The pair met again in Philadelphia on November 28, 1918, with most newspapers favoring Dempsey after six rounds. By then, the future champion had gained more experience against Miske’s troublesome methods.

Their third fight came on September 6, 1920, after Dempsey had taken the heavyweight championship from Willard. Miske was suffering from Bright’s disease and was knocked out in the third round of Dempsey’s first title defense.

His illness was not common public knowledge, so there is no basis for claiming Kearns selected Miske because he knew the challenger was dying. In hindsight, the physical decline made the title fight far less dangerous than their first meeting had been.

That knockout became the lasting image of their rivalry. Miske is now remembered primarily as the sick challenger who needed money, while Dempsey remains one of boxing’s most recognizable champions.

The familiar family story belongs mainly to the end of Miske’s life, not the 1920 title fight. A gravely ill Miske returned against Bill Brennan in November 1923, scored a fourth-round knockout, and used the money to give his family a memorable Christmas. He died on January 1, 1924.

Remembering only the tragedy reduces Miske to a sympathetic opponent in Dempsey’s championship story. Reports from 1918 present the fuller picture.

At that time, the St. Paul Thunderbolt was one of the sharpest technical boxers in the heavyweight division, possessing the timing, defense, and composure to frustrate Dempsey near his physical peak. He survived 10 rounds and forced the future champion to abandon many of his preferred attacks. The press left St. Paul unable to agree on a winner.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Claims Benn Overlooks His Ring Intelligence
Sports.content:
The less flattering side is his habit of retreating in straight lines until his back reaches the ropes. He often relies on a high guard, clinch, or awkward turn instead of circling into open space. Benn will attempt to close those exits, making Ryan’s footwork an immediate test of the boxing depth he is advertising.

Aggression also creates danger for the challenger. Benn was dropped twice by Cedrick Peynaud early in his career, and he can still rush inside without setting up his attacks. Those entries give Ryan opportunities to land his fastest counter.

Charging forward carelessly during the opening three rounds would leave Benn exposed. Ryan is at his most dangerous when an opponent supplies the movement and gives him a stationary target. One poorly timed leap may be all the champion needs.

The body offers Benn his clearest route to slowing Ryan. Gervonta Davis stopped him with a liver shot in 2023, and Benn throws heavy hooks downstairs when he gets within punching range. Sustained body work could reduce Ryan’s movement and take some of the speed from his counters.

Reaching that distance is the difficult part. Ryan owns the faster hands and is more dangerous from the outside, leaving his challenger dependent on close-quarters exchanges and a punishing pace.

Returning to 147 pounds raises another question for Benn. He added size for two fights with Chris Eubank Jr., and camp footage shows a noticeably leaner fighter coming back down to welterweight. If the cut weakens his legs or stamina, trapping Ryan will become increasingly difficult.

This is Ryan’s opportunity to support his claim. Knocking Benn out with another hook would confirm the power everyone already recognizes. Escaping the ropes, controlling distance, working inside, and adjusting to the body attack would demonstrate the boxing IQ he believes Benn has failed to appreciate.

Sports.title: Fury Calls Itauma A Billion-Dollar Loss
Sports.content:
A few soft opponents will not cause supporters to abandon Itauma. The real difficulty is finding fighters who can extend him without beating him.

To support his warning, Fury used his own career as the example Itauma should have followed.

“I did it the traditional route, and it’s done like that for a reason,” Fury said. “I was 27 years old when I fought Wladimir Klitschko; I was a 10-1 underdog [but] I was ready. If I’d have fought him at 21, I’d have got knocked out, too.”

There is some truth in that. Fury spent years fighting domestic and European opposition before receiving his first world title opportunity. He entered the Klitschko fight with a 24-0 record, making the November 2015 contest his 25th professional bout.

What his version leaves out is Klitschko’s condition at the time. The champion was 39 and nearing the end of his career. His reactions, punch output, and willingness to exchange had declined. Fury did not complete a traditional apprenticeship and then defeat a heavyweight champion at his physical peak.

With only 35 professional rounds behind him, Itauma was given a much more dangerous test. Hrgovic was experienced, durable, and able to force a hard pace after absorbing Itauma’s best punches.

The promotional obsession with Itauma breaking Mike Tyson’s record as the youngest heavyweight champion also helped accelerate his development. That age window had already closed by the time he fought Hrgovic, but the rush had shaped his career. Opponents were selected to produce quick knockouts and keep him moving toward a marketing milestone.

Those victories established Itauma’s destructive image without preparing him for the moment a world-class heavyweight refused to disappear.

Stories about Itauma handling leading heavyweights in sparring helped create confidence in his readiness. Fabio Wardley also confirmed that Itauma had completed 12-round sparring sessions despite an earlier interview clip suggesting otherwise.

Completing 12 rounds in a gym is not the same as fighting nine hard rounds under championship pressure. Sparring partners can reduce the pace and stop when instructed. There are no judges, title stakes, or thousands of spectators reacting to every punch.

Once the fight began, Hrgovic presented a psychological test that closed gym sessions could not reproduce. Itauma hit him hard, dropped him in the second round, and continued attacking, yet the older man kept coming. Every unsuccessful attempt to finish Hrgovic increased the physical and mental cost.

Nothing in Itauma’s professional experience had prepared him for an opponent absorbing that much punishment and returning with greater pressure after six rounds.

It would be too simple to blame roadwork or poor cardiovascular conditioning. Itauma exhausted himself through the way he fought.

Nearly every combination was thrown with maximum torque. He remained tense at close range and repeatedly searched for a damaging finish. He lacked a controlling jab that would allow him to maintain distance, score without spending heavily, and recover while remaining offensively active.

After Hrgovic survived the early assault, Itauma had no economical gear. His legs weakened, his punches lost their shape, and he no longer had the energy to defend himself or slow Hrgovic’s advance.

The jump in opposition was considerable, but the matchmaking alone did not cause the defeat. Itauma’s approach made an already difficult test even harder.

Proof that a young heavyweight can recover from a defeat is already available within Queensberry. Frank Warren continued working with Daniel Dubois after losses to Joe Joyce and Oleksandr Usyk.

After both fights, Dubois faced criticism, particularly when he took a knee and allowed the referee to count him out. Those defeats did not destroy his commercial value or end his title ambitions. Queensberry lowered the pressure, found suitable fights, and gave him another opportunity to develop.

Rather than watching a “billion-dollar” future disappear, Itauma may be following a rougher version of the Dubois route. The difference is that Queensberry must use the rebuilding period to correct an identifiable weakness instead of merely restoring his knockout streak.

“I just think that knocking out a low-level man is different to knocking out a world-class man; different power, toughness, everything,” Fury said. “It is totally different. “It’s about getting the balance right. Get him in with somebody who is durable, not that dangerous, who can take punishment and give him the rounds. He needs to get used to getting the rounds in.”

Here, Fury makes his strongest point. Queensberry needs durable opponents who can survive Itauma’s opening attacks, make him think, and force him to regulate his output. He must learn to vary the speed of his punches, take quiet periods, and stop treating every opening as a chance to produce a knockout.

Until he does, the Hrgovic blueprint will remain available. A mobile heavyweight can stay away during the early rounds, while a durable pressure fighter can absorb his power and wait for him to slow down.

Careful matchmaking can restore Itauma’s popularity, but it cannot disguise his stamina forever. If his engine remains suited to six rounds, the same ending will remain possible whenever an opponent lasts long enough to test it.

Sports.title: Hearn Says TKO Gave Joshua 90 Minutes for America
Sports.content:
“Yesterday, TKO went around the back again to try and offer Joshua money to do the fight in America,” Hearn told DAZN. “It’s a dirty, dirty game, mate, to be honest with you. It’s made it even harder for them because Josh just ain’t about that. You’ve got an hour and a half to make your decision. Mate, what don’t you understand? I signed to fight in Britain. I want the fight in Britain.”

The 90-minute demand is the major addition to Hearn’s story. A deadline that short would leave Joshua little time to study revised terms, consult his lawyers, or calculate the financial consequences of moving the event from Britain.

It sounds like an attempt to place a large number in front of AJ and force an immediate decision. No amount has been disclosed, but TKO presumably understood that a modest increase would not persuade him to surrender Wembley Stadium, his home support, and the protection Hearn says was written into the signed agreement.

“You can’t buy everybody,” Hearn continued. “Especially the ones who it means something to.”

Hearn said the approach strengthened Joshua’s determination to keep the Fury fight in Britain. The growing public support has also changed the tone of the venue negotiations. A week earlier, Hearn said there was “zero interest” in London and that New York was being treated as the only destination. He now claims Sela has asked him about contacting London Mayor Sadiq Khan to help make the British event possible.

The conflict with TKO has not ended. When asked if Matchroom would take action over the direct approach, Hearn said his team had already written to the company.

“What are you doing?” Hearn said. “You guys are on the New York Stock Exchange. What is this? Just coming around the back trying to bung someone a few quid. Come on. It doesn’t have to be like that. But it’s pushing the fight further away because of their behavior.”

That is the danger behind TKO’s alleged tactic. The company may have believed a quick financial offer would settle the American venue, but Hearn says it produced the opposite response. Joshua is now more committed to Britain, Matchroom has contacted TKO in writing, and the relationship between the parties has deteriorated.

Hearn placed the likelihood of Fury and Joshua fighting in Britain at 64%. That oddly precise estimate still leaves New York in contention, but it is more optimistic than his position a week ago.

The missing financial figure remains fascinating. If TKO wanted Joshua’s answer within 90 minutes, it must have believed the offer was large enough to make him reconsider everything he had signed for.

Sports.title: Muhammad Ali, Richard Dunn, And The AccuPunch
Sports.content:
Both stood 6’3″, but nearly everything else separated them. Ali traveled with an international promotional circus and commanded million-dollar purses. Dunn was a former paratrooper and working scaffolder who balanced his trade with professional boxing. Their meeting was not part of the original plan.

German promoters anticipated that Bernd August would win the vacant European championship and provide Ali with a German challenger. Dunn ruined the arrangement by stopping August in the third round at London’s Royal Albert Hall seven weeks before the Munich date.

That victory sent Bradford’s working-class champion into a fight with the most famous athlete in the world.

Dunn was Ali’s third championship opponent in barely three months. Ali stopped Jean Pierre Coopman in February, struggled through 15 rounds with Jimmy Young in April, and returned against Dunn only 24 days later.

The champion traveled between Puerto Rico, Maryland, and West Germany while completing three training camps and fulfilling three promotional commitments. Money helped drive the pace. His large entourage, expensive lifestyle, and business obligations required a steady supply of purses.

Ali’s performance against Young showed what the schedule was costing him. He looked slow, poorly conditioned, and frustrated as Young made him miss before leaning through the ropes to escape exchanges.

The judges awarded Ali a unanimous decision, but the scores did not erase the criticism. Young had exposed how much of the champion’s timing and movement had disappeared since his physical peak.

Munich gave Ali an opportunity to look dominant again. Dunn held three respected championships, but his direct, aggressive style offered fewer complications than Young’s movement and defensive tricks.

The promotion struggled before either boxer reached the ring. A dispute involving $225,000 from Ali’s purse and German taxes placed the event in danger only days before the fight.

A late compromise kept the card alive. Ali’s purse was reported at approximately $1.6 million after adjustments, while Dunn received about $100,000, easily the largest payday of his career. Ali also helped cover a shortage in the challenger’s money.

The champion spent another $100,000 purchasing 2,000 tickets for American servicemen stationed near Munich. Even that gesture did not rescue the live gate.

The main event began around 3 a.m. local time to place it on NBC during American primetime. That decision served the television audience but punished German ticket buyers. High prices and the brutal starting hour helped leave thousands of seats unsold.

Roughly 11,000 people were inside the 12,700-seat Olympiahalle, but about 4,000 reportedly attended with complimentary tickets. Estimates placed the promoters’ losses between $300,000 and $500,000. Ali and Dunn received their money. The local backers were left with the bill.

Ali frequently described southpaws as awkward opponents. Karl Mildenberger had given him uncomfortable moments from the left-handed stance during their 1966 championship fight, creating the belief that the alignment itself caused Ali trouble. Dunn demonstrated the limits of that theory. A southpaw stance changes punching angles, but it does not automatically provide timing or defense. Dunn approached Ali upright, followed him instead of cutting off the ring, and often began his attacks with looping punches.

Those wide shots gave Ali time to recognize what was coming. Dunn also advanced without consistent head movement, leaving a direct lane for the champion’s right hand.

A quicker and more deceptive southpaw might have punished Ali’s low left hand and tendency to pull away from punches. Dunn lacked the speed and disguise required to take advantage. His stance altered the angles, but his technical flaws gave Ali the solution.

Ali waited for Dunn to square himself and drove short rights through the opening. The fight showed that his difficulties were not caused by southpaws alone. They came against opponents who knew how to use the stance.

Dunn pressed forward from the opening bell and tried to force a physical contest. His activity kept Ali from treating the bout as an exhibition, but much of his work struck gloves, arms, or empty space.

The challenger’s bravery soon worked against him. He continued marching forward after Ali established his advantages in speed, timing, and power. Instead of changing his approach, Dunn kept presenting the same openings.

Ali was more than 10 pounds lighter than he had been against Young. He remained heavier and less mobile than the dazzling fighter of the 1960s, but the lower weight helped him look sharper.

The champion stayed patient during the early rounds, studied Dunn’s attacks, and gradually began sitting down on his punches. Once he committed to the right hand, Dunn lacked the defensive reactions to protect himself.

Ali dropped him three times in the fourth round. Each knockdown exposed the difference between determination and defensive ability at championship level.

Dunn rose from another knockdown in the fifth, but a short right sent him to the canvas again. Referee Herbert Tomser stopped the fight at 2:05 as Ali theatrically wound up his right arm from a neutral corner.

Ali later credited taekwondo instructor Jhoon Rhee for teaching him the short right used in the finish. Rhee called it the “AccuPunch” and said its quick delivery was based on a technique Bruce Lee had shown him.

The punch was designed to remove the physical warnings that normally precede a power shot. Instead of drawing back the hand or first rotating the shoulder, the boxer sent the fist directly toward the target and brought the rest of the body behind it.

That approach suited the opening against Dunn. The challenger was advancing with his head high and his guard separated. Ali released the right from close range before Dunn recognized the attack.

The exaggerated arm motion came afterward, when Ali knew the contest was finished and began performing for the crowd.

It gave him the 37th knockout of his professional career. Ali never stopped or officially knocked down another opponent.

The Dunn victory was the last time Ali increased the pressure, repeatedly floored an opponent, and ended a fight before the final bell.

His later victories depended more heavily on endurance, clinching, defense, and carefully rationed attacks. Ken Norton forced him through another punishing 15 rounds. Earnie Shavers hurt him badly before Ali rallied in the final round. Leon Spinks outworked him in their first fight and pushed him through 15 more rounds in the rematch.

Ali retained the ability to produce combinations and fight through exhaustion, but he was no longer an offensive finisher. His legs moved less, his punches carried less force, and too many rounds were spent on the ropes while opponents worked.

Dunn became the final opponent Ali was able to erase once he decided to attack.

Ali had little time to recover. Just 33 days after beating Dunn, he faced Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in a mixed rules exhibition at Tokyo’s Nippon Budokan.

Inoki spent much of the 15-round contest on the canvas, repeatedly kicking Ali’s legs while remaining outside punching range. Ali absorbed more than 100 kicks and left with severe swelling, bleeding, an infection, and two blood clots.

Three months later, he defended his championship against Norton at Yankee Stadium and escaped with a disputed decision after another exhausting 15 rounds.

The sequence captured the reckless pace of Ali’s career. He fought Young in April, Dunn in May, Inoki in June, and Norton in September. His body received little opportunity to recover between major events.

Thousands of people lined the streets of Bradford to welcome Dunn home. They honored a working scaffolder who had risen to challenge the most famous boxer in the world.

His championship run ended five months later when Joe Bugner stopped him in the first round. Dunn retired after a 1977 knockout loss to Kallie Knoetze.

The Munich promotion lost money, but the fight gained historical importance. Dunn became the final opponent Ali stopped, permanently linking the Bradford heavyweight to The Greatest.

Ghana News.title: Parrott scores again as Betis beat 10-man Lille
Ghana News.content:
The Republic of Ireland's Troy Parrott scored the winner as Real Betis came from behind to begin their return to Champions League football with an exciting win at Lille.

The former Tottenham man continued his strong run of form since joining Betis last month, having also scored the only goal in victory against Real Madrid on Friday.

Lille dominated the first half, but a strong performance after the restart - and a Lille red card - helped the Spaniards to victory.

Ayase Ueda, a summer arrival from Feyenoord, got his second goal in as many games when he nodded in from close range after a well-weighted delivery from Ethan Mbappe, the brother of Real Madrid star Kylian.

Lille began to assert dominance but Betis soon restored parity when Marc Bartra met a whipped Pablo Fornals cross and sent a diving header past Berke Ozer.

Both sides scored with their first efforts on target and Lille got back in front with their second when Alexsandro nodded in an outswinging Gaetan Perrin corner.

But Bartra levelled once again just three minutes after the restart when his slight headed touch directed an Isco free-kick past Ozer.

The Spanish side then got what would turn out to be the winning goal when Parrott rifled a low effort into the far corner.

Lille's night then rapidly worsened with Mbappe shown a red card after appearing to elbow Natan off the ball.

The French club pushed for an equaliser, bringing on attacking reinforcements including former Arsenal and Chelsea striker Olivier Giroud, but were unable to breach the Betis defence.

Lille travel to Arsenal for their next Champions League game on 13 October (20:00 BST), while Betis host Porto on 14 October at 20:00 BST.

Ghana News.title: Mbappe goes joint-fifth in the list as real Madrid beat Inter Milan
Ghana News.content:
Kylian Mbappe moved joint-fifth in the list of all-time Champions League and European Cup goalscorers as Real Madrid overcame Inter Milan.

The France captain, 27, opened the scoring for Jose Mourinho's side with a clinical 14th-minute finish from just inside the box - his 71st goal in 99 appearances in the competition.

Only Karim Benzema (90), Robert Lewandowski (109), Lionel Messi (129) and Cristiano Ronaldo (140) have scored more.

Three-time Real Madrid Champions League winner Raul scored 71 times in 142 appearances.

It was Real's first attempt on target and their next one brought a second goal in the 23rd minute after a horrible mistake by Inter's Spanish goalkeeper Josep Martinez.

Martinez lost possession after a back pass by Benjamin Pavard, with captain Federico Valverde dispossessing the keeper before tapping over the line.

Martinez made amends at the end of the first half with a double save to keep out Mbappe and Jude Bellingham before the post came to Inter's rescue.

Italian champions Inter had started well with Thibaut Courtois, making his 100th Champions League appearance, keeping out attempts by Hakan Calhanoglu and Lautaro Martinez.

Inter also hit the top of the bar through former Liverpool midfielder Curtis Jones, while they sent on John Stones - a Champions League winner with Manchester City in 2023.

In a game full of chances, Bellingham missed a golden opportunity to make it 3-0 for the record 15-time European champions before Carlos Augusto swept home in the 77th-minute to set up a grandstand finish between Mourinho's current and former clubs.

Despite the win, Real's fans were unhappy with their team's performance and made their feelings known during the game.

Ghana News.title: Police arrest suspects over murder, bank robberies, gold-related attacks
Ghana News.content:
The Police have arrested some suspects in connection with the alleged murder of a missing couple, attempted bank robberies and robbery and murder attacks targeting gold buyers in the Western and Ashanti regions.

The arrests were part of seven major breakthroughs recorded after weeks of coordinated, intelligence-led operations across the country.

Mr Christian Tetteh Yohuno, Inspector-General of Police (IGP), told the media on Monday that special intelligence teams, working with Regional Police Commanders, had conducted operations that led to the arrests and recovery of weapons, ammunition, vehicles and other exhibits.

He said the Police had arrested Abraham Awundok, 32, in connection with the alleged murder of Dr Jesse Amuah and his wife, Mrs Elizabeth Amuah Esi, who were reported missing in April 2026.

Investigations subsequently established that the couple had allegedly been murdered, leading to searches at their residence and other locations they were believed to have visited, with information provided by family members.

Their remains were later recovered and conveyed to the Police Hospital Morgue for preservation and autopsy.

The IGP said investigations established that Awundok, who worked as an errand boy for the couple, allegedly murdered them and took their mobile phones, money and private vehicle before leaving Ghana for the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

He was subsequently declared wanted through an INTERPOL Red Notice and deported from Dubai to Ghana on August 30, 2026, by investigators from the Anti-Armed Robbery Unit and INTERPOL.

The suspect allegedly admitted to the murders during interrogation, the IGP said.

He said the couple’s vehicle had since been recovered, while Awundok remained in Police custody to assist with the investigation.

The IGP said the Police had also foiled an attempted robbery at banks in Labone, Accra, last month, following a swift response by officers from the Office of the Special Operations Assistant to the IGP (SOA).

He said two suspects were shot dead, another escaped, while one was arrested.

The operation followed intelligence received in April 2026 about a suspected robbery syndicate that monitored bank customers, used master keys to open their vehicles and, in some cases, broke into them.

The group was also suspected of planning attacks on banks.

The IGP said the SOA was tasked to mount surveillance on suspected criminal groups operating around banks in the Greater Accra and Tema metropolitan areas.

He said the syndicate had operated around some banks on June 9 and 11, 2026, using a Toyota Highlander and a Hyundai Tucson.

On May 17, the suspects allegedly robbed a woman at Agbamaame in Tema Community Two of GH¢50,000 after she withdrew the money from a bank.

On June 11, the gang allegedly attacked a young man at gunpoint at Achimota after he had withdrawn an unspecified amount from a bank and was travelling home.

On August 13, the surveillance team received information that the gang had been spotted at a bank on the Spintex Road and was heading towards Labone and Cantonments.

The suspects were monitored in a black Hyundai Tucson, registration number GS 7915-19, and an ash-coloured Toyota Highlander, registration number GS 1434-18.

The Police identified the gang leaders as Harrison Chinedu and Dan, who were said to be regularly armed with pistols.

The suspects were later spotted at Labone, strategically positioned between Zenith Bank, GCB Bank and Ecobank, allegedly monitoring the banks in preparation for an attack.

The planned attack was foiled by the Police, resulting in two suspects being shot, one escaping and another being arrested.

A search of the Toyota Highlander led to the recovery of 13 vehicle registration numbers and a Blow F90 pistol.

Investigations allegedly established that the suspects brought vehicles into Ghana and replaced their Nigerian registration plates with Ghanaian ones to facilitate their criminal activities.

Augustine Okechuku Maazi, 49, has since been remanded by the court and remains in lawful custody.

In another operation, the Police dismantled a robbery gang operating in Wassa Akropong, Diaso, Dome, Abofour Camp and the Manso enclave.

The IGP said sustained intelligence-led operations conducted between August and September 4, 2026, resulted in the arrest of five suspects, while another suspect died during the operation.

The operations led to the recovery of three AK-47 assault rifles, five magazines, 357 rounds of AK-47 ammunition and two vehicles.

Those arrested included Clinton Mawuli, 33; Richmond Mensah, alias “Master Abey”; Daniel Sarfo, alias “Abedi”; Prince Duker; and another suspect.

The IGP said Seidu Salifu, 40, who was linked to other robbery incidents at Sakam near Offinso and was standing trial at the Nsuta Circuit Court over the robbery of gold bullion at Offinso Abofour in July 2025, died during the operation.

On August 21, 2026, the Western Regional Police Command also mounted an operation that led to the arrest of five suspects in connection with the robbery and murder of a 40-year-old gold buyer, Seth Kobina, at Agona Fie near Agona Nkwanta.

The suspects were identified as Amponsah; Christopher Seyiri, alias “Cross and Die,” 47; Bashiru Ibrahim, 20; and Thomas Odoom, alias “Wale,” 30, all of whom were arrested in the Agona Nkwanta area.

Another suspect, Isaac Quayeson, alias “Last Burial,” was arrested at Denyira Kwaboso in the Western North Region.

The Police recovered two locally manufactured pistols, five live BB cartridges, a metal bar and two cutlasses from the suspects.

The IGP said special teams had been deployed to the affected areas to strengthen security and ensure that residents could continue their activities without disruption.

Ghana News.title: Pragyia rider gets three months prison term for biting Police Assistant
Ghana News.content:
A 24-year-old tricycle (Pragyia) rider has been jailed for three months by the Nkawie Circuit Court in the Atwima Nwabiagya South Municipality of the Ashanti Region for biting a Community Police Assistant (CPA) at Nkawie.

Abdul Aziz pleaded guilty to the charge of negligently causing harm and was convicted on his own plea.

Police Inspector Kwaku Frimpong, the prosecuting officer, told the court presided over by Mr Robert Addo that the complainants in the case were officers from the Nkawie Divisional Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) of the Ghana Police Service.

He said that on September 03, 2026, at about 8:40am, the complainants, led by Chief Inspector Abedi Larbi, were on official patrol duty to ensure safety in Nkawie town and intercepted the convict, who was driving a Pragya tricycle with registration number M-25-A-3722.

He explained that, after a careful inspection, it was detected that the convict was without a license and other required documents, so Alhassan Seidu, the CPA, was instructed to lead him to the office for the next action.

On their way to the office, the convict took a different direction, so the CPA directed him to take the right route to the police station, but he disobeyed and attacked the CPA, and this led to a struggle between them.

In the process, the convict bit the CPA on the chest, so he shouted for help, and some nearby youth rushed to the scene and helped him arrest the convict.

In his caution statement, he admitted the offence, and after further investigations, he was charged and brought before the court.

Ghana News.title: Palm wine tapper jailed for stabbing farmer
Ghana News.content:
A Tarkwa Circuit Court has sentenced a 50-year-old palm wine tapper to 10 years’ imprisonment with hard labour for repeatedly stabbing a farmer in the back and stomach.

The convict, Obedie Brekpo, was charged with causing harm. He pleaded guilty to the offence and was convicted on his own plea by the presiding judge, Her Honour Bernice Mensima Ackon.

Detective Chief Inspector Bright Nkansah, prosecuting, told the court that the complainant, Paul Dabuo, and Brekpo resided in the same neighbourhood at Cape Town in the Tarkwa-Nsuaem Municipality.

He said on June 30, 2026, at about 0630 hours, Brekpo went to Dabuo’s residence and requested that he transport him on his motorbike to New Atuabo, a suburb of Tarkwa, to collect money owed to him by a customer.

The complainant agreed and accompanied Brekpo to the customer’s residence. However, upon arrival, they realised the customer was still asleep.

Detective Chief Inspector Nkansah said that while both men sat on the motorbike discussing their next course of action, Brekpo suddenly pulled out a jackknife concealed in his clothing and stabbed the complainant several times in the back and stomach.

The prosecutor said Brekpo further bit the complainant twice on the back and, when Dabuo attempted to wrest the knife from him, used the weapon to inflict cuts on his left fingers.

According to the prosecution, after inflicting multiple injuries on the complainant’s back, left ribs, stomach and fingers, Brekpo fled the scene.

Some residents who found Dabuo bleeding profusely rushed him to a hospital for medical treatment.

Detective Chief Inspector Nkansah said the complainant later reported the matter to the Tarkwa Police Station on the same day.

He said police investigations led to Brekpo's arrest on July 7, 2026.

During interrogation, Brekpo admitted committing the offence and told investigators that he did not know what had come over him.

He was subsequently charged with causing harm and arraigned before the court, where he pleaded guilty and was sentenced accordingly.

Ghana News.title: Travel and tour agent remanded over GH¢107,000 recruitment scam
Ghana News.content:
A travel and tour agent has been remanded into lawful custody for allegedly collecting GH¢107,000 from a civil servant and his relatives under the pretext of securing their recruitment into Ghana’s security services.

Clement Osei-Wusu is alleged to have promised to enlist the complainant and his relatives into the Ghana Armed Forces (GAF), Ghana Police Service (GPS), Ghana Immigration Service (GIS), and Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA).

He has been charged with defrauding by false pretences and pleaded not guilty before an Accra Circuit Court.

The court, presided over by Mr Joseph Y. Kunsong, remanded Osei-Wusu to reappear on September 22, 2026.

The prosecution, led by Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) Raymond Ackom, said the accused was a resident of Weija SCC, Accra, while the complainant was a civil servant residing in the Bono Region.

The prosecution said in October 2025, the complainant joined a WhatsApp group, “Limited Job Opportunities”, administered by the accused, where s for recruitment into the security services were posted.

The complainant’s cousin, Gbenyare Yahaya, who was also on the platform, contacted Osei-Wusu for further information and subsequently informed the complainant.

The prosecution said Osei-Wusu demanded GH¢15,000 for recruitment into the GRA and GH¢19,000 for the GAF and other security services.

On October 17, 2025, the complainant and Yahaya reportedly visited the accused’s office at Weija SCC and paid for two slots in the GAF.

During their discussions, Osei-Wusu represented that he also had slots available for recruitment into the GIS and GPS, prosecution said.

It said the complainant subsequently transferred GH¢35,000 into the accused’s Fidelity Bank account on December 24, 2025.

In 2026, the complainant allegedly made additional payments totalling GH¢20,000 through the accused’s Mobile Money wallet and two rural bank accounts for two slots in the GPS.

The prosecution said the accused later demanded an additional GH¢5,000 to facilitate the transfer of the complainant’s son, who was allegedly in the second batch of GAF recruits, to the first batch.

However, after collecting the various sums, the accused allegedly failed to fulfil his promises and blocked the complainant’s means of communication.

The complainant reported the matter to the Police on August 8, 2026, leading to the accused’s arrest.

Osei-Wusu admitted the offence in his caution statement, the prosecution said.

Ghana News.title: Taxi rank executives arrested over alleged attempted murder
Ghana News.content:
The Madina Divisional Police Command has arrested two executives of the Botwe Old Town Taxi Rank for allegedly plotting to murder a woman.

The suspects, Eric Tettey, former chairman of the taxi rank, and Abubakar Altine, the current chairman, are alleged to have contracted two armed men to kill Esther Danquah, a resident of Nanakrom and a susu collector operating at the Botwe Taxi Rank.

A police brief copied to the Ghana News Agency said officers received intelligence about the alleged plot about two weeks ago.

Acting on the information, a team of police officers conducted an operation in the area on September 3, 2026, at about 1930 hours.

The team, led by Deputy Superintendent of Police Maxwell Oppong, Madina Divisional Crime Officer, included Detective Chief Inspector David Kuavoga, Detective Chief Inspector Churchill Odzeyem, Detective Inspector Valeria Adegu, and Detective Lance Corporal Isaac Aboagye.

It said the officers laid an ambush and arrested the suspects while they were allegedly preparing to execute the murder plot against Ms Danquah.

Preliminary investigations indicate that one of the suspects owed the victim money and allegedly sought to avoid repayment.

The two suspects have been detained to assist with investigations.

Police said they would be arraigned after investigations were completed.

Ghana News.title: Galamsey operator who posed as pastor to defile student jailed 15 years
Ghana News.content:
A Tarkwa Circuit Court has sentenced a 20-year-old galamsey operator to 15 years’ imprisonment for defiling a 14-year-old student after posing as a pastor.

The convict, Kelvin Oppong, a resident of Nsuaem in the Western Region, pleaded guilty to the charge of defilement.

Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) Samuel Ahiabor, prosecuting, told the court, presided over by Her Honour Bernice Mensima Ackon, that the complainant was the victim’s stepmother and that both lived at Nsuaem.

He said the victim had completed Junior High School and was awaiting her Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) results to enrol in Senior High School.

ASP Ahiabor said on May 26, 2026, at about 0930 hours, the complainant sent the victim to sell sausage and gizzard in the Nsuaem township to raise money for her education.

According to the prosecution, at about 1100 hours, Oppong approached the victim under the pretext of buying some of the sausage and presented a GH¢100 note.

The victim, however, could not provide change. Oppong then lured her to his house, claiming he would give her money.

ASP Ahiabor said once at the house, Oppong pretended to be a pastor and told the victim he had had a bad dream about her. He prayed for her and gave her a concoction to drink, causing her to fall asleep.

The prosecutor said Oppong subsequently took advantage of the victim and forcibly had sexual intercourse with her on the veranda of his house.

After regaining consciousness, the victim realised she had been sexually assaulted and reported the incident to the complainant.

The matter was subsequently reported to the Nsuaem Police, who issued a medical report form for the victim to undergo examination and treatment.

The prosecution said the victim was taken to the Nsuaem Government Hospital, where she received medical attention. The endorsed medical report confirmed that she had been defiled.

ASP Ahiabor said on May 27, 2026, the complainant, with the assistance of some residents, spotted Oppong in the Nsuaem township, apprehended him and handed him over to the police.

Following investigations, Oppong was charged with defilement and arraigned before the court, where he pleaded guilty and was convicted on his own plea.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
