World.title: A friend’s letter to Abdulmumin at 50, By Ismaeel Ahmed
World.content:
I have also had the privilege of seeing him through both triumph and adversity. His political journey has had its share of difficult seasons, some of them difficult enough to discourage almost anyone. But Chairman has an extraordinary capacity to return. He reflects, recalibrates and rises again. Not because the fall did not hurt, but because he has always believed that a difficult chapter does not have to be the end of the story.

There is a particular privilege in knowing someone before the world decided who they were going to be; before the titles, the cameras, the offices and the public arguments. I have had that privilege with Abdulmumin Jibrin.

I knew Abdulmumin long before most people knew him as they do today; before the National Assembly and before the many chapters of public life that have since defined his name. So, as he turns fifty, I find myself writing not about the Honourable Member for Kiru and Bebeji, but about my friend, my older brother and school father. That distinction has always mattered.

I remember someone whose mind never seemed to rest. Chairman, as we fondly call him, could take an idea everyone else had accepted, turn it around repeatedly, question it from every direction, and continue long after the rest of us had become tired of the conversation. I used to tease him about it, and sometimes I still do. But over the years, I have come to understand that this intellectual restlessness is at the very centre of who he is.

It explains the businessman, the teacher, the politician and the scholar who earned a PhD in International Relations and, years later, returned to Bayero University Kano for another in Economics. Chairman has never believed that learning has an end point. He is always searching for the next question and, inevitably, the better answer.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Yet, for all his accomplishments, what I value most about him is something much simpler: his loyalty. He remembers people. He remembers friendships, kindness and those who stood with him when there was little to gain from doing so. Beneath the forcefulness that people see in public is a tenderness and generosity that those who know him closely understand very well.

I have also had the privilege of seeing him through both triumph and adversity. His political journey has had its share of difficult seasons, some of them difficult enough to discourage almost anyone. But Chairman has an extraordinary capacity to return. He reflects, recalibrates and rises again. Not because the fall did not hurt, but because he has always believed that a difficult chapter does not have to be the end of the story.

Perhaps that is one of the most important lessons of his first fifty years. We are not measured by never falling. We are measured by what we learn from the fall and whether we find the courage to rise again.

He also possesses a rare ability to remain connected to his roots, while engaging confidently with the wider world. Whether in the classroom, the boardroom, the political arena or among friends, he carries with him a strong sense of identity and responsibility. His journey has taken him through different institutions and experiences, but it has not separated him from the people, values and community that shaped him. That balance is not easy to maintain, and it is one of the reasons his story continues to resonate with many people.

Another quality I have come to admire is his ability to create room for other people to grow. He does not merely occupy spaces; he opens conversations, shares ideas and encourages those around him to think beyond their immediate circumstances. Many people have benefited from his advice, introductions, encouragement and willingness to challenge them to become better versions of themselves. That influence may not always be visible, but it is one of the lasting marks a person leaves in the lives of others.

He also possesses a rare ability to remain connected to his roots, while engaging confidently with the wider world. Whether in the classroom, the boardroom, the political arena or among friends, he carries with him a strong sense of identity and responsibility. His journey has taken him through different institutions and experiences, but it has not separated him from the people, values and community that shaped him. That balance is not easy to maintain, and it is one of the reasons his story continues to resonate with many people.

At fifty, therefore, I am less interested in counting Abdulmumin’s offices, businesses, degrees or political accomplishments. I think instead of the full measure of the man I have known: the businessman who understood risk, the scholar who never stopped learning, the politician who survived both victory and defeat, and the friend who still remembers to call.

Fifty is a beautiful milestone. It gives a man enough road behind him to understand the journey, and, God willing, enough road ahead to decide what he wants the rest of that journey to mean.

My Chairman, I hope the years ahead bring a little more patience to your restlessness and a little more peace to your ambition. Build more. Give more. Mentor more. Forgive quickly, as you have always somehow managed to do. And worry less about who receives the credit. History has its own way of separating noise from substance.

Happy fiftieth birthday, Sir. May the years ahead bring you more wisdom than ambition, more peace than pressure, more purpose than applause, and many more opportunities to give than reasons to receive.

Congratulationss.

Ismaeel Ahmed (OON), a lawyer, writes from Kano.

World.title: Why Peter Obi should stop ‘diplomatic approach’, embrace fierce resistance – Lawyer
World.content:
A human rights activist, Inibehe Effiong, has urged the 2027 presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, to stop his cautionary and diplomatic approach to issues and politics to exert his constitutional rights as a Nigerian.

Mr Effiong made the remarks in a post on his verified X handle on Tuesday.

The human rights lawyer was responding to a report that suspected political thugs disrupted Mr Obi’s visit to Benue State on Tuesday after they blocked his convoy from gaining access into the north-central state.

Tuesday’s incident was the second time Mr Obi’s visit to Benue State would be disrupted, following Governor Hyacinth Alia’s earlier stoppage of one of Mr Obi’s proposed visits to an internally displaced persons camp in April 2025, citing security and protocol concerns.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Alia, a Catholic priest, is a member of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) under which he won the state’s governorship election in 2023.

Why he should stop diplomatic approach

Mr Effiong, in the X post, argued that Mr Obi’s political adversaries had continued to undermine his right to freedom of movement and urged the NDC candidate to adopt a more confrontational stance to reverse the trend.

“Peter Obi’s cautionary and endlessly diplomatic approach to issues and politics is not going to deter the Tinubu regime, governors and his political adversaries who are continuously undermining his right to freedom of movement.

“At some point, he has to realise that fierce resistance and confrontation are necessary in certain circumstances to cure madness and end impunity,” he said.

The lawyer further contended that the ruling APC has no plans to ensure free and fair elections in 2027.

“Anyone who believes that the APC is ready for free and fair elections is delusional,” he argued.

World.title: Pitch Awards: Philips backs Tinubu’s reforms as Osimhen, Iwobi, others win top honours
World.content:
President of the Nigeria Pitch Awards, Shina Philips, has backed President Bola Tinubu’s ongoing reforms in Nigerian football, urging stakeholders and the media to support efforts to improve transparency, professionalism, and accountability in the administration of the game.

Mr Philips made the call on Tuesday at the 12th Nigeria Pitch Awards ceremony in Lagos, where Super Eagles stars Victor Osimhen, Alex Iwobi, Calvin Bassey and Stanley Nwabali emerged among the leading award winners.

Osimhen claimed two of the major honours, winning the Rashidi Yekini Award for Best Striker of the Year and the King of the Pitch award.

Iwobi was named Midfielder of the Year, while Bassey won Defender of the Year, and Nwabali received the Goalkeeper of the Year award.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Rasheedat Ajibade was named Queen of the Pitch, while Justine Madugu won Coach of the Year for his work with the Super Falcons. Remo Stars were recognised as Team of the Year.

Philips backs reforms

Speaking at the ceremony, Mr Philips said the awards came at an important time for Nigerian football, with reforms underway within the country’s football administration and regulatory institutions.

He commended President Tinubu for what he described as a bold step and urged stakeholders to support the reform process.

“The ongoing reforms within the relevant regulatory institutions present both opportunities and responsibilities. Reform, by its very nature, demands courage, transparency, accountability, and a willingness to embrace better ways of doing things,” he said.

Mr Philips specifically called on the media, which he described as the “powerful Fourth Estate of the Realm”, to support the presidential initiative.

He said the reforms should strengthen football administration, improve professionalism and transparency, protect stakeholders’ interests and create an environment where talent can flourish.

The Pitch Awards president also stressed the importance of recognising excellence, saying awards can motivate young footballers and acknowledge the contributions of coaches, administrators, referees, journalists and supporters.

He said the organisers had faced financial difficulties in sustaining the annual event amid rising costs of logistics, production, publicity and other requirements.

Despite the challenges, he said, the organisers remained committed to celebrating those contributing to Nigerian football.

Emerging Star category

Mr Philips announced that the Nigeria Pitch Awards will introduce an Emerging Star Award from its next edition.

The category will recognise Nigeria’s most promising football starlet under 18 and is intended to encourage competition and talent development at the grassroots level.

He also announced that voting for the 2026 edition will begin in December, while the 13th award ceremony, scheduled for 2027, will be preceded by a symposium.

The 12th ceremony was originally scheduled for an earlier date but was delayed. Mr Philips clarified that the awards being presented were for the 2025 edition.

Voting process

Mr Philips reaffirmed the credibility of the awards’ voting process, explaining that winners are selected by a College of Voters comprising sports editors from across the country.

He said the voting pattern would be published after the ceremony to allow nominees and voters to see how the votes were recorded.

READ ALSO: Eguavoen named interim Super Falcons coach ahead of Olympic qualifiers

Other winners

Kunle Soname, chairman of Remo Stars, received the Sam Okwaraji Award and also won the Sportsmanship Award.

The Nigeria Police Force and the Niger Delta Development Commission received the Special Achievement in Sports Award.

Lagos State won the award for State with the Best Grassroots Football Development Programme, while the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo was named Football Pitch of the Year.

Akwa Ibom State Governor, Umo Eno, won Football Friendly Governor of the Year, while MTN Nigeria received the Corporate Sponsor of Football Award.

In the journalism categories, Charles Diya of New Telegraph won the Print award, Cecilia Omorogbe of Channels Television won TV, Anthony Bekederemo of Brila 88.9 FM won Radio, and Samuel Ahmadu of Savid News/Nigeriafootball.ng won Online.

Mr Philips expressed appreciation to the National Sports Commission, Nigeria Football Federation, SIAO Partners and the Nigerian media for their support.

World.title: 2027: Security agencies strategise against election violence in Kogi
World.content:
Security agencies and other stakeholders in Kogi State have begun preparations for the 2027 general election, with a focus on preventing violence and other threats that could undermine the electoral process.

The stakeholders met in Lokoja under the Inter-Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) to review emerging security threats and strengthen coordination ahead of the elections.

The Kogi Resident Electoral Commissioner, Shehu Wahab, who spoke at the meeting, said the committee had a responsibility to deploy its experience and resources to ensure voters could exercise their franchise peacefully.

He said the meeting provided an opportunity for security agencies to review security concerns and determine measures required to safeguard the electoral process.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The meeting, which lasted about two hours, was held behind closed doors as members reviewed security concerns and other issues surrounding the 2027 elections.

The Kogi State Commissioner of Police, Naziru Kankarofi, subsequently urged political actors to comply with electoral laws and avoid hate speech, incitement and other actions capable of disrupting public peace.

He also called for responsible political communication and peaceful campaigns ahead of the elections.

Mr Wahab said the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) was putting measures in place to support the work of ICCES and strengthen efforts towards a peaceful and credible election in the state.

He acknowledged that Kogi, like other states in Nigeria, has areas facing security challenges, adding that the security committee was designed to address such concerns through collaboration among relevant agencies.

READ ALSO: Soldier injured as military repels ISWAP attack on military base

The development comes a day after PREMIUM TIMES reported that Governor Ahmed Ododo banned night arrests and urged traditional rulers to work toward peaceful, violence-free elections.

Mr Ododo, while addressing first-class traditional rulers at the Government House in Lokoja on Monday, directed security agencies not to invade homes or make arrests at night.

He also urged the monarchs to discourage political thuggery, intimidation and violence, and to ensure that political campaigns are issue-based rather than driven by religion or ethnicity.

The governor’s directive and the latest security meeting come as Kogi begins early preparations for the 2027 electoral process, with stakeholders stressing the need for security agencies, political actors and communities to work together to prevent violence.
