World.title: Re-elected MPs pledge continued development
World.content:
Re-elected Members of Parliament have pledged to continue driving development in their constituencies, with emphasis on infrastructure, social services and empowerment programmes under the Constituency Development Funds (CDF).

Bwana Mkubwa MP, Warren Mwambazi, says his major priority is to enhance road infrastructure development.

He stated that a Level One Hospital is already functional and awaiting commissioning, while a maternity annex and police station are under construction, pledging to ensure phase two of the projects are complete within the shortest possible time.

He explained that the constituency has embarked on the construction of roads covering 10.4 kilometers, which has faced delays, explaining that this will now be implemented as an immediate project.

“So these are some of the infrastructure developments which we quickly want to run with to ensure that we open up our constituency in terms of road network”, the Bwana Mkubwa law maker noted.

And in a Separate Interview, Chingola West MP, Chipoka Mulenga, stated that continued development will remain his focus, covering infrastructure, health, education, and social amenities.

He acknowledged gaps in facilities, noting that Chingola West lacked a mini hospital, a boarding school and a well-structured secondary school.

He pledged to work towards establishing these, while also addressing youth unemployment through socio-economic empowerment programmes, in line with President Hichilema’s ‘Grow Zambia’ agenda.

Mr Mulenga further indicated that his preoccupation was to identify sustainable and viable economic activities for the people, expressing confidence that resources were available to achieve these goals.

Meanwhile, Chiyenge MP, Favourite Musangu who was elected for the first time identified the Kashikishi-Luchinda road as her priority for completion.

She explained that the contractor was already on site emphasising that the upgrade of the road to bituminous standard will unlock the constituency’s vast natural resources and facilitate cross-border trade with the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Ms Musangu also highlighted youth unemployment as a pressing issue, noting that many were forced to travel outside the district for skills training.

She pledged to establish a training institute within Chienge, to motivate young people, while also empowering women and youths through loans and grants under CDF.

“The other issue which my constituents here experience is the challenge of safe drinking water. The way forward is that people should have access to safe drinking water. We want to have as many water schemes as possible so that people have access to safe drinking water”, she said.

World.title: ‎Nchelenge man jailed for 60 months for possessing crocodile carcass
World.content:
The Nchelenge Magistrate Court has sentenced a 50-year-old man to 60 months imprisonment with hard labour for unlawful possession of a crocodile carcass.

‎John Mukuka of Kapema village in Nchelenge district pleaded guilty to unlawful possession of a protected trophy, contrary to Section 130 of the Wildlife Act No. 14 of 2015 of the laws of Zambia, as read with Statutory Instrument No. 42 of 2016.

‎Particulars of the offence are that on August 28, 2026, in Chienge district, Mukuka was found in possession of a full carcass of a crocodile without lawful authority.

‎The court heard from State Prosecutor, Sinyinda Mbangweta, that on the same day, around 13:00 hours, officers from the Department of National Parks and Wildlife were patrolling in Lusenga National Park when they found Mukuka with the crocodile carcass.

‎

‎Mr Mbangweta said the officers asked Mukuka to produce documents authorising him to possess the protected trophy, but failed to show them the papers.

‎”He was subsequently apprehended and taken to Nchelenge Police Station where he was detained for safe custody, while the crocodile carcass was seized,” he said.

‎He added that the carcass was later examined and confirmed to be that of a crocodile, which is a protected animal.

‎‎When asked if the facts presented by the state were true and correct, Mukuka responded in affirmative.

‎‎Upon Mukuka’s own admission of the facts, Resident Magistrate Luckson Mbewe, convicted the accused accordingly.

‎In mitigation, Mukula pleaded with the court for leniency.

‎Magistrate Mbewe said he took into consideration the fact that Mukuka was a first offender who readily admitted the charge without wasting the court’s time.

However, being found in possession of a government trophy is a very serious offence.

‎”I am sending you to prison for 60 months with hard labour so that others can learn from you,” Magistrate Mbewe said.

World.title: Motorbike rider attacked, robbed in Chipata
World.content:
A 32-year-old motorbike rider was yesterday attacked and robbed of his motorcycle by two unknown men in Katopola area of Chipata district.

The incident occurred around 18:00 hours and was reported at Nabvutika Police Post, under Chipata Central Police Station around 19:30 hours.

Zambia Police Service Eastern Province Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba, identified the victim as Gift Mbao of Mchenga compound.

Mr Mweemba said Mbao was hired by the two suspects to transport them to Katopola area.

He said upon reaching Katopola, one of the passengers instructed Mbao to stop the motorbike before the other one produced a screwdriver and attacked him, inflicting a deep cut near the left ear.

Mr Mweemba explained that the victim became unconscious following the attack and, upon regaining consciousness a few minutes later, he discovered that his blue Savaja motorbike, valued at K28,000, had been stolen.

He said some people who passed near the scene contacted another motorbike rider who transported Mbao to Nabvutika Police Post, where he reported the matter.

Mr Mweemba said the victim was later issued with a police medical report form and is currently admitted to St. Luke’s Mission Hospital, where he is receiving treatment.

He said police have since commenced investigations, while making efforts to apprehend the suspects and recover the stolen motorbike.

World.title: ‎Barbra Banda  nominated again for Ballon D’or ‎
World.content:
Copper Queens and Orlando Pride star Barbra Banda has earned her third consecutive Ballon d’Or nomination, once again putting Zambian football on the global stage.

‎

‎According to the freshly released list, the Zambia captain has been named among the top 30 nominees for the prestigious award.

‎

‎Reacting to the nomination, Banda expressed gratitude.

‎

‎“Happy to get my third nomination for the Ballon d’Or,” Banda said.

‎

‎“It’s an amazing feeling to get this recognition. We keep working hard and thankful to my teammates, coaches, family and my management team for their support and input, it’s a team effort, grateful,” she added.

‎

‎The Ballon d’Or and the votes are organized every year by French magazine France Football.

‎

‎The ceremony is co-organized with UEFA.

‎

‎It rewards the best male and female player in the world, regardless of league or nationality.

‎

‎The reference period covers the entirety of last season, from 3rd August 2025 to 19th July 2026, including international competitions. For women, this includes the Women’s AFCON, which ended on 16th August 2026.

‎

‎The final three nominees will make the podium on 26th October 2026 in London.

‎

‎Banda is joined on the 30-player list by Malawi Women National Team star Temwa Chawinga, marking strong Southern African representation.

‎

‎Banda, who was named 2024 BBC Women Footballer of the Year and CAF Women Footballer of the Year, is among the most recognizable faces in the women’s game.

‎

‎She has graced two Olympics and a FIFA World Cup with the Copper Queens.

World.title: MUZ condemns continued loss of lives in mining accidents
World.content:
The Mineworkers Union of Zambia (MUZ) has condemned the continued loss of lives in the mining accidents.

MUZ is saddened by the continued loss of miners’ lives in mining following the death of 52-year-old miner Mambwe Nicolas in an underground accident at Tongguan Mining Company in Chambishi and four people in an illegal mining accident in Milenge District.

MUZ President Joseph Chewe said in a press statement availed to ZANIS that his Union is deeply saddened and conveys its deepest condolences to the families, colleagues and communities affected by these tragedies.

Mr Chewe said the sustained fatalities recorded in the mining sector this year are a painful reminder that much more needs to be done to protect the lives of people who work in and around mines.

“As a union, we are calling for stronger safety regulations, rigorous enforcement and more frequent inspections across the mining sector. Safety standards must not only exist on paper. Mining companies and operators must be held accountable, while workers must be provided with safe working environments, appropriate protective equipment, adequate training and effective emergency response systems,” said Mr Chewe.

He said MUZ was particularly concerned about the risks faced by workers in underground operations, where rock falls, ventilation failures and other hazards can have fatal consequences.

Mr Chewe called for a thorough investigation into the Tongguan incident, with the findings used to identify safety gaps and ensure that appropriate corrective measures are taken to prevent similar incidents.

The MUZ President pointed out that the deaths in Milenge further highlight the dangers associated with unsafe and unregulated mining activities.

“MUZ supports efforts to formalise artisanal and small-scale mining and urges authorities to strengthen monitoring, education and enforcement to ensure that miners do not resort to hazardous operations that put their lives at risk,” he said.

Mr Chewe emphasised that mining must never become a choice between earning a livelihood and losing one’s life.

He urged Government, regulators, employers and all stakeholders to treat occupational safety as an absolute priority, stressing that Zambia cannot continue to mourn miners who could have been protected through stronger regulations, strict enforcement and a zero-tolerance approach to unsafe mining practices.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

Nigeria Reportedly Agrees to Secret Ceasefire With Boko Haram

Nigeria has reportedly maintained a secret ceasefire with Boko Haram for the past three months, following negotiations that helped secure the release of 360 civilians abducted from Ngoshe village in Borno State. Three sources with contacts within the jihadist group told The New Humanitarian that the truce, which has reportedly stopped attacks around Ngoshe, is likely to be extended by another 40 days. The agreement allegedly involved a ransom payment of $3.7 million. The government has denied making such a payment. The reported ceasefire highlights a possible shift to talks after 17 years of conflict, even as the government publicly rejects negotiations with Boko Haram and continues with efforts to strengthen the military. Analysts caution that the truce may be only a temporary tactical arrangement rather than a path to lasting peace. Negotiations are further complicated by Boko Haram's rivalry with Islamic State West Africa Province, which is not part of the agreement.

Sudan Faces Fresh Scrutiny Over Alleged Chlorine Weapons



Sudan's war is facing renewed scrutiny over allegations that the Sudanese Armed Forces developed and deployed chlorine-based chemical weapons against the Rapid Support Forces during the battle for Khartoum. Investigations by The New York Times and The Washington Post, based on more than 150 leaked intelligence documents, photographs, videos and intercepted communications, reportedly detail an alleged programme that began in 2024, including plans for chlorine-filled warheads, testing operations and efforts to conceal the programme. The records also identify possible sources of chlorine, including a reported shipment that entered Sudan through Egypt and supplies stored at water-treatment facilities. However, there is no evidence that chlorine supplied by UNICEF for civilian water systems was diverted for weapons. Sudan's military has denied producing, stockpiling, or using chemical weapons. The United States previously sanctioned Sudan in 2025 over separate allegations of chemical weapons use. The latest claims are expected to increase pressure for an independent investigation to establish whether the weapons were produced or deployed, who authorised them and how the chlorine was obtained.

Namibia HIV Groups Warn of Impact From U.S. Funding Cuts

Namibia's planned phase-out of United States financial assistance for its HIV response has raised concerns among organisations supporting people living with HIV, despite the country being recognised for reaching key United Nations HIV targets for testing, treatment and viral suppression. The United States plans to provide $45 million for Namibia's HIV response during the 2027/28 financial year as funding shifts from direct financial assistance towards technical cooperation. Victoria Kamule, executive director of the Tonata People Living with HIV Support Network, said the reduction could have a major impact because many treatment, prevention and support programmes have relied heavily on donor funding. Tonata represents about 29,000 people living with HIV across six regions. Kamule warned that support groups and established community programmes could struggle without adequate government funding. More than 220,000 people currently receive antiretroviral treatment through Namibia's public health system. The government says it is committed to maintaining national ownership of the HIV response. Officials are also seeking alternatives to replace about N$730 million in annual HIV funding if an agreement with the United States cannot be reached over health data and specimen-sharing arrangements.

Mozambican Opposition Leader Faces Trial Over Post-Election Unrest

Mozambican opposition politician Venâncio Mondlane is preparing to face trial before the Supreme Court over five charges linked to protests that followed the disputed October 2024 presidential election. Prosecutors accuse him of public advocacy of crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to a crime, instigation to terrorism and incitement to terrorism, allegations he denies. Mondlane, who finished second to ruling party candidate Daniel Chapo, rejected the election result and claimed he had won, triggering months of protests in which more than 300 people were killed. He left the country after the election before returning in January 2025 and later held meetings with Chapo in an attempt to address the political crisis. The case gained further significance after Mondlane joined the Council of State and his immunity was suspended to allow the proceedings to continue. Legal and political observers say the trial could deepen concerns about using the justice system to resolve a fundamentally political dispute and could affect Mondlane's ability to contest the 2029 presidential election.

Close 

Morocco Earthquake Survivors Wait for Aid Three Years On

Three years after a devastating earthquake struck Morocco's Al Haouz region, killing more than 2,900 people and injuring over 5,500, reconstruction has progressed significantly in some communities but left thousands of families still waiting for assistance. In Ighermane village, about 90% of homes have reportedly been rebuilt, with 114 of around 150 families receiving some form of state support. But in nearby Azgour, one of the worst-hit areas, dozens of families are still waiting for reconstruction assistance, while some residents whose homes have been rebuilt elsewhere face problems accessing water and electricity. The High Atlas Development Agency says more than 54,000 homes have been built or rehabilitated and that the government has provided over 7.2 billion dirhams in assistance. However, more than 3,000 families have reportedly complained that they have received no state support, with some excluded because of residency or property-status disputes. Victims and advocacy groups are calling for greater transparency and an independent investigation into how aid has been distributed. Some survivors remain in tents or damaged homes nearly three years after the disaster.

World.title: South Africa: Police Union Demands Better Protection - South African News Briefs - September 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

Police Union Calls for Tougher Action Against Cop Killers

Twelve police officers who died in the line of duty between April 2025 and March 2026 were honoured at a ceremony at the Union Buildings in Pretoria, reports EWN. The number is lower than the 27 officers killed the previous year. The South African Policing Union (SAPU) has said that more must be done to protect police officers. It called for tougher laws and harsher consequences for those who kill members of the police.

Man Due in Court Over Fatal Spring Day Stabbing

A 53-year-old man accused of fatally stabbing 20-year-old Tshepang Nyathi during Spring Day celebrations in Refilwe, Cullinan, is set to appear in the Cullinan Magistrate's Court, reports SABC News. The incident allegedly occurred after young people splashed bystanders with water. The accused said to have retaliated by stabbing Nyathi through the heart. The killing has sparked mixed reactions within the community and fuelled national debate.

Inquest Hears Details of AKA's Call Before Anele Tembe's Fatal Fall

The inquest into the death of Anele Tembe heard that Kiernan "AKA" Forbes made a frantic call to hotel staff shortly before her fatal fall from the Pepperclub Hotel in Cape Town, reports EWN . A staff member testified that Forbes sounded panicked and said someone was on the balcony and wanted to jump, before she heard a scream and a loud bang. The testimony comes as the Forbes family has chosen not to be represented at the inquest. AKA's father, Tony Forbes, has previously indicated that he intends to testify.

World.title: Africa: NITDA, NDPC and Galaxy Backbone Back CyFrica 2026 as Nigeria's Leading Cybersecurity Summit Returns
World.content:
As Nigeria's digital economy accelerates towards an estimated $18.3 billion in 2026, the country is confronting an equally urgent challenge: protecting the digital infrastructure, data and financial ecosystems powering that growth.

With more than 281,500 accounts reportedly breached in the first quarter of 2026 alone, the widening gap between digital opportunity and cyber risk is placing cybersecurity firmly at the centre of Nigeria's economic and national resilience agenda.

Against this backdrop, CyFrica 2026 , Nigeria's premier cybersecurity summit, is set to return on 8 October 2026 at the Eko Convention Center in Lagos, bringing together leading government authorities, regulators, cybersecurity experts, technology innovators and enterprise decision-makers to address the country's most pressing digital security challenges.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The summit will provide a high-level platform for strategic dialogue on cyber resilience, data protection, emerging technologies and public-private collaboration, while exploring practical pathways for strengthening Nigeria's digital defences in an increasingly complex threat environment.

NITDA, NDPC and Galaxy Backbone Join as Supporting Partners

Adding significant institutional weight to this year's summit, the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) and Galaxy Backbone Limited (GBB) have joined CyFrica 2026 as Supporting Partners.

Their participation reinforces the summit's role as a strategic meeting point for Nigeria's cybersecurity and data protection ecosystem, bringing together policymakers, regulators and industry leaders at a critical moment in the nation's digital transformation.

The summit has also attracted major industry participation, with Anomali, TRINEXIA, ThreatLocker Zero Trust Platform, Heirs Technologies and others geared up to showcase their best at the platform. Organised by Tradepass, also regarded as the World's No.1 Events Company , the event will feature a growing roster of prominent organisations from across the cybersecurity, technology, financial services and enterprise sectors.

Senior Leaders to Drive Critical Cybersecurity Dialogue

CyFrica 2026 will place substantive industry dialogue at the heart of its agenda, with senior government officials and leading practitioners addressing issues ranging from cyber resilience and AI-enabled threats to regulatory compliance and data protection.

Among the distinguished speakers confirmed to take the stage are:

Dr. Ayodele Bakare, Assistant Director – Cybersecurity, National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA)

Dr. Vincent O. Olatunji, National Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer, Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)

Abdul-Hakeem Ajijola, Chairperson, African Union Cyber Security Expert Group (AUCSEG)

Dr. Muktar Bello, Head, Quality Control and Assurance Unit, Forensics & Crime Laboratory Services Department, Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC)

Folorunso Aliu, Group Chief Information Officer, Dangote

Obiora Awogu, Chief Information Security Officer, MTN MoMoPSB

Through keynote addresses, panel discussions and fireside conversations, speakers will examine how organisations can strengthen their cyber defenses while navigating an increasingly sophisticated threat landscape and evolving regulatory environment.

World.title: Ghana: Supreme Court Controversy - Bishops Call for Greater Caution, Not Resignation
World.content:
Accra — The Chief Justice of Ghana, Paul Baffoe-Bonnie, should exercise greater caution when making public statements, but there are no grounds to call for his resignation. This, in essence, is the position of the Ghana Catholic Bishops' Conference regarding the controversy sparked by remarks made by Baffoe-Bonnie on September 2, 2026, during working visits to the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT) and the Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF).

The Chief Justice made a critical reference to the "last eight years" which, in Ghana's political context, could reasonably be interpreted as a comparison between the current administration and the previous one. What might have been intended as an assessment of institutional performance therefore appeared, at least on the surface, to take on the character of a biased judgment, prompting strong criticism from the opposition.

In a statement signed on September 6 by its President, Msgr. Matthew Kwasi Gyamfi, Bishop of Sunyani, the Ghana Catholic Bishops' Conference stressed that "the independence of the judiciary is not only a matter of actual impartiality; it also depends on the visible and unmistakable appearance of impartiality. A judge, and especially the head of the judiciary, must be, and must be seen to be, above partisan political struggles."

"The Chief Justice, like any citizen, is entitled to his own convictions," the Bishops said. "The question is not whether he may hold them, but whether his public conduct in office should ever create room for reasonable doubt about where he stands."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Bishops nevertheless believe that "calls for his resignation on this basis alone strike us as disproportionate to the offense," adding that "the same standard of restraint must be asked of every public office holder, regardless of who occupies it or which party is in government."

"We continue to hold the Judiciary, and all who serve the nation in public office, in our prayers, and we pray that God may grant our leaders the wisdom to serve truth, justice, and the unity of our common home," the Bishops concluded.

World.title: Cold case takes grim turn after remains identified as runaway teen; homicide investigation underway
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Authorities announced a major breakthrough in a decades-old cold case, identifying human remains found nearly 49 years ago in North Carolina as belonging to a runaway 15-year-old girl who disappeared from Maryland.

The skeletal remains were discovered more than six months after Cindy Marcell Blizzard went missing in the spring of 1977, according to the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation (SBI).

Authorities said the manner of death remained undetermined, but the case was being investigated as a homicide. They said the remains were found in a wooded area near a Wilson County manufacturing facility roughly five hours south of Blizzard's home.

The "circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the probability of foul play, and the investigators are treating the case as a homicide," the SBI said.

TEEN FOUND IN SHALLOW CALIFORNIA VINEYARD GRAVE IDENTIFIED NEARLY 50 YEARS LATER AS FAMILY WARNS KILLER

According to officials, skeletal remains and clothing were found Dec. 29, 1977, near a Firestone plant that produces vehicle tires.

A medical examiner determined the remains had likely been there for six months to two years and belonged to a white female between 16 and 23 years old.

In the decades that followed, the case went cold as forensic technology was not advanced enough to identify the remains, authorities said.

"For years, investigators compared dental records against missing persons cases without finding a match," the SBI said.

GIRL KNOWN AS 'CHELSEA JANE DOE' ID'D 26 YEARS AFTER MUTILATED BODY FOUND HUNDREDS OF MILES FROM HOME STATE

The case was reopened in 2010 by a state anthropologist, who submitted the remains for DNA testing and cross-referenced the results with federal databases, officials said.

However, the investigation did not gain momentum until 2024, when the SBI’s Cold Case Investigative Team reviewed the case again using forensic tools that did not exist in 1977.

WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT

When the case qualified for advanced DNA testing, forensic scientists extracted preserved genetic material from a bone sample, according to the authorities.

"A genealogy service used the profile to trace potential relatives, pointing investigators toward a 15-year-old girl who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977," the SBI said.

The identification was made with assistance from the FBI’s NCIC Investigation and Operational Assistance Group, the Maryland Department of State Police Homicide Unit and the Raleigh Police Department’s Intel Unit, authorities said.

World.title: Establishment Dem defeats socialist challenger in crucial battleground Senate primary

Rep. Chris Pappas on Tuesday won the Democratic Senate nomination in swing state New Hampshire, in a key race that is a must-hold for the Democrats in the midterm elections.

Pappas defeated socialist rival and first-time candidate Karishma Manzur, the Associated Press reports, in the showdown to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the first woman in the nation's history elected governor and senator.

Republicans haven't won a Senate election in New Hampshire in 16 years, but they view the open Democrat-held seat as a top flip opportunity in the fight to hold their slim majority in the midterms.

The race between Pappas and Manzur was one of the final fights in a six-month primary season that saw the far-left score a slew of high-profile victories over centrists in what's been framed as a battle for the Democrats' ideological future.

"All he wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C. Go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is," she charged in a Fox News Digital interview.

The first-time candidate, scientist with a Ph.D. in biochemistry, and nonprofit leader who is a member of a local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) group, pushed for universal health care, raising the minimum wage to at least $20 per hour, abolishing ICE, and ending all military aid to Israel for what she argues is the Israeli government's "genocide" against the Palestinian people in their war against Hamas in Gaza.

Manzur argued that Pappas, who has been supported over the years by the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC, is a "genocide enabler."

"Chris Pappas has had his turn and has not been able to serve this state honorably. He hasn't done a good job in serving his corporate donors, his AIPAC foreign-aligned lobbies," she claimed.

Pappas, in an interview with Fox News Digital, said, "Israel's a historic ally of the United States, the only democracy in the region. And you can say that while you have vehement disagreements with the Netanyahu government as I've expressed."

And referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Pappas said, "I think Netanyahu's being incredibly reckless right now. He faces voters in a matter of weeks and could lose his election. And I think that would be important to set a new tone for the U.S.-Israel relationship."

Pappas, who was the frontrunner for his party's nomination ever since Shaheen announced early last year that she wouldn't seek re-election, enjoys strong establishment and union backing. And for over a year, as he runs for the Senate, Pappas also takes aim at what he calls a political system "rigged for billionaires."

Regardless, Manzur charged that Pappas took a page from her playbook.

"It's really embarrassing and insulting to the people of New Hampshire. He's been there for eight years. He has not provided any of that sort of populist messages, and now he's realizing, wait, he's dropping in the polls, and now he has to catch up," Manzur charged. "That's another one of those deceptions that... Chris Pappas always engages in."

Pappas defended his record, noting "I've been fighting to change Washington to get big money out of our political system since I got elected to Congress in 2018."

Pappas will face off in the general election against either former Sen. John E. Sununu or former Sen. Scott Brown.

World.title: Conflicting court rulings leave Missouri’s congressional map in limbo
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A fast-moving fight over whether Missouri Republicans can use a redrawn congressional map for this fall’s midterm elections was cast into chaos on Tuesday with two different courts issuing conflicting rulings.

In one, the U.S. Supreme Court, in an order issued by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling from last week that said the map could not be used while a ballot initiative that could lead to voters rejecting the newly drawn district lines moves forward. Kavanaugh handles emergency requests that arise from Missouri.

But soon after, a federal judge in Missouri ruled in favor of two GOP congressional candidates who argue that the new map, which was in place for the August primaries, must be used in November in order to avoid federal constitutional violations. That case could also quickly face U.S. Supreme Court scrutiny with time running out for the map to be finalized. The state’s deadline to finalize ballots was 5 p.m local time, and first ballots are set to go out Sept. 19.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, both Republicans, said on X Tuesday evening that the redrawn map would be used for the November election.

The two cases raise different legal issues, with the Missouri Supreme Court focused only on state law while the federal case raises questions under the U.S. Constitution.

The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave prompted by President Donald Trump, was designed to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

If the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remains in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election.

The new lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters.

The legal clash erupted after the 2025 redistricting plan was enacted.

A group called People Not Politicians Missouri, led by Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters.

The Missouri Supreme Court found that Hoskins should not have rejected the plan, unanimously concluding there is nothing in state law that says redistricting plans are exempt from the referendum process.

The referendum petition was “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found.

Under state law, whenever a proposed ballot initiative that overrides the Legislature is deemed valid, the law is automatically put on hold until after the people vote on it.

The court also said any confusion caused by its ruling was a result of Hoskins’ delay in deciding whether the referendum could move forward. Hoskins waited until the last minute to reject the proposal ahead of an Aug. 4 deadline and broke with the state’s typical process of putting a law facing a veto referendum on hold when enough signatures are submitted.

In the separate federal case, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, ruled that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary. Using the old map would violate the rights of candidates under the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and the provision of the Constitution that outlines how members of the House are elected, he found.

Hoskins argued at the Supreme Court that the state court ruling violated the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause, which he said delegates significant powers to state legislatures in overseeing elections. The Supreme Court rejected a similar argument in a redistricting case from North Carolina in 2023.

Hoskins’ lawyers told the justices that the state court ruling had created chaos because the new map was used in this year’s primary election. If the state has to revert to the old map, “hundreds of thousands of Missourians will see their votes in the primary election rendered pointless,” they wrote.

Lawyers for the referendum supporters said in court filings that Hoskins was seeking at the Supreme Court a “political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution.”

In May, the Supreme Court rejected a similar attempt by Democrats in Virginia who sought to revive their own congressional map that had been approved by voters. The Virginia Supreme Court had found legal flaws in the process that led to the referendum.

World.title: Trump escalates trade war with Canada, moving to ban the import of some autos, dairy and alcohol
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday moved to sharply escalate the trade war with Canada, seeking to block the import of some autos, dairy products and alcohol.

In a call with reporters, senior Trump administration officials said that the move was in direct response to Canada’s latest retaliatory tariffs. Those duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday.

The ban on the importation of Canadian alcohol in particular closely mirrors bans that provinces across Canada put in place in early 2025 on American alcohol. Those were imposed after Trump introduced sweeping duties on America’s longtime northern ally.

The measures announced Tuesday were signed into law under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, documents posted to the White House show. That trade law was never used until Trump implemented new tariffs on Canada under the statute in late August.

Other products banned from import include Canadian motorcycles.

A senior Trump administration official, speaking on the call with reporters, said the White House also completed “housekeeping” on tariffs already in place. Tariffs on cement, road salt and hospital pads were removed and replaced with duties on all-terrain vehicles, some cheeses and motor boats.

The import bans will go into effect in about three weeks — Sept. 29.

On Tuesday’s call, a White House official also said Trump’s plan for 50% duties on cars and trucks remains on the table. The president recently threatened to impose those on January 1.

Tuesday’s announcement comes as the U.S.-Canadian relationship severely deteriorates. For nearly a year, U.S. officials have taken issue with Canada’s retaliatory tariffs.

“I’ve got two countries in the world that have retaliated against the United States for trade measures: the People’s Republic of China and Canada,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in August. “That’s not the kind of company you really want to be running in.”

Days later, Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled the plug on negotiations with the U.S., citing “uneconomic” and “unfair” demands from American officials at the last minute. Trump administration officials have disputed that.

After the collapse of those negotiations, Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” Canadian officials have said they will ignore Trump’s renaming.

“We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period,” Canada’s Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly said on August 27. “While all these shenanigans are happening, we’ll just be smart, and we’ll be strategic, and we’ll fight back.”

On Monday, Trump ratcheted up pressure on Canada once again, threatening Canadian jet maker Bombardier. Trump, on Truth Social, wrote that the company should no longer be able to sell its products in the U.S.

Bombardier quickly pointed out that it supports thousands of U.S. jobs throughout its supply chain. White House officials said Tuesday night that Trump was still reviewing options with how to implement that idea.

Monday was also when Canada’s latest swath of retaliatory duties took effect, hitting hundreds of products, including steel, dairy, household appliances, farm equipment, paper, and electronics with duties of between 15% and 50%.

For Carney, Canada will not be returning to the negotiating table any time soon.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said last week.

Since Carney terminated trade talks on Aug. 21, top officials such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have mocked Canada and its economy. Trump has also posted numerous AI memes on social media about Canada, and the White House’s official X account posted an image of a bald eagle stepping on what appears to be a Canadian goose.

On Sunday, Bessent likened Canada to “a little yippy dog” in an interview with Fox News Channel.

Carney remained steadfast Tuesday, even as he said that the Trump administration was trying to “break” Canada with tariffs.

“With a resilient economy and the strongest fiscal position in the G-7, we have everything we need to pivot and prosper,” Carney said in a YouTube video.

Carney’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Tuesday’s actions.

As trade talks with Canada remain on ice, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is set to travel to Mexico on Wednesday, according to Mexico’s trade minister. In a post on X, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Lutnick would meet with Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum to discuss the two countries’ trading relationship.

World.title: U.S. strikes five Iranian tankers after attempted attacks on Navy warship, CENTCOM says
World.content:
The U.S. military struck five Iranian tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in response to attempted attacks by the IRGC on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

“CENTCOM forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days,” U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. “The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed.”

Four of the tankers were attacked in the Gulf of Oman and one was hit near Kharg Island, according to CENTCOM.

“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM said in a statement.

A U.S. strike hit an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil terminal, which has been repeatedly threatened by President Donald Trump, according to the semiofficial Tasnim news agency. The U.S. military hit a second tanker near the port city of Jask, according to Iranian state TV.

Two American warships were attacked and damaged by ballistic missiles, the IRGC said in a statement, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

The IRGC also said in a statement Tuesday that they had retaliated by launching missiles at American forces on the Al Azraq military base in Jordan, according to the semi-official Fars news agency.

Jordanian air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles and two missiles fell in unpopulated areas, the spokesperson for the Jordanian armed forces said Tuesday, according to Jordanian state media.

The strikes on the Iranian tankers Tuesday come after the IRGC attempted to hit an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer over the weekend, resulting in a U.S. response in which the U.S. sank one tanker and permanently disabled two more.

Iran also threatened to target oil tankers in Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for the U.S. strikes on Tuesday.

“Following the actions of the American military in targeting several Iranian oil tankers, we warn all oil tanker crews in the areas around the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which are hosting these forces and are complicit in their actions, to immediately evacuate their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement posted by the semi-official Fars news agency.

The Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war, has become the key battleground in the conflict as both the U.S. and Iran have attacked tankers.

The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

World.title: Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas win New Hampshire Senate primaries, setting up battleground race
World.content:
The battleground New Hampshire Senate race is set between Republican former Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, NBC News projects, after both prevailed in their primaries Tuesday night.

Pappas defeated scientist Karishma Manzur, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, in his primary, leading 62%-36% with about one-fifth of the vote counted. But it appears he could fall short of the support from primary voters that the Pappas campaign touted in recent internal polling.

Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., talks with voters in Warner last month. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images file

The race could be key to the fight for the Senate majority in November. Republicans are confident that Sununu, a member of a well-known political family, can put the race in play. But Democrats dismiss GOP optimism in a state that President Donald Trump has never won.

Trump endorsed Sununu in the primary against former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown, who also served as an ambassador during Trump’s first term. Sununu had 70% support to Brown’s 25% with about a sixth of the vote counted.

First elected to the House in 2018, Pappas has long been viewed as the frontrunner in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. And Pappas had already started to focus on the likely general election contest against Sununu, launching an attack against Sununu in mid-August.

“In Congress, Sununu gave huge tax breaks to pharma companies and sided with the insurance industry, and then he went to work for them and made $35 million,” Pappas said in the ad. “In Washington, I’m taking on this kind of corruption, refusing corporate PAC money and fighting to lower costs.”

Republicans, meanwhile, have already begun to attack Pappas. One Nation, the non-profit arm of the GOP super PAC Senate leadership fund, launched an ad knocking Pappas on taxes. The spot alleges the congressman “gave out tax breaks to New Yorkers for their million dollar homes” when he supported a sweeping climate and social safety net measure in 2021.

Trump’s approval rating is down and voters are raising concerns about the economy and the Iran war as the midterms approach. But Republicans are still optimistic with Sununu on the ballot in New Hampshire.

Sununu’s father and brother both served as governors of the state, and Sununu himself represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 through 2008 after serving in the House.

He lost his bid for re-election in 2008 to Shaheen, who then served three terms before retiring this year.

Republicans believe they could have an opening with independent voters in the state who are averse to higher taxes, and they have GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte on the ticket as she runs for a second two-year term. Ayotte is the last Republican to win a Senate race in New Hampshire, winning her first term in 2010 before losing re-election in 2016.

But Democrats dismiss Republicans’ optimism about New Hampshire.

Lauren French, a spokesperson for the Democratic super PAC Senate Majority PAC, acknowledged in a recent interview the New Hampshire race would be competitive, but said Democrats were confident they would prevail.

“New Hampshire feels like wish casting in a lot of ways,” French said of Republican optimism about the state. “We continue to put states that they didn’t even think were going to be competitive on the board, so they need to continue to assure donors, right, that they are also doing the same.”

World.title: Lindsay Clancy juror speaks after mistrial: "There was so much doubt"
World.content:
A woman who served as a juror in Lindsay Clancy's high-profile Massachusetts murder trial provided a look at deliberations, saying there was too much doubt for her to reach a guilty verdict.

Clancy's murder trial ended in a mistrial on Friday due to a hung jury. According to a note sent to the judge by the foreperson, there was an 11-1 split among jurors.

A woman who was juror No. 5 spoke to WBZ-TV's Kristina Rex, though she asked to remain anonymous.

"At the end of the day, there was so much doubt," the woman said. "The prosecution didn't have a figurative smoking gun. There was not a single moment throughout the presentation of that case where you could say 'Yup, 100% I'm certain she did it' or that she didn't do it. There was too much gray area."

Lindsay Clancy juror interview

The juror said that from the start of deliberations, the majority of the room was trying to sway the lone holdout.

"The majority of people, it doesn't matter what side they were on, were very firm in their stance and their belief from the beginning," she said. "The stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side. So, I'm going to kind of defend that individual in a sense. There were some big personalities in that room. But at the end of the day, it just came down to an inability to move past your convictions."

The juror who spoke to WBZ-TV said at first, she believed Clancy should be found guilty and was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children.

"And maybe I still believe that in a certain way. I think that this is a woman who was not mentally healthy. She was someone who was in the throes of a significant mental health crisis," the juror said. "I really just felt like she was so deep in it that she couldn't see her way out."

Juror will "never be the same" after hearing 911 call

Clancy's attorney attempted to have the holdout juror thrown off the jury because he argued they were refusing to apply the instruction of the law to reasonable doubt.

"At the end of the day, to not follow that reasonable doubt and to acknowledge that it's there, you morally and legally cannot convict somebody for that. And that was therefore a violation of her constitutional rights," the juror said. "Essentially, that is what we were there as a jury to do is to uphold that Constitution and give someone a fair trial of their peers. And I don't necessarily think she was getting that with that juror. It's not simply because of the fact that he had an opposing view or this person felt like she was guilty. It was the inability to back that up with any logic."

When it came to sitting on such a high-profile case, juror No. 5 said there were moments of devastating testimony. Particularly, she said hearing the 911 call from Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's now ex-husband, was something she will never forget. The call was played in the courtroom, but not broadcast during the trial.

"I will never be the same after that 911 call," she said. "After the trial, I saw all the conspiracy theories about how Patrick did it and that he somehow convinced Lindsay that she had done it when it was really him. All I could think was that if these people could have heard that visceral, blood-curdling scream, I don't think I could name a single actor or actress that could have performed that the way he did, and not that he performed it, but I will never be the same after that. It was horrifying. Just to imagine living through that and being the person to find your children in that scenario, it shakes you."

Prosecutors have not yet said if they will retry the case a second time after the mistrial.

World.title: Trump administration to ban some Canadian motorcycles, dairy, alcohol
World.content:
The Trump administration moved Tuesday to ban imports of Canadian motorcycles, some dairy products and most types of alcohol starting later this month, intensifying the trade war between the two countries.

The bans were announced less than 24 hours after Canada imposed steep tariffs on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods — a measure that was issued after the U.S. slapped tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods. The Trump administration has accused Canada of unfair trade practices, but Canadian officials have accused the U.S. of making unreasonable demands.

Senior administration officials told reporters Tuesday night there will be an outright ban on a majority of Canadian alcohol coming into the U.S. starting at 12:01 a.m. on Sept. 29. Bans on Canadian motorcycles, whey, molasses and nonalcoholic beer are set to take effect on the same day, according to a set of proclamations signed by President Trump.

The administration will also slap an additional 50% tariff on cheese products, steel, aluminum and bamboo furniture from Canada starting next Tuesday. Some existing tariffs on toilet paper, cement and fishing rod parts were terminated after more government research on the tariff impact, according to a senior administration official.

In Tuesday's trade actions, the White House alleged Canadian officials "ceased negotiating in good faith" and "did not remove" trade barriers during last-minute negotiations to avert a set of tariffs threatened by Mr. Trump last month. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and his administration have vowed to match the U.S.'s tariffs "dollar for dollar," and many Canadian provinces have maintained boycotts of American alcohol that began last month.

Despite the deepening economic fallout between the two close trading partners and allies, the White House insists that conversations with Canadian trade leadership are ongoing and there remains hope for an off-ramp.

A senior administration official said Canada has expressed interest in finding an "alternative pathway" and the U.S. remains open to negotiation.

Still, Mr. Trump is not backing down from a 50% tariff on all Canadian automotive imports, trucks, auto parts, and steel, effective Jan. 1, 2027, if a deal is not reached, according to administration officials.

The president said Tuesday he would ban Canadian-made products from federal government contracts unless the Canadian government opens up to U.S. imports. He also threatened to ban the sale of Bombardier, a Canadian airplane maker, in a post Monday on his social media platform Truth Social.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren't good enough!" Mr. Trump wrote, adding they must build in the United States.

Bombardier says the company employs thousands of Americans across nine major facilities. Republican Sens. Roger Marshall and Jerry Moran of Kansas publicly defended the Montreal-based company, saying it creates thousands of jobs in their state.

"I'm going to fight to keep Bombardier's over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I've already taken that concern inside the Oval Office," Marshall wrote on X.

World.title: New Hampshire Senate race set between Pappas and Sununu after projected primary wins
World.content:
Washington — Former GOP Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will face off in November after winning their primaries for U.S. Senate on Tuesday night, CBS News projects.

Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's decision not to seek reelection kickstarted the competitive race for an open seat in the Granite State, which could be key to determining which party controls the Senate. As her successor, Shaheen endorsed Pappas, who is one of the state's two representatives in the House. But Pappas faces a formidable opponent in a Republican with widespread name recognition in the state, hailing from a political family that's spent decades in its leadership.

Sununu, 61, represented New Hampshire in the House and Senate for more than a decade, before he was ousted by Shaheen. The son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu, his name carries significant weight in New Hampshire. In the GOP primary on Tuesday, he defeated former Sen. Scott Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate from 2010 to 2013.

Pappas, 46, has represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019, where he's a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. On the campaign trail, he's billed himself as an independent voice for New Hampshire. And he defeated a progressive candidate, medical scientist Karishma Manzur on Tuesday, despite a number of victories by insurgent Democrats elsewhere in the country this cycle.

Although Republicans have controlled New Hampshire's governor's mansion since 2017, the state hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2010, and a Republican hasn't won in the state at the presidential level since 2000. But Pappas has acknowledged that the race is "highly competitive," telling CNN last month that "it will continue to be tight until the very end."

With 53 Republicans in the Senate, Democrats would need to flip four seats to gain control of the upper chamber, while defending a handful of seats, like in New Hampshire.

World.title: Federal judge backs Missouri's new House map after Supreme Court rebuffs case
World.content:
A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Missouri should use a new congressional map that favors Republicans for now, hours after the U.S. Supreme Court left in place a ruling from the state's highest court directing Missouri to use an older map.

The Supreme Court rebuffed an appeal from Missouri officials who wanted to use new congressional districts backed by President Trump in the November election, marking a defeat for Republicans who had hoped the new map could help them hold on to their slim House majority. The justices let stand a decision by Missouri's top court, which said the new districts cannot be used in the November elections because they were superseded by a citizen petition demanding a statewide vote.

But shortly after, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate challenge to Missouri's Supreme Court decision, writing that the plaintiffs faced "irreparable harm" otherwise because "many Missouri voters would have to cast their general-election votes for candidates whom they had no role in nominating."

The decision adds further confusion about which boundaries will be used in November.

The new House maps, passed by the state legislature last year, would dramatically redraw longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-area district, making it GOP-leaning.

Missouri's new districts were used in the August primaries. But the Missouri Supreme Court ruled last week that the state must revert to districts adopted after the last census.

Republican state Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, who appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, had argued it would violate federal rights to switch districts for voters between the primary and general elections. She also said it would cause confusion.

"A federal-election-administration disaster is unfolding in Missouri," Hanaway wrote in an emergency application for the U.S. Supreme Court to put the ruling on hold, warning it could lead to "unprecedented chaos" and render the primary "utterly pointless."

She continued: "Looking forwards, the State is genuinely unsure whether it can switch its governing congressional map in time to run a timely federal election."

Richard Von Glahn, who sued over the new maps, urged the U.S. Supreme Court not to intervene, writing that the state "waited as long as possible to manufacture the present dispute over Missouri's congressional districting map" by not moving to reject the petition for a referendum until last month.

Hanaway's request for the U.S. Supreme Court to step in was rejected by Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday.

Missouri currently is represented in the House by six Republicans and two Democrats who were elected under districts that Republican state officials approved in 2022.

But at Mr. Trump's urging, Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe called the Legislature into a special session last year to redraw congressional boundaries to their advantage ahead of the midterms.

The revised map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Cleaver. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver's district far eastward into rural Republican areas.

Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. State Sen. Rick Brattin won the Republican primary in the reshaped district.

On the same day as the primary, Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected a petition with thousands of signatures seeking to force a November referendum on the map. Hoskins asserted that Missouri's Constitution doesn't allow a referendum on congressional redistricting. A lower court agreed, but the state Supreme Court reversed Hoskins' decision.

The state's top court said the new districts were retroactively frozen in December, when the petition signatures were submitted, and thus never became law. Hoskins on Tuesday assigned the redistricting referendum as Proposition A on the November ballot, in compliance with the state court order.

The Missouri Constitution does not specifically say that a referendum can be used for congressional redistricting. But the state Supreme Court said a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on "any act" of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting legislation.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to respond to Mr. Trump's call last year to redraw congressional districts. Several other states followed. All told, Republicans had hoped to win as many as 16 additional seats from new House maps enacted in eight states — Texas, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Florida, Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama.

Democrats, whose counterattack faced several setbacks, think they could win up to six additional seats from new districts in California and Utah.

It remains to be seen whether the redistricting works as intended for Republicans. The president's party historically has lost congressional seats in the midterms, and Mr. Trump's poor approval ratings could provide an extra hurdle for Republican candidates.

World.content: Supreme Court rebuffs Missouri's request for new House map favoring Republicans The Supreme Court on Tuesday denied an emergency application to block a Missouri Supreme Court ruling barring the state from using its new congressional map, which favors Republicans.
