World.title: Sydney's busiest emergency departments revealed in new health data
World.content:
South Western Sydney Local Health District is doing the heavy lifting across the city's hospitals in a range of categories, new public health data reveals.

The latest Healthcare Quarterly data from April to June 2026, released by the Bureau of Health Information (BHI), paints a picture of NSW's health system.

Overall for NSW, more elective surgery procedures were performed on time and more emergency department patients were treated on time compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

But demand across the state's hospitals remained ever-present.

The median time from arrival to leaving the emergency department for all NSW patients was 3 hours and 49 minutes, up 5 minutes compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

Sydney's busiest emergency departments

Royal North Shore Hospital had high attendance numbers. (ABC News: Heath McPherson)

The data captured emergency department attendance.

In Sydney's north, Royal North Shore Hospital had 22,805 attendances, Hornsby Ku-ring-gai Hospital had 13,153 attendances and Ryde Hospital was the lowest at 6,954.

Northern Beaches Hospital recorded 16,009 attendances, but this hospital only transitioned into the public system from April 29, so any results prior to this date cover publicly contracted services only.

Northern Beaches Hospital was also considerably busy. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

In the south-west, Liverpool Hospital had the greatest attendances at 23,773, followed closely by Campbelltown Hospital at 23,664.

The lowest rates in this local health district were Camden Hospital (3,014) and Fairfield Hospital (9,099).

Other particularly busy Sydney hospitals included St George Hospital at 21,038 attendances, and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital at 20,832.

What the data shows is the high demand faced by the South Western Sydney Local Health District, which covers an area of 6,243 square kilometres from Bankstown to Bowral.

Treatment times at Sydney hospitals

As for the percentage of patients starting treatments on time at Sydney hospital emergency departments between April to June 2026, the data showed major improvement in one key local health district.

At Liverpool Hospital, 77.5 per cent of patients started treatment on time, a 7.8 per cent increase compared to the previous year's reporting period.

The data showed treatment time improvement at Liverpool Hospital. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Campbelltown Hospital saw one of the biggest improvements, from 53.8 per cent between April to June 2025, to 68.2 per cent in this year's period.

Camden Hospital recorded 84.1 per cent for the 2026 reporting period, Ryde Hospital had 83.5 per cent and Royal North Shore Hospital was 74.6 per cent.

As for the lesser performing hospitals in this category, Fairfield Hospital stood at 49 per cent, and Prince of Wales Hospital was 52.6 per cent.

Blacktown Hospital was also one of the lower rates at 49 per cent, though it was a 9.3 per cent improvement from the previous year's period.

Health Minister Ryan Park acknowledged there was "still a lot to do in our emergency departments".

When asked on 702 ABC Sydney about one caller's experience of waiting 20 hours at Westmead Hospital, Mr Park said it was "not good enough".

"But one of the challenges is … there has been a massive increase and nearly doubling of the patients that are categorised two and three," Mr Park said in reference to the past 15 years in NSW.

Category two refers to emergency cases, and category three refers to urgent cases.

"They're the sickest patients in the system. They need to spend more time in an emergency department," he said.

Episodes of mental health care at Sydney hospitals

Royal Prince Alfred Hospital saw a high number of mental health care cases. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Patients admitted for mental health episodes of care at Sydney hospitals were also recorded.

The inner west saw great demand, with Royal Prince Alfred Hospital having one of the highest rates at 690 episodes, along with Concord Hospital at 529.

The city's south-west also did heavy lifting at Campbelltown Hospital (532), Liverpool Hospital (382) and Nepean Hospital (345).

Elective surgeries at Sydney hospitals

Across NSW in the reporting period, 85.6 per cent of elective surgeries were performed on time, not including the Hunter New England Local Health District, as centralised data from this district was not available for the report.

There were 697 NSW patients on the waiting list that had waited longer than clinically recommended.

As for Sydney specifically, only a few hospitals recorded considerable rates of patients waiting longer than recommended for surgery at the end of the quarter.

At Prince of Wales Hospital, 71 patients waited longer than recommended. (ABC Radio Sydney: Declan Bowring)

Prince of Wales Hospital recorded 71 patients waiting longer than recommended and St George Hospital had 49.

Mr Park said the system was under pressure from 1,300 beds being taken up every day from people who were medically fine but waiting on NDIS or aged care spaces.

"That's the equivalent of two Sydney hospitals not to be used," he said.

World.title: How Ned overcame a decade of pain to return to running
World.content:
The doubts that occasionally flit across Ned Buckell's mind are likely to be familiar to runners whatever standard they're at.

Buckell's story is different to most, though.

A life-threatening infection as a teenager.

A year-and-a-half on crutches.

Another serious infection just when it felt like things were on track, resulting in a hip replacement before he was 21.

And a race number from the 2016 Melbourne Marathon Festival pinned to his wall, reminding him that there is still a destination to reach despite the darkness.

"There's definitely been times when you think to yourself, what am I doing this for?" Buckell tells ABC Sport.

"Why am I still trying to get back running at a reasonably high level?

"I think the biggest thing is because I knew I would do it.

"Those thoughts always creep into my mind like, 'Why am I still going? You're not going to get the most out of it,' but I can get the most out of what I can, and I've always told myself I can.

"That's probably why I haven't given up.

"Even though there've been countless times when you want to, when you keep getting struck down, there are signs, and the universe is telling you to stop.

"You have to just sort of not ignore them, but just push them aside and prove that it's not."

'If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me'

Running was Ned Buckell's life. After his injury and illness, it still is. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell was always going to be a runner.

His dad, John, was a runner and both Ned and his twin brother, Matt, would tag along to cross-country races around Bendigo and run from the age of five.

Theirs was an early introduction to the lung-busting freedom that a pair of trainers and the open trails of the countryside can afford.

"Me, my twin brother and my two older brothers were all always very competitive," Buckell says.

"That turned us into sporty individuals that always want to be better than each other.

"I've always been a runner, but it wasn't until maybe 14 or maybe 13 where I quit footy and was trying to focus on it a bit more.

"I knew me and my brother had some sort of talent, that we could take it to the next level.

"My twin brother has done that, but I haven't. I've just been struck down with this, really."

Sometimes you have to really love running to get up in the freezing cold of winter. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell's issues all stem back to an infection he got when he was 14 years old, just after he turned to running seriously.

"The night it all happened, I was playing basketball with my mates at his house," Buckell recalls.

"It was a warm September night, the boys were in shorts and T-shirts, and I was in trackies and a hoodie, I was getting these fevers.

"We were all thinking that something's not right, so I rode home with Matt and then the fevers got really bad."

Buckell's parents were away, so it was up to his Nan and Pop to take him to the local GP, who initially diagnosed a twisting hernia, with Buckell struggling to stand due to the pain.

The GP sent Ned to a specialist, who instantly transferred him to the emergency department, where the scale of Buckell's issue became terrifyingly clear.

A staph infection had entered Ned's hip, driving up his temperature to dangerous levels.

"I ended up getting four hip washouts; three in Bendigo, which had no effect, basically, and then they sent me to the Royal Children's Hospital for another one," Buckell says.

The then-14-year-old spent the next three-and-a-half weeks in hospital, fortunate to be alive.

"I was on the cardiac ward because the infection had spread to my heart," Buckell explains.

"If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me.

"I never realised how severe it was, probably until now that I've finished my degree."

'Sometimes it's impossible to see that light'

Ned Buckell says the support of his family was essential. (Supplied: 2045)

Ned was discharged from hospital just in time to celebrate his 15th birthday.

It was a bittersweet moment.

The teenager spent the next 18 months on crutches, "torture" for a kid who described himself as "one of the most active that you'd meet".

"There were times that I, you know, I'm very lucky that I've had a supportive family," Ned says, understandably struggling to find the words to recall what had been a horrendous time.

"If I hadn't had that support around me, I definitely wouldn't be here today.

"There were times when you just wanted a way out.

"I knew that I couldn't do that, but watching all my brothers start work, play their sports … I was never jealous, but I was so sad all the time about missing out.

"It was extremely tough. You wouldn't wish that upon anyone, really."

Buckell says he gets goosebumps talking about this period of his life, underlining what a tough topic it is to address even 10 years on.

But despite all the darkness, Ned says that he always kept an optimistic mindset, something which he knows helped him a lot.

"It has been pretty important just to try to find the good in things," Buckell says.

"It's a hard topic for me to talk about, but it's something that I've acknowledged, and I'm just grateful to be where I'm at right now, to be honest.

"I know everyone battles their own shit, and I think the way I've looked at it all is there's always a light at the end of the tunnel.

"And sometimes it's impossible to see that light. And sometimes it's not there.

"But you just have to keep going forward and pushing through.

"It's hard, but I think talking about it does help me try to word things a little bit better."

Running is 'just something I do'

Ned Buckell has had to deal with serious illness and a traumatic injury, but has found peace in running. (Supplied: 2045)

The positivity was tested in 2022 when, having fought his way back to a high level, running 14:42 at the Bendigo 5km Frenzy to break a local under-20 record, his hip started playing up again.

He was diagnosed with avascular necrosis, the death of bone tissue due to a lack of blood flow.

Surgery couldn't fix it, leading to a hip replacement and yet more time watching the rest of the world run away from him.

"I think it comes from within," Buckell says of his perseverance.

"It's something inside of me that hasn't allowed me to give up at all, me knowing that I'm capable of more."

Buckell can sometimes forget that he has a new hip as he runs, finding the same freedom that he had as a child chasing his two older brothers and his twin.

He describes the hip replacement as being "life-changing".

The reminders that things are different come afterwards, when the muscles that had to be so violently contorted to insert the new joint begin to ache.

But that's not enough to stop him.

"I feel like I don't reflect enough on it afterwards," Buckell says of his relationship with running now.

"I did a race the other week, and I won it, and people like my Nan and Pop cried to me on the phone and told me how proud they are, and I forget to realise everything that I've been through.

"I really do have to reflect deeply on how much I've actually endured and overcome. But for me, it's just like something that you do without thinking about it."

Perhaps running is just a part of him?

"It is, yeah," Buckell says.

"And I don't need to over complicate it more than that. It's just something I do, really.

"But I do have to look back and think of how lucky I actually am, to be more offline and running at the level I am because I was told that it was going to be impossible."

Ned Buckell's race number from a decade before has helped spur him on. (Supplied: 2045)

In October, he will prove that impossible is just a word, lining up at the Melbourne Marathon once more, this time in the 5km race.

The race number that he wore the last time he ran the Melbourne streets as a teenager, just before the universe hit pause on his ambitions, is still stuck to the wall of his childhood bedroom.

"I probably won't actually ever realise how big it has impacted me," Buckell says.

"It was kept there as a reminder that I've got work to do to get back to where I want to be.

"And for a while it sort of just stayed there, and it didn't leave. And I was like, yeah, this is my constant reminder that things don't go your way, but I can get back to what I want to do.

"I feel like I've been working so hard for so long, and you just keep getting shit thrown at you, but honestly, I'm confident enough to say that this is sort of the end of it and I can actually test myself now."

World.title: Suspect images released as police offer $1million reward over cold case murders
World.content:
Police have offered a $1 million reward for information leading to the conviction of suspects in two cold case murders.

Forensic artist impressions of two people believed to be linked to the suspected murders of two men from the Queensland–New South Wales border region 24 years ago were released by Queensland Police on Wednesday.

In 2002, 45-year-old Iain Stewart Hogg from Tweed Heads and 67-year-old Frederick Hugh Rosson, also known as "Slim Johnson", went missing.

Detective Sergeant Scott Chapman said the public should take a moment to look at the images of the suspects.

"Someone may recognise or know these men or remember something that seemed insignificant at the time but now could be important," he said.

"People who may once have been afraid to speak may no longer feel that way. It is never too late to come forward."

Last reported sightings

Mr Hogg was reported missing on March 12, 2002 after he did not turn up for work at a Burleigh bottle shop.

He was seen driving his 1992 red Toyota Celica coupe to his apartment at Teemangum Street in Currumbin Beach in the late afternoon of March 10, before speaking to his elderly mother on the phone at about 6pm.

The car, with Queensland registration plate 861 GBW, was last spotted between 1am and 3am, NSW time, in a car park near the Volunteer Marine Rescue Boat pontoon on the northern bank of Tweed River in Coral Street.

Witnesses reported seeing a number of people standing around the car, before a flash and loud bang, believed to be caused by the firing of a gun.

Police said Mr Hogg's body may have been thrown into the river, immediately adjacent to the Tweed River mouth's northern rock wall.

Days later, on March 14, Mr Rosson was shot and killed at his Pademelon Pass residence at Mount Nathan, north of the border.

Police said Mr Rosson was phoned by a man in the Coolangatta–Tweed Heads area about a 9mm CZ handgun he had listed for sale in the local Trading Post classifieds.

It is believed Mr Rosson was in the process of selling the handgun when he was shot.

Both the gun and ammunition were stolen, with witnesses reporting seeing two men in a red Celica visiting Mr Rosson at the time.

The car was found abandoned on 15th Avenue, Palm Beach, on March 20.

Police do not believe either Mr Hogg or Mr Rosson were known to each other, or involved in any criminal activity.

Indemnity from prosecution may also be offered to any accomplice who did not directly commit the alleged crimes but provides information to police.

World.title: Australians sleep at Heathrow after UK air traffic control failure
World.content:
Australian travellers have been left stranded at one of the world's busiest airports after an air traffic control failure led to flight cancellations across the United Kingdom.

Up to 1,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday, according to tracking website FlightRadar24, and delays are expected to continue throughout today as airlines work through a significant backlog.

A fault in the flight data processing system operated by the UK's air traffic control provider, National Air Traffic Services (NATS), caused the disruption.

Many passengers are in for an uncomfortable wait. (Supplied: Monique Whiting)

Perth woman Monique Whiting and her partner Frank are sleeping on the floor at London's Heathrow Airport after their flight to Iceland was cancelled.

The couple boarded their Icelandair flight shortly before 1pm local time and remained on the aircraft for more than four hours before being told to disembark.

The Whitings are sleeping on the airport's floor after their flight to Iceland was cancelled. (Supplied: Monique Whiting)

"We knew pretty early on that there was a bit of a delay, and I could see through the window that there was a bunch of planes lining up to go," Ms Whiting said.

She said the airline provided snacks and water, but later that afternoon passengers were told the flight would not be leaving.

Ms Whiting said Icelandair told passengers to arrange their own accommodation and offered to reimburse them up to a certain amount, but nearby hotels were full.

"A bunch of other things had already been cancelled, and a lot of the close-by accommodation was obviously already booked out," she said.

"You can imagine how busy it is and there's lots and lots of people still at the airport.

" We're all staying here overnight and not getting any sleep. "

Debbie Payne was four days into a European holiday when she arrived at Heathrow for an 8:50pm flight home to Australia via Singapore.

After travelling to the airport by car, train and the London Underground, she discovered flights had been cancelled.

Debbie Payne got caught up in the delays after holidaying in the UK. (Supplied: Debbie Payne)

"People weren't sure what to do," she said.

"You just had to wait around and hope."

Ms Payne said passengers were initially prevented from passing through security, while some travellers were stranded aboard aircraft on the tarmac.

"There were people on planes who couldn't get off because there were no ramps," she said.

"It was hard to know what was going on.

"I felt sorry for people who didn't speak English and those with young babies."

Backlog to cause further delays

A fault in the flight data processing system operated by NATS caused the disruption.

The system processes flight plans and other operational information controllers use to manage aircraft travelling through UK airspace.

NATS said it had fixed the problem, but warned it was taking longer than expected for normal operations to resume.

Chief executive Martin Rolfe apologised to affected travellers and told the BBC there would be a full investigation.

Stranded passengers gather after some departing flights were cancelled at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 5. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported that up to 1,000 flights had been cancelled.

The worst-affected airports included Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham, while airports in Scotland and Ireland also reported disruption.

EasyJet cancelled about 200 flights, and British Airways cancelled or diverted more than 100.

Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers experienced delays of up to eight hours.

World.title: Shops selling illegal tobacco in Victoria face closure from today
World.content:
Stores that sell illegal tobacco products can be closed by inspectors from today under new laws introduced by the Victorian government.

Shops that get hit with closure notices will be publicly listed on Tobacco Licensing Victoria's website.

The government is promising dozens of Tobacco Licensing Victoria inspectors will be out in force conducting spot checks of stores across the state.

Victoria Police officers also have the power to issue closure notices from today if officers uncover illegal tobacco products being sold.

Premier Ben Carroll said stores found in breach of the laws will be closed. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The closure notices initially cover a period of up to 90 days, but long-term closures can also be pursued through the Magistrates' Court.

"If you are selling illegal tobacco, expect an inspector any day at any moment and expect a fluoro sign on the front of your door saying this shop has been closed," Premier Ben Carroll told ABC News Breakfast.

" There are too many and we are shutting them down and smoking them out and that starts today. "

Business owners who ignore closure orders face fines of up to $2.5 million and 20 years' jail.

Public health organisations welcomed the new measures, arguing the changes helped bring Victoria in closer alignment with other Australian jurisdictions.

Research commissioned by the Cancer Council Victoria recently found 72 per cent of adults in the state agreed shops should be shut "straight away" if caught selling illegal tobacco.

Cancer Council Victoria chief executive Todd Harper said the state government should take a "zero-tolerance approach to the illicit trade".

"There is still more work to do," he said.

Quit director Rachael Anderson said Victorian laws needed to go further "to include action on vapes and nicotine pouches".

"Victorian enforcement officers are unable to shut down retailers found selling vapes or pouches, even though it’s illegal to do so," she said.

Quit director Rachael Andersen. (Supplied)

Debate over how to tackle illegal tobacco

The new laws come into effect as debate continues at a federal level over the tobacco excise, with both the Coalition and One Nation vowing to slash the tax on cigarettes if elected.

The Coalition is promising to cut the excise by 80 per cent, which it claims will kill the black market for illegal tobacco.

One Nation wants to slash the tax on cigarettes by 75 per cent and freeze indexation for three years.

The Victorian government would not support any move to cut the excise on tobacco products. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Both parties argue high taxation has created the market for illegal tobacco products.

Mr Carroll said the Victorian government would not support moves to cut the tobacco excise.

"I think we need to put more money into public health. We shouldn't be on the side of [tobacco company] Phillip Morris, we need to be on the side of public health," he said.

"We've seen this exercise previously in Canada where they cut excise and it just ensured that the black market came back."

Experts are divided on how best to tackle the black market.

Some argue lowering the excise would reduce demand for black market tobacco products, while others say criminals will simply lower the price of illegal products in response.

World.title: Voters want greater say over national policy as dismay with major parties grows
World.content:
Australians still believe in the ideals of their democracy and government, but their declining faith in politicians and the political system is putting that trust at "profound risk".

A clear majority of voters think ordinary citizens should have a greater say in setting the country's policy priorities, with many feeling politicians prioritise their own self-interest and the interests of lobby groups and corporations over the community's desires.

Why Labor lost safe seat to One Nation WA Labor will be conducting a post-mortem of its crushing defeat in the Secret Harbour by-election to see where it went wrong.

Those are some of the key findings from the latest annual Purpose of Government Pulse, published by the centre-left Centre for Policy Development (CPD) think tank this month.

"It is clear that voters are losing patience with politics as it has always been done," the report warned.

"People are voicing their frustration with the traditional two-party system by branching out to independents and minor parties like One Nation.

"People increasingly feel like the current political system doesn't listen to their concerns and that major decisions are made without their input or consultation.

"[But] despite this frustration, Australians have not given up on their vision for what government and democracy can, and should, deliver," it found.

The data is drawn from 10 survey waves conducted by Essential Research between October 2015 and February 2026.

Huge support for universal health care

The report was published on Friday, but the media didn't cover it widely.

Perhaps its findings weren't considered newsworthy enough, since you can only say the same thing so many times before it loses its novelty, and "everyone knows" Australians are increasingly frustrated with their political system.

A 'serious moment in Europe' The weekend win by Alternative for Germany in the state of Saxony-Anhalt has sent shivers across the continent, and could embolden the right across Europe.

But the report had important insights.

First, it found that, despite decades of political messaging about the need for smaller government and less intervention, the overwhelming consensus is that government should play a direct role in improving people's long-term wellbeing.

It found the vast majority of Australians say health, education, and child care must be free or affordable for all, with targeted extra support provided to those who need it most, and that government must maintain the capability to deliver social services directly.

Second, it showed two-thirds of Australians had consistently said for the past decade that voters should have a greater say in setting the government's core policy priorities.

Third, it found that while Australians had clear expectations of what they wanted government and democracy to deliver, they were increasingly sceptical that politicians would deliver it.

Little say over strategic future

Now, if you look for evidence of voters' growing frustration with Australia's political system, you won't be short of examples.

The CPD report didn't mention it specifically, but an obvious example of voters' concerns about their lack of control over Australia's future is manifest in the current public inquiry into the AUKUS deal.

That inquiry is an extremely unusual phenomenon.

Loading...

If you haven't heard about it, the public hearings, which began in June, have no backing from the federal government and are not funded by taxpayer money. The Australian Peace and Security Forum has coordinated them, with former Labor minister Peter Garrett as lead commissioner.

Former public officials, retired military and naval officers, strategists and academics, and lawyers and union leaders have been dedicating their time to the inquiries to try to uncover basic information about the AUKUS "security partnership" that will lock Australia into a particular security arrangement with the United States for decades.

They want to know why ordinary Australians have been largely excluded from one of the biggest defence decisions in Australia's history.

"The AUKUS deal was conceived in secret and with deception — and continues to be shrouded in secrecy despite the incredibly high stakes and massive cost," the inquiry's website says.

It has been asking questions like: Will AUKUS jeopardise our sovereignty? Why are we joining the US to go to war against China potentially, our major trading partner? Will AUKUS make us safer or turn us into a nuclear target?

In a society more responsive to citizens' concerns, one would expect a publicly funded inquiry (rather than a crowd-funded one) to ask such heavy questions about Australia's strategic future.

Loading...

Concerns about AI, data centres, and surveillance

There are examples of voter unease in other areas.

For instance, anxiety is growing across the political spectrum about the pace at which data centres are being built and how little say local communities have over their construction.

Backlash over data centres brewing While the government is trying to assure people there is nothing to fear from AI, many think technology is moving too quickly for authorities to keep up.

"Increasingly, I'm hearing from people from all walks of life how concerned they are with the pace of AI growth," former Labor industry minister Ed Husic told the ABC's Patricia Karvelas in June.

"Again, if we think new One Nation voters are attracted to the idea of giving the system a kick, look how we're managing [the] massive wave of data centre construction.

"Most local communities have absolutely no say about the construction of these centres in their area, leaving average residents fuming.

"When they resist, they're told these data centres are important for the economy. So if they're so important, why aren't they being built in Bellevue Hill instead of Blacktown?" he said.

Concerns about government contracts

And what about the concerns people have about controversial companies winning major government contracts?

In April, journalist Cam Wilson, writing for Crikey (he now works for the ABC) reported that the federal government had spent $60 million on contracts with the Trump-aligned surveillance and intelligence data company Palantir Technologies, with little public scrutiny, and the Future Fund held $165 million worth of the company's shares.

As Europe rearms, where is Australia's Future Fund investing? As defence spending ramps up across Europe, Australia's Future Fund is investing in weapons manufacturers, Tesla and Palantir Technologies.

"The company has been mired in controversy for alleged human rights violations, its close association with the Trump administration, and the outspoken pro-American political rhetoric of its co-founder, Alex Karp," Wilson wrote.

It would be interesting to see how Australians would vote, given the opportunity, on whether Australian governments should sign contracts with companies like that, or whether the Future Fund should invest in them.

But Australian voters rarely get a say over that kind of thing.

Last week, Nine newspapers broke the story that Coles Supermarkets will cut ties with Palantir after its three-year contract ends in 2027. The move follows a pressure campaign from the activist group GetUp! and growing public concerns about the company.

We need more than minor policy tweaks

At any rate, when it comes to formal politics, the CPD report says voters' scepticism about Australia's political system is clearly being reflected in the declining primary vote share of our two major parties and the rising popularity of minor parties and independents.

It also said the "core challenge" for governments and politicians was to address the widespread belief that Australia's political system was failing to deliver on the vision voters had for the future.

Confidence in democracy lower outside major cities, study finds Experts warn Australia's democratic institutions need more protection as confidence falls.

When the report was released, CPA chief executive Andrew Hudson said voters wanted to be heard.

"They want to know that their concerns are being listened to and that their long-term interests are being prioritised," he said.

"Unfortunately, the majority of Australians currently don't feel that is the case."

And the report said fixing that "disconnect" would require far more than minor policy tweaks.

"The historic fall in the primary vote share for the major parties is a clear, direct message from voters that they are losing patience with government as it has always been done," it said.

"They want a system that prioritises the needs and concerns of communities in decision-making, and a distinct shift away from a system they see as increasingly captured by powerful, vested interests."

World.title: LIV Golf players used to 'turbulence' as league files for bankruptcy
World.content:
LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy in New Jersey, saying it intends to restructure its business with a $US49.6 million ($68.7 million) bankruptcy loan provided by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) of Saudi Arabia.

The company has between $US500 million and $US1 billion in liabilities and between $US100 million and $US500 ‌million in assets, according to its Chapter 11 petition.

LIV Golf said the bankruptcy will allow it to move forward with the support of a new backer, BC Partners Advisors ‌LP, and transition to a player-first ownership model.

BC Partners and other ⁠potential minority investors are expected to provide exit financing and ‌sponsor the company's debt restructuring, LIV Golf said.

LIV has been ‌preparing for its next iteration ever since the PIF said in April that further investment in the rebel circuit no longer aligned with its strategy and that it would cut funding at the close of the 2026 season.

PIF owns 100 per cent of LIV Golf's equity, according to its bankruptcy petition.

McIlroy fires shot at returning LIV Golf stars Masters champion Rory McIlroy says LIV Golf players who want to return to the PGA Tour face a tough road ahead.

The PIF has invested more than $US5 billion in LIV Golf since its ⁠launch in 2022 and the breakaway circuit ‌used massive signing bonuses to ‌poach big-name players from the PGA Tour like Australian Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau, Jon Rahm and Dustin ‌Johnson.

Rahm, DeChambeau and Johnson are the company's top three unsecured creditors, according to the petition. Each is owed more than $US5 million.

Speaking in the build-up to the Irish Open, before news of the Chapter 11 petition broke, Rahm was asked if he knew what the future held.

"Yes and no, it hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis a few weeks ago," the two-time major winner said.

"And there's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen, and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell.

"To be fair for us, people that joined LIV, I'm pretty good at dealing with turbulence.''

LIV ‌Golf said bankruptcy is ⁠meant to keep the league in business while transitioning to an innovative player-first ownership model. The company hopes to exit from bankruptcy by early 2027.

"We believe deeply in LIV Golf's future, the opportunity in front of ⁠us, and the people who will help us realise it," LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said in ‌a statement.

The ‌professional men's golf league laid off most of its workforce in August, while it worked to secure new funding.

World.title: New map could reshape the way you see the world
World.content:
For centuries, human understanding of the size, shape and bearing of nations has been laid out by one map based on a single projection of the way the world looks.

The Mercator projection was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

UN adopts a new world map The United Nations has voted to adopt a map that makes Africa and Australia bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.

It has been the most commonly accepted visualisation of the world since at least the 18th century.

But the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) voted this month to change that, approving a new "equal area" map aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses.

It's called the "Equal Earth projection", and some experts say it could reshape how people see the world.

But first, what did the UN vote on?

A proposal introduced on behalf of 54 African countries by the continent's western nation of Togo pledged to correct an "imbalance inherited from the past", a UN statement said.

Togolese Foreign Affairs Minister Robert Dussey argued distorted maps could affect education about and global perception of continents, including Africa.

Robert Dussey wants the UN General Assembly to adopt a more equitable, accurate depiction of the world. (Reuters: Alain Jocard)

"How do we represent the world? How do we teach it? How do generations learn to see our planet?" he said before the vote on Friday.

"Correcting the map means recognising that every region of the world deserves to be represented accurately and with dignity.

"Our approach is not directed against any nation, any civilisation or any cartographic tradition.

"A fair map does not change the geography of the world; it changes how we see the world."

Of the 171 nations represented during the UNGA vote, 164, including Australia, voted in favour and six abstained.

A single nation, the United States, opposed it. Its representative, Yaryna Ferencevych, described the plan as a "barnacle" and a "reason this institution is losing its credibility".

Among the abstentions, Ukraine said it supported the idea but would not vote in favour because the Equal Earth map shows Crimea in grey as contested territory amid the ongoing war with Russia.

What is the new world map?

The Equal Earth projection "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," according to the proposed UNGA resolution.

Launched by cartographers in 2018, it makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania, including Australia, appear much larger.

Loading

It also reduces the size and scale of North America and parts of Europe, while placing Africa slightly more centrally.

The projection does not redraw national borders or coastlines, but shows continents in their true proportions, whereas the Mercator projection skews the scale of landmasses the closer they are to the North and South Pole.

The Equal Earth projection (in blue) shows the world to scale in its true proportions, while the red Mercator projection skews landmasses larger the closer they are to the poles. (Supplied: Mike Bostock/Observable)

Geographer Greg Lauer, from the OSGeo Oceania geospatial organisation, believes the Equal Earth change is mostly symbolic and the Mercator projection "is not wrong".

"It's right, particularly for navigation, but it's wrong for comparison … I'd say it was misused, not mistaken," he said.

Why is there no 'perfect' world map?

Recognisable world maps rely on the accurate projection of four fundamental principles — shape or angles, area, distance and direction — according to geospatial technologist Alex Leith.

He said the challenge for cartographers has always been converting the three-dimensional globe into a two-dimensional map without skewing the appearances of the world's landmasses.

"You have a choice about what you preserve, and you can't preserve all of it," he told the ABC.

"Mercator maps preserved direction, so that's about sailing from somewhere to somewhere else.

"This [new map] preserves area exactly, and approximately the shape."

The Mercator projection and other traditional world maps prioritised the shape of landmasses for ease of navigation, but skewed their total area and measure of distance. (Reuters: Jose Manuel Ribeiro)

Mr Lauer also said projection models sacrificed one or more of the key principles, based on what a map was trying to show.

"The Mercator is more distorted to the north and to the south, whereas Equal Earth is more distorted to the east and the west," he said.

"Projection is the maths that decides what gets sacrificed."

Will Equal Earth change how we see the world?

Mr Lauer said he did not expect the UN vote to spark an immediate social shift or for mandates to be rapidly implemented across the world to adopt the map projection.

He said most people's global perception stemmed from an ingrained mental image of the Mercator-aligned world map, which they had seen for most of their lives.

"Most people form their mental images of the world from a single map, and when you see it thousands of times from childhood, you never question it," he said.

Loading...

He also acknowledged that someone's understanding of the significance of certain parts of the world was shaped by the maps they used, and that a new map could alter future generations' outlooks.

"Size reads as importance," he said.

"If Africa looks the size of Greenland, it's easy to say, 'Africa doesn't matter.'

"I would imagine the African Union suggesting it's a representation issue with rural, economic and diplomatic consequences. They want Africa to be seen equally with the rest of the world."

Mr Lauer said that significance also extended to the continent shown at the centre of world maps, meaning less emphasis could be placed on the US.

For much of his second term, US President Donald Trump has sought to alter world maps to reflect growing American power.

He has repeatedly spoken of plans to make Canada the "51st state" of the US and seize Greenland as an American territory.

Mr Trump also signed executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and changing Lake Ontario to Lake America.

An image shared online by Donald Trump that shows Canada, Mexico and Greenland as US territories emblazoned with the country's flag. (Supplied: Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump)

But the new map projection suggests a shift in the perception of global power away from central Europe and the Americas, according to Mr Leith.

"It's just a reasonable, rational decision that provides a better representation of the world," he said.

"This is about equity and representing data in a more equitable way."

Will Australian school maps change?

While Togo says it will become the first country worldwide to update geography textbooks with the new map, the change is not legally binding, and the Mercator projection should still be used for navigation.

Australia's national education curriculum does not specify which maps schools should use to teach students.

The ABC understands some Australian schools may choose to incorporate the Equal Earth projection into their teaching, but no national mandate requires them to use any specific world map.

"While the Australian government plays a national leadership role in school education, it is state and territory governments and non-government education authorities who are responsible for the day-to-day delivery of education programs," a spokesperson from the federal department of education told the ABC.

"This includes decisions about how best to implement the Australian Curriculum, and in this case which maps to use and for what purpose.

"The Australian Curriculum supports students to read, interpret and create maps, developing their spatial reasoning and geographical skills to better understand Australia and the wider world."

The ABC has contacted the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority for further comment.

World.title: Elon Musk offered his ex $40m to not take part in a new doco about him. She did it anyway
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema Elon Musk offered his ex $40m to not take part in a new doco about him. She did it anyway Stephanie Bunbury September 9, 2026 — 10:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Venice: A four-hour documentary tracing the life and work of Elon Musk – maker of electric cars, rockets, Starlink satellites, right-wing propaganda and “a legion of children” from his own loins – has proved the pivotal talking point of the Venice Film Festival. Alex Gibney, the prolific director of documentaries about subjects including Enron, Edward Snowden and Scientology, tells the story of his rise to dizzying power – and phenomenal riches – in Musk, which confronts the question of how and why anyone has been allowed so much influence. Gibney usually interviews his subjects, but Musk refused to participate. Filmmaker Alex Gibney (middle) with tech journalist Zoë Schiffer (left) and Musk’s former girlfriend Ashley St Clair, at the Venice Film Festival this week. AP Photo/Scott A Garfitt It wasn’t easy to find other willing interviewees. “There was a fear of talking. Among his critics, his business colleagues and his friends, very few agreed to speak,” Gibney said at a festival press conference. One exception was the film’s trump card, a former MAGA influencer and Musk’s ex-girlfriend Ashley St Clair, who gave birth to one of Musk’s 14 children in 2024.



St Clair was close to Musk during the heady few months when he was head of President Donald Trump’s newly minted Department of Government Efficiency, striking out entire project budgets and sacking thousands of government employees. Loading “Elon is a nuke,” St Clair told the cameras. St Clair, who was in Venice with the film, alleged he had offered her $US40 million not to participate in the documentary. “When you’re offered something like that it really causes a debate in your head about what your speech means,” she says. “How valuable that is – and why do they want to offer me that much money not to speak?” She has her own answers. “It has to do with his sense of unreality, Elon’s relationships are complicated in general but, especially, he has a complicated relationship with the truth.” Gibney put his own spin on this by putting Musk’s extreme pronouncements into the mouth of a graphic avatar in a space suit. He says he was picking up on Musk’s obsession with video games.



“But also, so much of what Elon Musk says has an air of unreality to it.” He soon realised that what looked like a story about new technology and its overlords was “the story of old wine in a new bottle, the story of the confidence man. His wealth and power come from inflated stock.” Elon Musk was appointed head of the Department of Government Efficiency and took to the task with gusto. AP It was Enron all over again. He maintains a measured tone, however, as he covers the tech lord’s troubled South African childhood, his command over the satellites crucial to many countries’ military operations, his acquisition and manipulation of Twitter, now called X, his alliance – and fall-out – with President Trump and his $158 billion Tesla remuneration package. We see his beginnings, devising and then selling an online business directory, then taking and selling a slice of Peter Thiel’s Paypal, which provided him with working capital. Gibney spends a good deal of time debunking Musk’s promise of an imminent life on Mars. The research is meticulous, even if nothing is new. “I think it’s bearing witness and reaching out to witnesses,” says Gibney. “And also trying to understand. Particularly in this bewildering world of inputs from social media and 24-hour news access. There are so many trees that I think it’s worth stitching together a narrative that shows the forest. The film attempts to reframe the story.”



There were mutterings before the press screenings about the prospect of having to watch a four-hour documentary half-way through an exhausting festival, but the film proved a literal eye-opener that drew an energetic critical response. Editor's pick Film Festivals Hidden cameras, no script: Oasis documentary goes inside the Gallagher brothers’ split “A chillingly forensic hatchet job,” said the Telegraph; “a poleaxing portrait of the tech titan as a con man,” read the Hollywood Reporter’s headline; “an epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man … excellent”, according to the Guardian. It is Musk’s involvement in political influence, especially on the eve of the mid-term elections in the United States, that feels least transparent and thus the most troubling aspect of his influence. “We know during DOGE, the boys (Musk’s team of very young men who carried out mass sackings from government departments) had super administrative status at all agencies,” says Gibney. “That meant they had access to an extraordinary amount of data on American citizens - and moving that data would be as easy, as I understand it, as copying a file into a folder.



“Would that folder be at Space X and might he be using that information for an AI (tool) to influence the election? Yes. I don’t know that it will happen but it might happen. It was a warning.” So, asks one journalist at the press conference, one short answer: is Elon Musk dangerous to democracy? “Extremely,” says Gibney. “There’s your short answer. He’s very dangerous.” Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Almost half of Victoria’s roads in poor condition, as decline outpaces repairs
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Almost half of the state’s government-managed roads are in poor or very poor condition, with decline outpacing repairs, according to a new report from the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO).

Tracking the deterioration of Victoria’s “state roads” – major arterials owned and operated by the Department of Transport and Planning which span 23,000 kilometres – the report released on Wednesday found current government funding to maintain or improve state roads was insufficient.

A report by the Victorian auditor-general has found state roads are deteriorating faster than repairs are made. Joe Armao

“This has meant it [funding] focuses more on reactive and safety-critical repairs rather than preventative works,” the report found.

The vast majority of state roads are in regional Victoria, and carry most of the state’s traffic and freight vehicles. About 48 per cent of state roads were considered in poor or very poor condition in 2024 – jumping by almost a quarter from 39 per cent in 2021.

World.title: ‘Wants to be stuck with me’: Ellidy Pullin announces engagement
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSex & relationships ‘Wants to be stuck with me’: Ellidy Pullin announces engagement Abby Seaman September 9, 2026 — 10:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ellidy Pullin has shared the news of her engagement to Brock Wadsworth. Pullin, 38, confirmed the development via an Instagram post captioned, “HE WANTS TO BE STUCK WITH ME FOREVER” while holidaying in Europe with Wadsworth. The internet personality and podcast co-host of Darling, Shine! went public with the relationship in late 2025. Just hours after announcing the news, the couple’s post was flooded with well-wishes for the happy couple.



Related Article Sunday Life 36 hours after losing her partner, Ellidy Pullin made a life-changing decision The engagement comes six years after the sudden death of Pullin’s partner, Olympic snowboarder Alex “Chumpy” Pullin. Pullin met Wadsworth through mutual friends and knew each other for years before it is believed they began dating, about February last year. In November, they made the relationship Instagram-official while on holiday in Bali. Pullin later confirmed the details of their courtship in a December podcast episode, where she also spoke about navigating feelings of grief while falling in love.



“Of course, I love Chumpy, I still love him so much. I’ll never not love him,” she confessed. “Grief is absolutely f---ed.” Pullin admitted that she felt guilty about how happy she felt: “I was making things up in my head, now I’m just like all of those things were in my head ... I was just scared of my feelings.” Just days after her partner’s sudden death, Ellidy Pullin made the decision to retrieve his sperm. Hannah Sugarman In 2021, 15-months after Alex’s death, Pullin gave birth to their daughter, Minnie, who was conceived via IVF after she chose to undergo a post-mortem sperm retrieval. “The idea of having a baby on my own, a constant reminder of what I’d lost, was hard enough without having to deal with other people’s judgment,” Pullin wrote in her 2022 memoir, Heartstrong.



“Until someone has been in my shoes, I don’t think they’d ever be able to understand what I went through.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

Dwyer then took Greenwood to texts he sent to Sharangan Maheswaran detailing the efforts of the right faction, and warning that Charles Perrottet was at risk of losing his influence in the faction if Beckington didn’t receive money promised by Jean Nassif.

World.title: Creamy, silky and, err, fibrous: The saucy social media trend making tinned beans sexy
World.content:
Tips & adviceBeans Creamy, silky and, err, fibrous: The saucy social media trend making tinned beans sexy Beans are budget-friendly and high in fibre but can be a bit of a hard sell. However, have you ever tried drowning them in satay sauce? Now we’re cooking! Jane de Graaff September 9, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In case you missed it, it’s the year of “maxxing” everything. Protein-maxxing, looks-maxxing, Nanna-maxxing – we’re not just leaning in to the things we love any more, we’re maxxing out on them. And that includes fibre-maxxing – or the practice of consciously increasing fibre in the diet, with a focus on potential health benefits, including gut health and blood sugar management. Enter an unlikely poster-child for the fibre-maxxing trend: beans. Now, I personally love beans (tinned, dried, refried, souped), but I’d hesitate to call them sexy. And yet, the latest social media trend for dressing them up in creamy, silky and downright decadent-looking sauces – that still aim to support health goals – is making humble beans look, well, decidedly sexier than they did before. Welcome to the world of sexy bean recipes that are flooding social media and might just get you serving some up tonight. Katrina Meynink’s creamy marry-me chickpeas recipe has the big flavours of the original, minus the meat. Katrina Meynink The sexy-creamy-beany trend The trend itself is simple: sauces that you might usually see on pasta or noodles are being drizzled over or simmered with beans as a way of introducing more fibre-rich ingredients into the diet, without compromising on flavour. The beans are, essentially, a sauce delivery system.



Variations include cacio e pepe beans (pepper and cheese), green goddess or pesto, velvety french onion and creamy curry beans – and that’s just the tip of the beanstalk. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Championed by content creators such as Ohio-based @dietitiandebbie Deborah Murphy (with her social media recipe series “No Boring Beans”), one clear favourite has bubbled to the top: satay-style beans. This creamy, dreamy recipe is sliding into feeds everywhere, with iterations running from super spiced and topped with fresh herbs, to mild, mellow and sweet. Is it really better for us? It’s easy to see why this dish has caught on. It relies on flavours that we already know – such as peanutty, spiced and sweet satay-style sauce – and it’s made with just a handful of pantry-staple budget-friendly ingredients. It also promises to edge us closer to potential health goals, ticking off the golden quartet: quick, budget-friendly, healthier and tasty.



But, as always, we take health-related social media claims with a grain of (ahem) salt. “The fibre-maxxing trend and rising interest in gut health has a lot to do with the popularity of these recipes,” says food and nutrition scientist Dr Emma Beckett. “But I also think it comes back to cost. People are looking for ways to make things healthier without it costing the earth.” ‘These kinds of dishes – that you already like – will be better for you if you do them with beans. There’s not much of a downside to that.’ Dr Emma Beckett, food and nutrition scientist Beckett notes that younger generations are moving away from health foods that charge a premium and towards budget-friendly foods, with the bean trend appealing to that. “I’m all for it,” Beckett enthuses. A teacher of culinary nutrition, her students note that social media is a font of easy inspiration when cooking feels overwhelming. So, seeing a trend that capitalises on the “easy factor” while also introducing a healthier ingredient is a win.



“This trend is about adding the beans to something people already want to eat. It’s not saying to get rid of anything, and it’s not saying beans are the silver bullet. It’s saying these kinds of dishes – that you already like – will be better for you if you do them with beans. There’s not much of a downside to that,” she says. Related Article Seven inexpensive sources of fibre to add to your grocery list “I like to say ‘use the delicious to access the nutritious’,” she adds, with a laugh, “and I think this trend is exactly that. If you just say ‘eat more beans’, how boring! But if you say: ‘Did you know you can add some beans to this satay-style dish?’ – well that’s a really great way in. It’s meeting people where they are.” The short answer is, yes, this trend helps with health goals, as long as we’re mindful about what else we’re adding to the sauces. And while the beans are a win on the fibre front, Beckett recommends checking salt content or rinsing your tinned beans first, if necessary. Jessica Brook’s creamy braised beans with lamb meatballs. James Moffatt



Does it taste any good? If you like creamy sauces, yes, these recipes win. You can’t really go wrong with a creamy sauce served over tender beans. “When we’re talking about flavours like satay and chilli oil, it’s sort of a twist on the condiments we add to silken tofu as a snack,” says Lisa Liu, creator of Saucy Wench condiments, whose satay sauce and chilli oil have won gold at Melbourne Royal and Sydney Royal shows respectively. “Tinned beans have that same kind of effect. That kind of rich, beany flavour with a soft texture that goes very well with these two things. So it makes sense and definitely makes beans more approachable,” Liu says. The real trick is to find the beans you like because there are plenty of varieties with different flavours and textures to play around with. Right now, though, it’s butter beans and white cannellini beans that are lending their milder flavour to this trend.



No-cook creamy satay-style butter beans Jane de Graaff Jane de Graaff’s no-cook creamy satay-style butter beans You can swap out the butter beans in this recipe for any cooked or tinned beans of your choice, and while this is a no-cook recipe, you can also warm the sauce gently in a pan for a comforting twist, just don’t reduce the sauce too much. Perfect with a soft-boiled egg on the side and some hot buttered sourdough, but also an ideal bowl on its own. INGREDIENTS



1 x 400g tin of butter beans + 2 tbsp reserved bean brine

2 tbsp crunchy peanut butter

½ tbsp chilli crisp oil

½ tsp tamari

2 spring onions, white and green parts, finely sliced

pinch of brown sugar (optional)

2 tbsp coconut cream, divided

juice of 1 lime Toppings ½ tbsp toasted sesame seeds

sprigs of fresh coriander

½ a small red chilli, finely sliced (remove the seeds for a milder result)

1 x soft-boiled egg

Hot buttered sourdough, to serve METHOD Reserve 2 tbsp of the bean brine and then drain the beans and rinse them. Soft boil and peel your egg and set aside. Toast and butter your sourdough. In a bowl, mix together the peanut butter, chilli crisp oil, tamari, sliced spring onion, brown sugar (if using), ½ the coconut cream and ½ the lime juice to make a sauce. Thin with a little bean brine if necessary for a loose consistency. Add the drained and rinsed beans to the sauce and toss through to coat. Spoon the beans into a dish, drizzle with the remaining coconut cream and lime juice, and top with toasted sesame seeds, fresh coriander, and chopped fresh chilli. Serve with a side of hot buttered sourdough toast and a soft-boiled egg.

World.title: Two children die, six injured in school pick-up tragedy near Bacchus Marsh
World.content:
A 34-year-old mother had just picked up children from school when her 4WD ran off the road and rolled at Melbourne’s western fringe on Tuesday afternoon, leaving two children dead and six people injured. A car containing seven children was travelling west on Nerowie Road in Parwan before it “inexplicably” rolled onto a nature strip about 4.28pm on Tuesday, police said. Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating a fatal single-vehicle rollover in Parwan which occurred on Tuesday afternoon. Nine News A seven-year-old girl died at the scene. An 11-year-old boy died overnight in hospital, police said early on Wednesday. The scale of the crash required a huge response from emergency services. Two air ambulances and nine paramedic crews were dispatched to the area, transporting seven people to hospital.



Three boys were taken to the Royal Children’s Hospital, two of them in the air ambulances with upper- and lower-body injuries, with one of the two in a critical condition. The third boy was taken in an ambulance with upper-body injuries in a stable condition. The scene of the fatal crash near the intersection of Parwan-Exford Road and Exford Road. Eddie Jim A further three children – a female toddler with minor injuries, and a teenage boy and primary school-aged boy with upper-body injuries – were taken to Sunshine Hospital, all in a stable condition. On Wednesday morning, the children’s hospital said the patients being treated there were stable. The driver was taken by ambulance to the Royal Melbourne Hospital in a stable condition. That hospital has been contacted for comment.



Loading On Wednesday morning, shattered windscreen glass remained on the roadside. A single black sneaker, belonging to a child, lay nearby. Local farmer John Bibby, whose fence was cut by responders to try to reach the children, said the nearby road was in good condition compared with other parts in the area. “It’s just horrible – especially when kids are involved,” he said. The scene on Wednesday morning. Eddie Jim



Detective Sergeant Tony Gentile said police were still investigating the circumstances of the crash. “From my understanding, the scene was quite hectic, people everywhere. Witnesses who witnessed it, they stopped and rendered assistance,” he said. “Obviously, with seven children, they were distressed, and they were cared for by paramedics, members of the public and police.” “This is just a really sad set of circumstances. Really very sad.”



Police said it was not apparent that drugs or alcohol were involved and have urged anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam footage to contact police. Intensive paramedic crews and advanced life support crews were at the scene. Nine News In May 2023, 13 children were taken to hospital after a truck hit a school bus carrying 45 primary school students on the same road. Seven children were left with serious injuries, including a 10-year-old who lost her arm. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Where’s Karl?’ Podcast falls silent as advertising deal ends
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ‘Where’s Karl?’ Podcast falls silent as advertising deal ends Calum Jaspan Updated September 9, 2026 — 10:23am ,first published September 8, 2026 — 6:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Karl Stefanovic’s independent podcast has not uploaded new content in more than two weeks, raising questions about the program’s future as his main advertiser ended its contract with the former Today host. The Karl Stefanovic Show has not posted new podcast episodes or social media content across all social channels since August 24, leaving Stefanovic’s subscribers asking whether the former TV star will be returning at all. Karl Stefanovic’s independent podcast has not uploaded any new content in more than two weeks. YouTube The former TV host was sacked by Nine after he interviewed British far-right figure Tommy Robinson just over two months ago. After he was forced from his multimillion-dollar contract, Stefanovic said he was finally “free” and “truly independent”, allowing him to properly pursue his podcast. Country clothing brand Ringers Western confirmed its sponsorship deal with the independent show has ended, with no plans to renew the deal, when approached by this masthead over the show’s inactivity. A spokesperson from the brand said the deal was planned to end in September.



Stefanovic’s video content heavily promoted Ringers Western, with Stefanovic often appearing in videos in its clothing, including during an interview with One Nation leader Pauline Hanson in August. Related Article Opinion

On Background Billionaire brings former Gold Walkley winner back from the cold Calum Jaspan Media Writer The Karl Stefanovic Show has not posted any content since its last episode was published, featuring an interview with men’s surgeon Dr Buck Parker, discussing whether humans can de-age through “reprogramming ageing cells”, peptides and wellness treatments. In the week prior, Stefanovic uploaded five full episodes and often uploaded episodes several times per week to his YouTube channel, including almost daily posts on his Instagram and TikTok pages. Both Stefanovic and his business partner and producer Keshnee Kemp did not respond to requests for comment when asked to explain the absence on Tuesday afternoon. Kemp did also not respond to questions regarding the show’s ongoing funding after its partnership with Ringers Western came to an end.



Stefanovic posted a video on his personal Instagram page on August 29 showing him attending Griffith’s Taste of Italy Festival. Related Article Radio Stefanovic takes aim at TV’s ‘beige’ hosts after Nine departure Brand partnerships and sponsorships are key to Stefanovic’s funding model, which also relies on ad revenue from different social media platforms, largely YouTube. A company linked to Kemp’s digital marketing company August One owns 45 per cent of Stefanovic’s new venture, while Stefanovic owns 45 per cent himself. The final 10 per cent is owned by celebrity accountant Anthony Bell, as reported by the Financial Review in June. Some recent episodes published in August appeared without a brand partner, with Ringers Western the only partner listed on most videos on Stefanovic’s YouTube page. Some interviews were also sponsored by payroll platform Tanda. Stefanovic conducted the interview with Hanson in Mount Isa wearing Ringers Western clothing, while the One Nation leader appeared in a custom orange S Kidman hat, the clothing brand owned by party donor Gina Rinehart.



Pauline Hanson wearing what appears to be a custom-made hat made by Gina Rinehart’s Kidman Clothing company. A wellness supplement company Revive5 publicly backed Stefanovic in June after his sacking, but has not appeared on any recent episodes. Related Article Opinion

On Background Karl Stefanovic’s love affair with the British far right blooms Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Stefanovic launched the new podcast at the start of this year, agreeing to a deal with Nine which allowed him to launch his own show while continuing to present the Today program. It quickly became clear that the podcast, pitched as an unscripted and uncensored platform for him to uncover “bloody good stories”, was instead an attempt to capture the growing chunk of Australians moving toward far-right, populist politics alongside the rise of One Nation in the polls.



One Nation politicians including Hanson and Barnaby Joyce became regular fixtures, as did Family First senator Gerard Rennick, who is a regular guest alongside conspiracy theorists and foreign far-right figures such as British MP Rupert Lowe. Related Article Updated

Media & marketing Today show host Karl Stefanovic to leave Nine after Tommy Robinson podcast fallout Stefanovic’s followers have begun leaving comments on his various social media accounts, asking if the show will be returning at all. “Karl we miss you mate hope you’re ok!“; “wheres karl??“; “Where’s the podcast gone?!” commenters wrote on his social media pages. Stefanovic’s interview with Robinson, who is a fascist and convicted criminal, was the final straw for Nine, despite Stefanovic removing the interview shortly after it was uploaded.



“Here’s what I believe in: the public deserve to hear perspectives,” Stefanovic said in a statement published online shortly after he was dismissed by Nine. “On my show, I have spoken to people who have different perspectives; I know that winds some people up. Sometimes I agree with everything a guest says, sometimes I don’t. But importantly, you get to make up your own mind.” During the interview, Stefanovic took a deferential tone with Robinson, at one point telling him “god, I love ya”. World.title: ASX gains in early trade even as Wall Street drifts, oil hovers near $US100
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX gains in early trade even as Wall Street drifts, oil hovers near $US100 Staff writers Updated September 9, 2026 — 10:14am ,first published September 9, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket opened higher on Wednesday, shrugging off losses on Wall Street and another rise in oil prices to bounce back from a six-month low in the previous session. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 23.20 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8944 as of 10.06am AEST. The ASX slumped 1 per cent on Tuesday for its lowest close since late July. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.23¢. Wall Street has retreated after returning from a long weekend, with rising oil prices weighing on investors. Bloomberg On Wall Street overnight, US stocks fell in their return to trading from a three-day weekend after the latest fighting in the war with Iran pushed oil prices higher. The S&P 500 sank 0.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite dipped 0.3 per cent. US stocks felt pressure from rising oil prices after a barrel of Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $US99.46. It later settled at $US97.92, up 0.9 per cent, to continue its run from roughly $US72 in early July as increased fighting in the Middle East keeps the global flow of oil constricted.



Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump The Taxman v Trump: ATO opens new front in fight with Big Tech Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer More expensive oil has worsened worries about the high inflation weighing on people and companies across the country, which gives extra heft to a couple reports coming later this week. On Thursday, the US government will release its August report for inflation at the wholesale level, which economists expect will show an acceleration to 5.4 per cent from 4.7 per cent in July. The more closely watched report on inflation that US consumers are feeling will arrive on Friday. That update will show how much more people are paying for groceries, clothes and other costs of living than a year earlier, and economists expect it eased a bit to 3.3 per cent from July’s 3.4 per cent inflation rate. That, though, remains well above the 2 per cent target that the Federal Reserve has set as its goal. This week’s updates on inflation will be the last before the Fed meets next week to decide whether to cut, raise or hold interest rates steady. The traditional move for the Fed when inflation is high is to raise its main interest rate. That in turn would filter out into the rest of the bond market, make it more expensive for companies and people to borrow, slow the overall economy, undercut prices for investments and hopefully rein in inflation. But President Donald Trump has been lobbying for lower interest rates instead, which could give the economy — and inflation — an extra kick. The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, has meanwhile said he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed plans to do with interest rates in the short term.



That all has traders betting on a nearly 60 per cent probability the Fed will raise its federal funds rate at the conclusion of its next meeting on Sept. 16, according to data from CME Group. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.79 per cent from 4.78 per cent and is near its highest level since the autumn of 2023. Higher Treasury yields put more pressure on companies to grow their profits in order to lift their stock prices. On Wall Street, Boston Scientific fell 5.9 per cent after saying that a network outage earlier this summer caused by a cybersecurity incident means it’s unlikely to meet forecasts for sales and profit for the third quarter and for the full year of 2026. It expects to make back some of the revenue as it continues to ramp operations globally, fulfil customer orders and reduce remaining backlogs, but it doesn’t yet know the full impacts. Shares of Novartis that trade in the United States tumbled 13.9 per cent after the Swiss pharmaceutical company gave a discouraging update on a study of a therapy for people living with myotonic dystrophy type 1, a neuromuscular disease.



Qualcomm helped limit the market’s losses after rising 3.2 per cent. It announced a deal to collaborate with Amazon on large-scale AI data centres. The deal also gives Amazon the right to acquire up to 25 million of Qualcomm’s shares at $US161.26 per share. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Fighting the bully: Canada throws a punch back at Trump Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In stock markets abroad, Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 1.7 per cent under the weight of losses for major exporters, which were hurt by the continued rise for the Japanese yen against the US dollar. A stronger yen erodes the value of sales made in US dollars when Toyota Motor, Panasonic Holdings and other exporters translate them back into the Japanese currency. The Bank of Japan is also scheduled to meet next week on interest rates, and speculation is climbing that it could raise interest rates, which could further strengthen the yen. In China, indexes fell 0.4 per cent in Hong Kong and rose 0.2 per cent in Shanghai after the world’s second-largest economy said its exports jumped 25 per cent year-on-year in August, driven by strong demand for autos and high tech items.
